items.x: A personal study and revision notebook for Modern Indian History, built only from the material you provided: the Sarrthi IAS handout chapters (the "book") and the class slides with the teacher's board notes. Nothing is added from outside. Where the teacher's slide and the handout differ, the notebook says so in a note box instead of quietly choosing one. Each chapter follows the same pattern: sections in the order of the class, the teacher's ink in teacher boxes, traps in alert boxes, then a mind map, timeline, flow charts, tables, connections, recall sheet, quiz and flash cards. Teacher: Source for this course = only the Sarrthi IAS handout. After the batch is over, add the new NCERTs (from the Sarrthi IAS Foundation YouTube channel).

Teacher: Saffron box: what the teacher wrote or said on the board or slide. Red box: a trap, a Prelims alert or a common mistake. Blue box: a note, a clarification, or a difference between the handout and the slides. Green box: a takeaway to memorise. Mnemonic: Purple box: a memory hook (acronym, rhyme, story or peg) for a war, treaty, year, list or sequence. Each chapter also ends its notes with one "chapter in one breath" story. The Mnemonics page collects all of them.

Story so far: nothing yet. Before any dynasty, we need the words: power, State, sovereignty. Ask: what is a State, and who is it ruling? The teacher opens with vocabulary. Every later chapter uses these words (power, state, sovereignty, centralisation), so this section is worth reading slowly once. Source for this course = only the Sarrthi IAS handout (the "book"). After the batch is over, add the new NCERTs (go to the Sarrthi IAS Foundation YouTube channel for those). Feudal, non-modern and modern Feudal = old in time and regressive. Modern = usually new in time and progressive / better / more efficient. Old is not always feudal or backward. Old can be gold (the handout's example: Lata Mangeshkar). Raja Ram Mohun Roy, the Father of Modern India, wanted a return to the pure past of Vedantic traditions. Teacher's ladder: Feudal → Non-modern (the transition period) → Modern. Feudal is old in time and regressive; non-modern is the transition period; modern is usually new and progressive. Power and its six forms Power = Economic + Political (decision-making) + Military + Social (influence over people, or awe in their hearts) + Intellectual/Technological + Spiritual. A rise or fall in one form of power drives a rise or fall in the others. Example from the handout: a social-media influencer's popularity raises his or her economic power, while a scandal can hurt a politician's political power. Power and its six forms (W1 to W6), with the teacher's notes: Mao, "person-power fit", and the joint-family example. Person-power fit. Think of a joint family. The strong personality of the grandparents holds all the power. After years a weak personality follows, and power gets decentralised. Mao: power flows from the barrel of a gun (written beside Military). Baba Ramdev example: social power turns into money power (Patanjali, plus coaching). One power rising lifts another. It is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality Power centralises itself in a strong personality. That personality can be a human or an institution. When the personality weakens, power leaves in one of two ways: vertically downwards (decentralisation) or by horizontal displacement (another personality replaces it). Teacher's example of horizontal displacement by an institution: Kodak → smartphones. Rise and fall of super-powers: a wave between centralisation and decentralisation Reading the wave. Till 1707: strong Mughal emperors (all-India power). After 1707: decline of the Mughals, decentralisation of power to regional powers. Then the Maratha empire by the 1750s, broken at the Third Battle of Panipat, 1761, and then the EIC (circled in red) rises. The teacher draws a grandparent with four children as the Mughal picture. Beside it are the initials "SS, RS, AA", which I could not decode from the handwriting. Check your own notebook. Country, nation, state Country = territory (Desh). State = the organisation that rules or governs a country and its people (Rajya). To rule = to make laws, implement them and settle disputes (L, E, J) over domestic affairs. That is also called governance. Nation = the summation of people who are one (fraternity), equal (equality) and supreme (liberty). This is the definition given by the French Revolution (1789). The teacher links it to "We the People" in the Preamble = Nation (Rashtra). Teacher's board: State = organisation that rules a territory (country) and its people (nation) State rules a territory and its people. Country = the territory. Nation = the people. The State talks, trades or fights with the outside world, but it rules only its own country and people. State structure Teacher's tree: Symbolic sovereign (= President, Head of State) sits over the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary. This structure repeats at the Centre and at the Province. The Executive = the Council of Ministers, which works through military servants and civil servants. The handout says the primary purpose of any constitution is to create the State structure. Teacher's board: State structure A modern State structure has separation of power, a well-defined internal structure with clear goals and functions, and mechanisms that keep the whole structure stable from top to bottom. A non-modern State structure has no institutional separation of power and is prone to instability. Student confusion resolved (handout). NCERT says a Modern State has "centralised power exercised over a clearly defined territory". In class we say a Modern State has separation of power. Both are right. A State can be vertically centralised (a strong Union Government with authority over the provinces) and at the same time have horizontal separation of powers at the Union level: Parliament makes laws, the Prime Minister implements them, the Supreme Court resolves disputes. Like parents who centralise power over the home, yet divide it between mother and father. The word "province" is better than "state" for the units of a federation, otherwise it causes confusion with State = the ruling organisation. "Republic of India" and the point of Modern Indian History "Republic of India" = the name of the State (organisation) ruling the Territory and People of India since 26 January 1950. Key goal of the Constitution = to define and create this State (organisation). MIH = the history of the States that ruled the territory of India and its people, for example the Mughal State, the Maratha State, the Awadh State, and the Company State by the EIC. INM (Indian National Movement) = a people's movement. Teacher's board: "Republic of India" is the name of the State (organisation) ruling the territory and people of India since 26 January 1950. Its goal: end the British colonial State and establish the Nation State (the Republic of India). Keep one picture: a State is an organisation. Every dynasty in this course is just one such organisation, and each can be studied by the same questions: who rules, over what territory, with what structure, and why did it weaken? Types of State Military State Set up and sustained by military power Police State Sustained by overuse of the police Kingdom / Empire Head of State decided by bloodline. An Empire = a sum of kingdoms Company State Set up by a company, for example the EIC's Company State (1765–1858) in India Nation State Set up by the people / nation Types of State, with the teacher's notes: a Military State is established by military victory and ended by defeat; all States until 1950 were of this kind. Military State = established by military victory, ended by defeat. Example: all States until 1950. Game of Thrones picture: an empire = seven kingdoms. Each kingdom has a king (or queen), and the emperor or empress sits above K1, K2 ... Kn. Dynasty = bloodline-based succession for the Head of State. It is named on the basis of family, name or ethnicity (example: the Bourbon dynasty). Dynastic rule = monarchy. By contrast, a Head of State who is a representative of the public = Republic. Teacher's board: dynasty = bloodline-based succession of the Head of State; a Head of State who represents the public = Republic. Organisations and their motives Family Welfare of its members Private company Profit for shareholders NGO A social motive Political party Power over the State (the 1886 INC rule: take up only political issues, not social issues, so the INC is a political party, not an NGO) State Territory, and ideally the people's welfare (example: a Nation State) The common man does not want to be an MP, MLA or minister. She wants security: physical, economic, socio-cultural and spiritual. The State's motive is territory. A State will make no compromise with its own territory (defensive), but it may also seek territorial expansion (offensive). Social power and the common man. The common man wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural: religion, language, art and so on). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises. If social power rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example given: 1971, Indira Gandhi, and the hit song of the time. Sovereignty Sovereignty = symbolic sovereignty + the power to make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes (legislative, executive, judicial power), over external and domestic sovereign functions. Symbolic sovereignty Who is the head of the State The three powers Make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes (L, E, J) External sovereign functions Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs: war and diplomacy (including trade) Domestic sovereign functions Everything else: Home, Finance, Agriculture, Industry, Infrastructure, Health, Education, Transport and so on "Rule" / "Govern" Always means exercising those powers over domestic affairs Sovereign functions are also called subjects or affairs. The 7th Schedule of the Constitution (COI 1950) divides the domestic affairs between the Centre and the provinces. What is Sovereignty? Teacher's notes: symbolic sovereignty (real power = 0), the power to do L, E, J on external sovereign functions and on domestic affairs. Symbolic sovereignty: real power = 0. (The head of State is only a symbol.) Second part: the power to do L, E, J on (a) external sovereign functions = D, C, FA and (b) internal / domestic affairs = Home, Finance, Education, Health. Affairs = subjects = sovereign functions = the items in the 7th Schedule of the COI. External functions: Defence goes to the Defence Minister (war) External functions map to ministers like this. D (Defence) → Defence Minister → war. C (Communications) and FA (Foreign Affairs) → MEA → diplomacy + trade. Foreign Affairs has an economic and a political side. Separation of powers in a modern State Teacher's board: modern State structure Teacher's board, "Today": a modern State has horizontal separation of powers (L, E, J) and vertical separation of powers (federalism). Modern State structure = symbolic Head of State over L, E and J, at the Centre and provinces. The aim is separation of power, with neither over-centralisation nor an over-weak centre. Horizontal SoP = L / E / J. Vertical SoP = federalism. Inside the executive too: Head of State, PM, Council of Ministers, then the military servants ("gun power") and the civil servants ("political power"). Teacher: notice the separation of powers here also, for example a DM and an SP (more than one civil servant) share district power. Non-modern State (example: Mughal). An absolute monarch, extremely powerful, with ministers, aristocrats and mansabdars below him. The mark is excessive centralisation. Feudal State. The king is powerless, and feudal lords, ministers or aristocrats are powerful. There is no centralisation of power in the king: a very weak central authority. The non-modern (Mughal) and feudal states compared with the modern structure. Modern INM: the phases Moderates 1857–1905 "the Pen" Extremists 1905–20 "the People" Revolutionaries 1907–47 "the Gun" Gandhian Era 1920–47 — Many Voices of the Nation — Working class, women's empowerment, Dalit issues How the teacher says to remember battles and wars War = Σ (the sum) of battles. For any named battle or war, hold four things: Geography / place, Duration (example: the Seven Years' War), Participants, and Reason (example: the Austrian War of Succession, 1740–48). Passages: how regions connect Khyber Pass = India's entry pathway from the North-West. A passage can be natural: on land a pass (Khyber); on water a strait (Gibraltar; the Dardanelles linking the Black and Mediterranean Seas). Or man-made: on land bridges and tunnels; on water canals (the Suez; the Panama Canal). Two places that are strategically important are joined by a passage, and the passage makes them so (teacher's sketch of A and B with a link, natural or man-made). Teacher's method: remember every battle or war by its Geography/Place, Duration, Participants and Reason. A war is the sum of battles. Gibraltar joins Europe and Africa. 1914 = the most important development in the rise of the USA (written next to the Panama Canal).

items.t: 2 · The Mughal monarchs: a quick reference
items.x: Because a State is an organisation with a head, we list the heads of this one. Ask: where do the reign codes pass the baton, and where do they drop it? The dates in each name follow a coding convention to help you remember reign years: Babur26-30 means reigned 1526 to 1530. 1 Babur26-30 1526–1530 2 Humayun30-40 1530–1540 & 1555–1556 3 Akbar 56-05 1556–1605 4 Jahangir05-27 1605–1627 5 Shahjahan27-58 1627–1658 6 Aurangzeb58-07 (Alamgir) 1658–1707 7 Bahadur Shah07-12 (Shah Alam I) 1707–1712 8 Jahandar Shah12-13 1712–1713 9 Farukhsiyar13-19 1713–1719 10 Muhammad Shah19-48 (Rangila) 1719–1748 11 Ahmad Shah Bahadur48-54 1748–1754 12 Alamgir II54-59 1754–1759 13 Shah Alam II60-06 1760–1806 14 Akbar II 06-37 1806–1837 15 Bahadur Shah Zafar37-57 1837–1857 Humayun 30-40 is the only Mughal ruler with two reign periods: overthrown by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 in 1540, in exile for years, back on the throne in 1555, dead the following year. The list ends in 1857, the year of the great uprising. The last powerful emperor, Aurangzeb 58-07 (Alamgir), died in 1707. His successors, from Bahadur Shah to Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 (Bahadur Shah II), are the Later Mughals, ruling with ever-shrinking authority until 1857, when Zafar was deposed and exiled by the British. The Mughal State began with a cannon blast at Panipat in 1526 and ended with cannon blasts in Delhi. Simple picture of the Mughal State. Mughal State = 1526–1858, with an intermission 1540–55. The teacher's line-by-line: 1526 set up; 1540 demolished; 1555 re-established; Jan 1556 demolished (Humayun 30-40 dies); 1556 re-established. Akbar 56-05's reign is marked 49 years. Teacher's board: Mughal State 1526-1858, intermission 1540-55

Because the Lodis were fragile and Kabul was poor, a prince from Fergana turned to India. Ask: what beat numbers at Panipat? Who were the Mughals? Babur 26-30 was born in 1483 to Umar Shaikh Mirza, ruler of Fergana, a semi-autonomous State in present-day Uzbekistan, roughly half the size of modern Haryana. Fergana belonged to the Timurid Empire, and Babur 26-30 was a descendant of Timur (Tamerlane). "Mughal" is a Persian corruption of "Mongol". The Mughals were a Turko-Mongol dynasty. Maternal Genghis Khan (1206–27) Mongol Empire (1206–1368) Paternal Timur (Tamerlane) (1370–1405) Timurid Empire (1370–1507) Self-identity Timurids Pride in Timur, who had captured Delhi in 1398 They took greater pride in the paternal ancestor, so they called themselves Timurids, not Mughals. Map: lands of the Empire of Timur (campaigns 1379 to 1405). Delhi is marked as sacked in 1398-99. Map: the Fergana Valley, Babur's homeland (Kokand, Andijan, Osh, Namangan, Fergana, Jodzend). Why Babur 26-30 turned to India Khanates of the Mongol Empire, about 1300 (handout figure). Babur 26-30 came to power young but could not hold Fergana; by 1512 his Central Asian ambitions had collapsed. He held Kabul (captured 1504), but Kabul was economically poor. India was wealthy but politically fragile under the Lodi dynasty. With artillery support from the Ottoman Empire (expert gunners), Babur 26-30 began attacking the Delhi Sultanate from 1519. Map: the conquests of Babur, 1516 to 1529 (Kabul 1504, Khyber Pass, Panipat 1526, Agra 1528, Gwalior and the east 1529) Babur 26-30's map: Kabul = "eco" (poor). The Khyber Pass is underlined. The dates 1526 (Panipat), 1528 (Agra) and 1529 (Gwalior and the march east) are underlined. First Battle of Panipat (1526) Babur 26-30 entered India through the Khyber Pass and met Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty (1451–1526), on the plains of Panipat. Babur 26-30's army was smaller (about 12,000 men), but his small bronze cannons were decisive, a technology the Lodis could not match. Lodi was killed, the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) ended and the Mughal Kingdom was born. This was still a kingdom, not yet an empire. It became an empire under Akbar 56-05 and reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07. Tech power. Babur 26-30's edge over a fragile Lodi Sultanate was technology, not numbers. The teacher underlines "small bronze cannons", "about 12,000" and "Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)". Why three great battles happened at Panipat Three of the most consequential battles in Indian history, 1526, 1556 and 1761, were all fought at Panipat. Geography chose Panipat; the commanders merely followed: 1. Panipat lay close to the Khyber Pass, the primary invasion route from Central Asia. 2. It sat in the narrow corridor between the Thar Desert (south) and the Himalayan foothills (north), a natural bottleneck. 3. The Yamuna to the east acted as a defensive choke-point, ruling out flanking manoeuvres. The Kala Amb memorial in Haryana commemorates the 1761 Third Battle, not the 1526 one. Babur 26-30 and the Mughal Kingdom (1526) Babur 26-30 in Fergana; Timurid descendant, loses Fergana by 1512 Kabul held from 1504; economically poor India: rich but politically fragile under the Lodis Ottoman gunners and small bronze cannons; attacks from 1519 First Battle of Panipat 1526; Babur 26-30 (about 12,000) defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi Delhi Sultanate ends; the Mughal Kingdom is born (a kingdom, not yet an empire)

Because a kingdom is easier to win than to keep, the son lost it to Sher Shah. Ask: which reforms of the winner did Akbar later build on? Babur 26-30 died in 1530; his son Humayun 30-40 succeeded. Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 was an Afghan-Pathan, born Farid Khan in Bihar, c. 1486. He was no foreign invader: his ancestors migrated to India under the Lodis and settled as Jagirdars in Bihar. He won the title Sher Khan by killing a tiger single-handed while serving Bahar Khan Lohani (Governor of Bihar under the Lodis till 1526, then independent Sultan Md Lohani, who refused Mughal sovereignty). Sher Shah 40-45 defeated Humayun 30-40 at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540), founded the Suri dynasty (1540–55) and pushed the Mughals out of India entirely. Humayun's loss and return: 1530 succession, 1539 Chausa, 1540 Kanauj, 1555 Sirhind, Jan 1556 death and Hemu seizes Delhi Two defeats: Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540). The Suri interregnum 1540–55 is a gap / intermission in the Mughal movie. Sirhind (1555) is boxed. Sher Shah 40-45's three reforms The Suri dynasty lasted only fifteen years, but Sher Shah 40-45's administrative innovations outlasted it: 1. Revenue. A standardised system of land measurement and revenue assessment, the precursor to Akbar 56-05's Zabti system. Each peasant got a Patta specifying his revenue obligation, and the State took a Qabuliyat, a written agreement, from the peasant. The two-document system gave both State and cultivator an enforceable record. 2. Currency. The silver Rupiya, a coin of standardised weight and purity, the ancestor of the modern Indian rupee. 3. Infrastructure. He upgraded the Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Sonargaon in Bengal, transforming communication and trade across the subcontinent. Patta and Qabuliyat. The Patta is a document given by the State to the ryot: land details, ryot's name, the LR to be paid. The Qabuliyat is proof that the ryot agreed to pay the LR; it is given by the ryot to the State. Sher Shah 40-45 was the first to introduce this bilateral / mutual agreement system. In ancient times a Patta existed but it was not two-sided: the State gave the Patta (Tamra Patra, a copper inscription). Sher Shah 40-45 died in 1545. The Suri dynasty held Delhi until 1555, when Humayun 30-40 recaptured the throne. Much of what Akbar 56-05 later systematised had its roots in Sher Shah 40-45's innovations. Humayun 30-40 returns, with Safavid help To retake his throne, Humayun 30-40 turned to the Safavid dynasty of Iran. The Safavids agreed at a political price: Humayun 30-40 had to adopt Shia practices and outward observances, cede Kandahar to Iran, and promote Persian culture in India. Whether this was genuine conversion is debated; Humayun 30-40 publicly assumed Shia forms as the price of the alliance. Lasting consequences: Persian language and art became embedded in Mughal court culture, and a distinct Irani group of Mansabdars later emerged in the Mughal administration. Teacher's board: the Safavid dynasty of Persia's conditions for helping Humayun: convert to Shia, promote Persian culture, make Persians mansabdars (link: the Irani group With 14,000 Iranian troops, Humayun 30-40 defeated the Suris at the Battle of Sirhind (Punjab, 1555). In January 1556 Humayun 30-40 fell from the stairs of his library, struck his head and died. Hemchandra Vikramaditya (Hemu), from Rewari in present-day Haryana, who had served as chief commander and minister of the Suris, seized Delhi and declared himself Samrat.

items.t: 5 · How the Mughal Kingdom was re-established (Panipat 1556)
items.x: Because Hemu seized Delhi after Humayun's death, a boy's guardian had to win it back. Ask: why is Akbar's code 56? On one side stood Hemu, controlling Delhi. On the other, the Mughal army under Bairam Khan: general, strategist and guardian to the thirteen-year-old Akbar 56-05. Hemu was defeated. The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) secured the Mughal State in India for the next 150 years. Humayun 30-40 to Akbar 56-05: the intermission Babur 26-30 enters through the Khyber Pass; First Panipat 1526 Humayun 30-40 defeated by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 (Chausa 1539, Kanauj 1540) Suri dynasty 1540–55; Mughals lose India Safavid alliance; 14,000 Iranian troops; Sirhind 1555 Humayun 30-40 dies Jan 1556; Hemu seizes Delhi Second Panipat 1556: Bairam Khan defeats Hemu; Akbar 56-05's reign secured

items.t: 6 · How Akbar 56-05 built the Mughal State: the Mansabdari System
items.x: Because the kingdom was re-won, Akbar built a machine to run it. Ask: who is a Mansabdar, how is he paid, and what is the fatal weakness? Babur 26-30 founded the Mughal Kingdom. Humayun 30-40 nearly lost it. Akbar 56-05, ruling for fifty years (1556–1605), built the machinery of the Mughal State: the Mansabdari System, a military-bureaucracy that decided how the State was administered, how its army was maintained and how the King kept control over a vast and diverse territory. What is a Mansabdar? Mansab = a post or rank. Mansabdar = the holder of the post. Every Mansabdar had a dual function: military and civil-administrative. The same man who commanded troops also governed territory. That is why it is called a military-bureaucracy. Teacher's board: the Mughal Emperor over Mansabdars (= ministers and senior officers) Posts in the State structure. "O" = a post = mansab. A DM or minister = mansabdar; DM-ship or minister-ship = mansab. Mansabdars = the ministers and senior officers of the Mughal State. Five questions the teacher sets for the topic: What is a mansab? What is a mansabdar? Salary? Ranks? How to become a mansabdar? Rank: Zat + Sawar Each Mansabdar carried two ranks: Zat = personal rank, governing seniority and status. Sawar = the number of horsemen he must maintain and provide to the King. Net rank = Zat + Sawar. Example: Zat 2,000 + Sawar 3,000 = net rank 5,000. Mansabdari, Zat plus Sawar No separation of power between civil and military. Zat is like today's rank (A); Sawar = the army, i.e. the horsemen (B); net rank = A + B. Eligibility. "Lineage, not merit" in most cases. The primary rule was hereditary, with the exception of Birbal, who was not from an aristocratic family. Zat-Sawar graph. Most nobles lie on the rising line (more Zat, more Sawar). Outliers: the favourite of the emperor = "Anshu" and the distrusted = "Piyush". The teacher's two names sit at opposite corners of the graph (Piyush high on Zat, Anshu high on Sawar). Who could become a Mansabdar? Lineage, not merit. If your ancestors had been Mansabdars, you had the opportunity. Talent alone was not enough, not unlike pre-revolutionary France, where only sons of nobles could enter the nobility. This rigidity later became a serious weakness. How Mansabdars were paid: Jagir, Khalisa, Inam A Mansabdar could be paid in cash (a Naqdi Mansabdar) or by a Jagir: a specific piece of land whose land revenue he pocketed directly. This revenue paid his salary and covered the cost of maintaining his army. A Jagir given in lieu of salary = a Tankha Jagir; its holder = a Jagirdar. Iqtadar of the Delhi Sultanate is like the Jagirdar Mansabdar of the Mughals. (Iqta = Jagir in Persian.) Mughal land was divided into these categories: 1. Jagir land: revenue to Mansabdars. 2. Khalisa land: royal land. Revenue goes directly to the King and pays Naqdi Mansabdars plus other State expenses. 3. Inam land: gifted land. Revenue goes to a chosen beneficiary (for example a man of exceptional talent) to sustain himself. 4. Mashrut Jagir: a temporary "top-up" or extra allowance given to an official to cover the extra costs of a specific, difficult assignment. It is revoked automatically when the assignment ends. (Like "base salary" versus "the bonus".) By the early 18th century there were over 8,000 Mansabdars, and four-fifths of all LR came from Jagirs, only one-fifth from Khalisa land. Teacher's board: land of the Mughal empire Salary in those times. The key source of power was control over land and its resources (today it is money). Mansabdars were about 4,000 to 5,000 at the peak of Mughal power (17th century); about 80 out of every 100 of LR went to them and about 20 to the King. Therefore the richest single person was the King. Worked example for LR: ₹100 of wheat is cultivated by the ryot / peasant / Khudkasht. Tax = LR = 1/3 to 2/3 of gross produce. (For the changing LR share by era, see section 7.) Teacher's board: salary is cash (Naqdi Mansabdar) or allocation of a Tankha Jagir (Jagirdar Mansabdar) Three rules for Tankha Jagirs 1. Transferable. The King could rotate Jagirs among Mansabdars, or convert a Jagirdar into a Naqdi Mansabdar at will. 2. Capped extraction. A Jagirdar could collect only the pre-determined LR, not a rupee more. Royal supervision existed to prevent oppression of peasants and zamindars. 3. Confiscation on death. On the death of a Tankha Jagirdar, both the Jagir and all accumulated wealth were confiscated. The predictable result: Mansabdars spent lavishly in their lifetimes, since saving made little sense. Tankha Jagir: the King gets his army from it From a Tankha Jagir the King gets his army. Teacher's example split: LR = ₹30 pays for personal salary; LR = ₹70 must be used to maintain the army as per Sawar. Military corruption (post-1707) = the expected army is not being maintained. Watan Jagir Watan = hereditary and permanent. Unlike Tankha Jagirs, a Watan Jagir could be passed down and was not subject to rotation or confiscation. Given mainly to Rajput chieftains and autonomous rulers who had submitted to the Emperor, so they could collect revenue in their ancestral domains in exchange for military service and loyalty. The holder paid 10% of LR to the King as Peshkash (tribute), acknowledging the King's ultimate authority and compensating him for giving up his right to reclaim the Jagir. Do not confuse an ordinary Zamindar's Milkiyat (hereditary personal property within his zamindari tract) with a Watan Jagir (a political grant to a chieftain, carrying sovereign-like privileges). Inam vs Watan: Inam is a pure gift and is confiscated after death like Tankha Jagir. Watan is hereditary, given to a Mansabdar doing duty for the King, and passes to heirs. Nature Salary grant Hereditary, permanent grant Heritability Confiscated on the holder's death Passes to heirs Transfer King could rotate it at will Not rotated Typical holder Any Mansabdar Rajput chiefs / rulers who submitted Tribute — Pays 10% of LR as Peshkash to the King Teacher's board: power of a Mansabdar W = Watan / Vatan = hereditary = permanent = 10% of LR to the King as tribute. TJ = temporary = the emperor can take it away = transferable. In the teacher's picture, a Jagirdar with both gets 90% of the LR of the Watan portion, the king taking 10%; on Tankha land the Jagirdar takes 100% of the LR. What held the system together, and its fatal weakness The system ran on a patron-client relationship: the King gave rank and Jagir, and the Mansabdar pledged personal loyalty and maintained the army. This co-opted powerful individuals who might have challenged royal authority. But the loyalty was personal, not institutional. A Mansabdar's loyalty was to the King as a person, not to the State as an institution or to any law. It was transactional and conditional: give and take. If the King could not deliver Mansab and Jagir (land shortage, financial pressure, weak authority), the loyalty dissolved, and dissolved loyalty meant political instability. This differs from a modern State, where bureaucrats and military officers owe their position to merit and service rules: impersonal loyalty to institution and law. Because the whole military strength depended on Mansabdars actually maintaining the Sawar armies, weakened royal supervision meant hollowed-out armies on paper, far fewer men in reality, a silent erosion of State power from within. The weakness of the Mansabdari System Patron-client bond; King gives Mansab + Jagir, Mansabdar gives loyalty and maintains the army Loyalty is personal; to the King, not to the State or any law King cannot deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir Loyalty dissolves; the bond was transactional and conditional State erodes; hollow armies on paper, fewer men in reality The Mansabdari weakness: an institutional / organisational / systemic weakness Teacher's board: Mansab plus Jagir given by the King; loyalty and army given back Institutional / organisational / systemic weakness. Impersonal loyalty (non-human) means loyalty to the State, law, religion, land or language, not to a person. The teacher's reading of the flow: "King cannot deliver" = cannot deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir (the teacher crossed out the handout's "land/revenue runs short" line and replaced it with this). The end state: on paper a 2 lakh army, in reality a 1 lakh army. Post-1707: if Mansabdars did not get their desired Mansab and Jagir, they became disloyal. The patron-client picture: the patron is senior and gives; the client is junior and takes.

Because the Mansabdars had to be paid, the State needed a revenue machine. Ask: who assesses, who settles, who collects, and who gets what? Usually people think all rights in a property are with the owner. That is not correct. Rights in land belong to four stakeholders: The owner (in the Mughal system, ultimately the King) Right to sell, lease out, rent out, and to get money from these; right to fair tax The tenant / ryot Right to occupy and cultivate; right to fair rent The collector of tax Right to collect tax; right to be paid for the service The State Right to assess / fix tax, enforce the demand and receive tax LR was the financial backbone of the State: it paid the Mansabdars, maintained the army and kept the treasury alive. Assessors fix the demand using past data of production and of LR, and so assess the LR demand. The two systems, Zabti and Ijaradari, are ticked. Who collected revenue, and how was it supervised The State did not collect directly. It relied on Zamindars (non-state actors) in zamindari tracts, who also held police duties. Rule of thumb: State actors get salaries. Non-State actors get a commission or profit for service performed for the State. The revenue hierarchy ran through record-keeping, assessment, settlement, collection and oversight: A1 Record keeping Village Patwari Maintains ledgers (Bahi / Bahi khata or Khasra) of individual peasant holdings and crops. A non-state accountant paid by the village community. Like the Kulkarni of Maharashtra, but the Patwari had no watan / vatan (hereditary) right; it was a customary right, not a customary vatan right A2 Record keeping Pargana Qanungo Consolidated Patwari data; a state official and hereditary custodian of historical tax rates (had vatan right) B1 Assessment Pargana Amil The State's executive revenue officer at the pargana level; assessed the official demand and audited accounts B2 Assessment Sarkar (district) Amalguzar Supervisor of the Amil at the sarkar level; assessed the demand and audited accounts C Settlement Ryot Patta and Qabuliyat See below D Collection Village Muqaddam Village headman who collected from cultivators E Oversight Pargana / sarkar Amil and Amalguzar Under Akbar 56-05's Zabti system Patta (the title deed) = the official paper given to the individual peasant by the government. The government used the Patwari's ledger / Khasra to create it. It told the peasant exactly how much land he officially held and how much LR he must pay, and so served as a check against over-extraction. Qabuliyat (the acceptance deed) = the document signed by the peasant and given back to the government, promising to pay the LR written on the Patta. Khudkasht vs Pahikasht A Patta has two pieces of information: which field / plot is cultivated by which ryot and how much LR is to be paid. It is a "safety tool for the Khudkasht / ryot". Zamindar = holds the right to collect LR from a land. Jagirdar = holds the right to consume LR from a land. Physical collection and the Zabti system Muqaddams collected from cultivators. In zamindari tracts they deposited to Zamindars (who extracted through their own Amlas). Where there were no intermediaries, Muqaddams paid directly to the State. In later periods contractual revenue farmers, the Ijaradars, also collected (covered below). Under Akbar 56-05's Zabti system, the State did not trust Zamindars with autonomous authority. State officials (Amil at pargana level, under the Amalguzar at sarkar level) scientifically measured the land and fixed the exact demand. The land records were archived by the Qanungo at pargana level. LR was calculated as a percentage of gross produce (more LR from more fertile areas). Mughal LR demand was a percentage of Gross Produce, not Net Produce. Subtracting the cost of cultivation before taxing was a British reform, much later, and only after the gross-produce method had caused widespread agrarian ruin. Mansabdari versus Zamindari / Zabti Mansabdari = a system of the Mughal State structure (king and mansabdars; roles and responsibilities, salaries, hierarchy and ranks). Zamindari / Zabti = a system of collection of LR: assessment (how much LR) by the State, collection by the Zamindar. Don't mix the two. The zamindar's position The Zamindar was an obedient collection agent under strict supervision, making sure the surplus went to the central treasury, not his pocket. His legally fixed commission, about 10%, was called Nankar or Malikana. His own personal lands were Milkiyat, on which he paid LR like any other landholder. Abwabs = customary tributes, extra demands passed from State to Zamindar to peasant. Teacher's diagram of the LR chain (Zabti): King gets LR from Khalisa lands; Jagirdar Mansabdars from Jagirs; Intermediary Zamindars (1000-3000 villages) and Primary Zamin Intermediary Zamindars = big Zamindars who received LR from Primary Zamindars and collected LR themselves where no Primary Zamindar existed in their assigned land. They passed LR from Khalisa lands to the Imperial Treasury and from Jagir lands to Jagirdars. Sometimes Primary Zamindars sent LR straight to the treasury or the Jagirdar. The Zamindari system The quantum of LR is decided by the State, not the zamindar. In the teacher's circle (the rural economy): ryots pay LR up to the Zamindar; he sends LR to K (king) and J (jagirdar); he keeps 10% as commission, Abwab, and has police duties. Zamindar roles. He also had police duties (the teacher compares it with an SHO's work) and was the traditional leader of ryots. Abwab from State to Zamindar = levies; Abwab from ryot to Zamindar = tribute. Teacher's board: the Patta (name of ryot, LR to be paid, details of fields) is the safety tool for the Khudkasht; the Zamindar is a non-state actor, not a govt employee;  A Zamindar is a non-state actor: a private person, not a govt employee. Salary is used only for employees. His payment for services to the State (LR collection and police duties) is the 10% of LR. A classroom ladder of power (vehicle analogy): King = helicopter; Jagirdar = Ferrari; Intermediary Zamindar = Fortuner; Primary Zamindar = Honda City; Khudkasht = cycle / Luna; Pahikasht = on foot. The teacher's vehicle analogy for the LR ladder: King (helicopter), Jagirdar (Ferrari), Intermediary Zamindar (Fortuner), Primary Zamindar (Honda City), Khudkasht (cycle/ Ryot (Khudkasht / Pahikasht) Pays LR Primary Zamindar (or Muqaddam, or directly to State in non-zamindari areas) Enough to sustain himself Primary Zamindar (smaller; 100–300 villages) Ryots Intermediary Zamindar About 10% (Nankar / Malikana) Intermediary Zamindar (big; 1000–3000 villages) Primary Zamindars King (Khalisa) or Jagirdar (Jagir) About 10% (Nankar / Malikana) King / Jagirdar Zamindars — King: Khalisa LR. Jagirdar: Jagir LR Two kinds of ryot Land worked The same land year after year Different lands each season (often share-croppers) Occupancy rights Customary occupancy: cannot be removed None; no fixed attachment to land Standing Small landowner-cultivator; holds a Patta Landless and rightless (Vagrant / Banjara) Khudkasht = occupancy rights of cultivation, NOT ownership. The King owned all land. A Khudkasht could not be arbitrarily removed, but could not sell or mortgage the land either. Khudkasht vs Pahikasht: the Khudkasht holds a Patta; the Pahikasht is a landless, rightless vagrant or Banjara. Pahikasht = cultivates different lands (within a village); landless and rightless. Revenue farming: Muqatai, Ijaradari, Farming System The logic: instead of collecting through the Zamindar network under State supervision, the right to collect all revenues from an area (land, traders, shopkeepers) was auctioned to the highest bidder, called an Ijaradar or Revenue Farmer. A farmer, in the economic sense, works with a profit motive; a peasant works for food security. The Ijaradar was not a cultivator but a merchant or moneylender who bid purely for profit. He farmed revenue, not land. The Ijaradar paid the bid amount, fully or partially in advance, to the Jagirdar (on Jagir land) or to the State (on Khalisa land), then collected his investment plus profit from the peasants and traders. Contracts were typically 3 to 5 years. His incentive was to extract as much as possible within that window, with zero interest in irrigation, peasant welfare or long-term growth. If he failed to deliver, the contract was re-auctioned. Ijaradars were urban bankers and merchants with no roots in the countryside: no long-term stake in the land, no relationship with the peasants. Teacher's board: the Ijaradari system arises when there is need (war, bad harvest, a State short of LR) or greed (for example a Jagirdar who wants to maximise earnings, o Why Ijaradari arises: need or greed, for ↑LR. Need = war, bad harvest, LR collection of the State falling short. Greed = for example a Jagirdar who wants to maximise his earnings, and a weak Mughal State. Teacher's auction analogy: the right to collect revenue from an area is sold like a painting The painting analogy. Bidders in the auction are all rich. "HK" (the seller) gets the best price, as a result of competitive bidding, and gets the money in advance. "Bhaskar" (the buyer) then gets the painting. Bhaskar and the other bidders have profit as the motive: he plans to sell it at ₹2 crore, so ₹1 crore is the investment and the return he expects is ₹1 crore. In Ijaradari the right to collect revenue is the painting. Teacher's board: auctions are held by the Jagirdar (in Jagir areas) or the King/State (on Khalisa lands) Who auctions: the Jagirdar (in a Jagir area) or the King/State (on Khalisa lands). They get money in advance (no wait till harvest) and the best price. Participants are men of money: merchants, moneylenders and bankers = Ijaradars. Motive = profit: collect such LR from ryots as covers the bid/investment plus profits. The teacher writes contract time as 3-4 years (the handout says 3 to 5). The Zamindar suffers a temporary loss of his Watan right to collect LR. The mechanics: the Jagirdar auctions the right to collect LR over an area; merchants and moneylenders participate; the winner pays the bid amount to the Jagirdar in advan Who is happy and who is not under Ijaradari: King/Jagirdar happy (advance, best price); Ijaradar happy (profits); ryots unhappy (no Patta); Zamindar unhappy (lost Watan r Who wins and loses in Ijaradari: King/Jagirdar: happy (advance, best ₹). Ijaradar: happy (profits). Ryots: unhappy (no Patta). Zamindar: unhappy (lost Watan right and earnings). A revolt needs a leader (L) and followers (Fo). If both (Zamindar as leader, ryots as followers) are unhappy: strong revolt. If the leader is unhappy but followers are happy: no revolt. If the leader is happy but followers unhappy: weak revolt. Example: Churaman Jat, a Zamindar-led peasant revolt (about 1695), the grievance being high LR, led to the Jat Kingdom. Example: Churaman 95-21 Jat = Zamindar-led peasant revolt (~1695); grievance = high LR; it led to the Jat Kingdom. (Taken up in Chapter 5.) Zamindar vs Ijaradar: why it mattered to the peasant. A Zamindar's right was tied to his bloodline; he and his descendants had to live with the peasants forever, so he rarely squeezed them to starvation. His commission was a state-mandated ~10% (Nankar / Malikana). An Ijaradar promised the State a fixed lump sum (say 1 lakh); if he extracted 3 lakh through torture and extortion, he kept the entire 2 lakh profit. The Zamindar's extraction was capped by law; the Ijaradar's was capped only by the peasant's capacity to endure. Basis of right Hereditary and traditional leader of rural society Won an auction; an urban moneylender / merchant Time horizon Permanent Short 3–5 year contract Extraction cap Capped (about 10% commission / Nankar / Malikana) No cap Peasant impact Subsistence living possible Ruined How LR is fixed Detailed survey Auction Settlement with (i.e. LR to be paid agreed with whom) Ryot (has Patta) Revenue farmer (Ijaradar), who also has the responsibility to deposit LR to the State Collection by Zamindar Ijaradar Motive of collector State-mandated commission Profit motive Peasant protection Patta gives legal right No protection The Ijaradari story across history: rise and decline Auctioning the right to collect tax is ancient, but it was formally institutionalised in the subcontinent during the Delhi Sultanate as the Muqatai system. It lasted until Akbar 56-05 practically abolished it. Ijaradari maps almost perfectly onto the rise and decline of Mughal authority: abolished when the State was strong, revived when it was weak. (Babur 26-30 had no time for revenue reforms in his four-year reign; the decisive break came under Akbar 56-05.) Ijaradari across the centuries Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526); Muqatai, the first formal institutionalisation of revenue farming Akbar 56-05; practically abolished it, replaced with the Zabti system Jahangir 05-27; re-emerges marginally as control over Jagirdar-Mansabdars loosens Shahjahan 27-58; reintroduced properly, but only for ruined or devastated lands Aurangzeb 58-07; expanded it significantly; the Deccan campaigns made quick cash irresistible Jahandar Shah 12-13; institutionalised in Punjab and Bengal, the richest provinces Farukhsiyar (1713–19); extended into royal Khalisa lands Successor states; Awadh under Sadat Khan 22-39 and Hyderabad under Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 continue it Warren Hastings 73-85 (1772); formalised as the EIC's Farming System in Bengal Ijaradari rise and decline, with the teacher's notes: notice the pattern; Shah Jahan for ruined lands (banjar); Jahandar Shah in fertile regions; Farukhsiyar's extension  Notice the pattern down the chain. Akbar 56-05: Zamindari system (the teacher writes it beside "Zabti"). Shah Jahan: ruined lands = "banjar". Aurangzeb 58-07: wars. Jahandar Shah 12-13: fertile regions. Farukhsiyar: Khalisa lands, the first time (1st), which hurts the Emperor's social power. Warren Hastings 73-85's Farming System = Ijaradari. Wars need money, so the LR demand rises. Akbar 56-05 1/3rd Shah Jahan (1627–58), Aurangzeb 58-07 High extraction: 1/3rd to 1/2 Later Mughals (1707+) Extreme extraction: 1/3rd to 2/3rd Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor of Bengal Presidency from 1772 and Governor General of Bengal Presidency from 1773–75 (the Regulating Act of 1773 made him GG, but he formally assumed office as GG in 1774). He formalised revenue farming as the Farming System in 1772. What began as the Muqatai system under the Delhi Sultanate, was abolished by Akbar 56-05 and revived under weaker successors, had become standard practice across large parts of the subcontinent by his time. The ryot at the bottom paid the price at every stage.

items.t: 8 · Akbar 56-05's religious vision: Sulh-i-Kul, Ibadat Khana, Mahzar, Din-i-Ilahi
items.x: Because the Emperor ruled a diverse realm, Akbar also built a religious vision. Ask: what is the order of the four steps? Akbar 56-05's approach to religion shaped the political character of Mughal rule for generations. He moved in a clear sequence: 1. Ibadat Khana (1575). A House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri where scholars from different faiths debated. It exposed him to the diversity of religious thought and to the bitter rivalries among the Ulama. 2. Mahzar, the Infallibility Decree (1579). It gave Akbar 56-05 the authority to adjudicate religious disputes: the Emperor, not the clergy, was the final word on matters of faith. 3. Din-i-Ilahi (1582). A syncretic spiritual order borrowing from Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism and Christianity. It is best understood as a religio-political experiment, not a movement: not many joined, but its real significance lay in the principle it expressed. 4. Sulh-i-Kul: universal peace. The State must treat all religions with equal respect, and no single faith should dominate policy. It became the ideological foundation of Mughal governance under Akbar 56-05 and influenced Mughal politics long after his death. The goal of each step. Ibadat Khana: a mid-path, to reduce conflict. Mahzar: the Emperor is the final word on faith. Din-i-Ilahi: a syncretic religio-political order (a new hybrid religion borrowing from multiple faiths); goal = social peace. Sulh-i-Kul: universal peace via equal respect for all faiths; goal = social peace / order.

items.t: 9 · Who actually introduced Jizya in India?
items.x: Because religion shaped policy, here is a side question on Jizya. Ask: who first imposed it, and who institutionalised it? Jizya is a tax on non-Muslims. It is often associated with the Delhi Sultanate, but it predates the Sultanate by several centuries. Muhammad bin Qasim first imposed Jizya in Sindh during the 8th-century Arab conquest. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 and his successors institutionalised it as a formal instrument of revenue and policy across the Delhi Sultanate from the early 13th century. The distinction matters: Jizya arrived in India with the Arabs, but became a pan-subcontinental administrative practice only under the Sultanate. Who introduced Jizya? First imposed by Muhammad bin Qasim in Sindh (8th century); institutionalised by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and successors across the Delhi Sultanate.

items.t: 10 · Two maps to fix in memory
items.x: Because a State is about territory, fix the map before the end. Ask: why had Babur no coast, and what did Akbar add? Pre-1526 Indian subcontinent. Teacher's Deccan triangle: Bijapur, Golconda, Goa and Vijayanagara (VN, 1336-1646). Pre-1526 subcontinent. In the Deccan, the teacher marks Bijapur and Golconda with Goa on the west coast, and Vijayanagara (VN) 1336–1646 in the south. Mughal Empire 1530 to 1707: extent of Babur (1530), Akbar (1605) and Aurangzeb (1707) State = organisation that rules a territory and people; territory = the motive of the State. Babur 26-30: no coastal territory. Akbar 56-05: rich coastal trade added to the economy. Babur 26-30 = founder; Akbar 56-05 and Aurangzeb 58-07 = expanders of the territory of the State.

items.t: 11 · The teacher's revision boards on the land revenue (LR) system (Lecture 4)
items.x: Last scene: the teacher redraws the land revenue machine on four boards. Ask: can you redraw the ladder, the survey, the four steps and the Amlas? At the start of Lecture 4 the teacher redrew the whole LR machinery. These four boards are the best one-page revision of Section 7. A State is an organisation. Power centralises in a strong personality, and when that personality weakens power leaves either vertically downwards (decentralisation) or sideways to another personality (horizontal displacement, as Kodak gave way to smartphones). A State is the organisation that rules a territory (the country) and its people (the nation), by making laws, implementing them and settling disputes (L, E, J). Sovereignty adds a symbolic head of State. The Mughal ledger. There are fifteen Mughal monarchs, from Babur 26-30 to Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, and the reign codes pass the baton from one to the next. Humayun 30-40 is the only one with two reign periods. The teacher writes the Mughal State as 1526-1858 with an intermission 1540-55. A prince without a home. Babur 26-30 was born in 1483 in Fergana, a Timurid descendant (the Mughals are 'Mongol' in Persian, but they took pride in Timur, who captured Delhi in 1398). He lost Fergana by 1512, and Kabul (1504) was economically poor. India was rich but politically fragile under the Lodis, and with Ottoman gunners he began attacking from 1519. Panipat, 1526. Babur 26-30 had about 12,000 men but small bronze cannons, and Ibrahim Lodi was killed. The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) ended and the Mughal Kingdom was born, a kingdom and not yet an empire. Panipat saw battles in 1526, 1556 and 1761 because it lay near the Khyber Pass, in the corridor between the Thar Desert and the Himalayan foothills, with the Yamuna as a choke-point. The son loses it. Humayun 30-40 was defeated by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540), and the Suri dynasty (1540-55) pushed the Mughals out. Sher Shah's three reforms outlasted him: the Patta and Qabuliyat revenue system, the silver Rupiya, and the Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Sonargaon. Persia's price. The Safavids of Iran helped, at a price: Shia forms, Kandahar ceded, Persian culture promoted. With 14,000 Iranian troops Humayun 30-40 won at Sirhind (1555), but in January 1556 he fell from the stairs of his library and died. Hemu seized Delhi and declared himself Samrat, and Bairam Khan, guardian of the 13-year-old Akbar 56-05, defeated him at the Second Panipat (1556). Akbar's machine: the Mansabdar. Every Mansabdar held a mansab (a post), with a military and civil role, and two ranks: Zat (personal) plus Sawar (horsemen to maintain). Lineage mattered more than merit, with Birbal the exception. Pay came in cash (Naqdi) or by Jagir, and Mughal land was Jagir, Khalisa, Inam or Mashrut; four-fifths of LR came from Jagirs. A Tankha Jagir was transferable, capped and confiscated on death, while a Watan Jagir was hereditary with 10% Peshkash. Land revenue: who gets what. Four stakeholders hold rights in land: owner, tenant, collector and State. The State assessed through the Patwari, Qanungo, Amil and Amalguzar, settled with a Patta and a Qabuliyat, and collected through the Zamindar (about 10% as Nankar / Malikana) and the village Muqaddam. LR was a share of gross produce, and the Khudkasht had occupancy rights while the Pahikasht had none. The flaw. Mansabdari was a patron-client bond: the King gave rank and Jagir, the Mansabdar gave loyalty and an army. The loyalty was personal, not institutional. After 1707, if the King could not deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir, loyalty dissolved, and the end state was an army of 2 lakh on paper and 1 lakh in reality. The auction door. Ijaradari (revenue farming) arises from need (war, bad harvest, a short treasury) or greed. The Ijaradar paid in advance, worked for profit on a contract of 3 to 5 years, and gave the peasant no Patta. It began as the Muqatai of the Delhi Sultanate, was practically abolished by Akbar 56-05 and then revived by weaker rulers (Jahangir, Shahjahan, Aurangzeb, Jahandar Shah, Farukhsiyar) until Warren Hastings 73-85 formalised it as the Farming System in 1772. When the Zamindar (leader) and the ryots (followers) are both unhappy, a strong revolt follows, as with Churaman 95-21 Jat about 1695. Akbar's faith ladder. Akbar 56-05 built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri (1575), issued the Mahzar (1579) making the Emperor the final word on faith, and set up the Din-i-Ilahi (1582), a religio-political experiment rather than a movement. Behind them all stood Sulh-i-Kul, universal peace through equal respect for every faith. Jizya, by contrast, was first imposed in Sindh by Muhammad bin Qasim and institutionalised by Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 and his successors.
