items.t: 1 · The middle path between king and rebel
items.x: Because the Mughals were too weak to crush every rebel, they offered a deal. Ask: what does each side give, and whose core interest is met? Teacher's board: in case of rebels establishing their rule in an area When rebels establish their rule in an area, the emperor has two options: (1) continue fighting and end the rebellion; (2) lose the territory (T) and let the rebel establish an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts to be a Mansabdar of the emperor, accepts the Mughal as emperor, sends tribute to Delhi, agrees to maintain an army / help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts: dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference in the rebel's rule. Teacher's board: both sides' core interest is met The middle path, king and rebel King (Mughal) The rebel provides an army; the empire does not shrink Rebel Opportunity as a Mansabdar at the centre (recall successor states); dynastic governor status; the king accepts the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir Except for the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once, in 1707), this pattern appears among the Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad, Mysore and Rajputs. The teacher's ink ties this to Article 370 status (a state within a state on special terms) and sorts the regional powers: SS (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad); RS (Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad; plus the Sikhs); AAS (Rajputs, Mysore; plus Travancore). The Sikhs [RS] and Travancore [AAS] were not legally in the Mughal empire.

Because the deal was on offer, three more rebel States used it. Ask: which three, and what did none of them manage to build? Apart from the Marathas, there were three more Rebel States in the 18th century: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, and the two Afghan kingdoms, Farrukhabad (est. 1714) and Rohilkhand (crystallised 1737-40). All three used the opportunity created by the weakening Mughal Empire to convert local military power into territorial rule, but none could establish a large, sustainable empire.

Because harsh land revenue and lost autonomy angered the Zamindars, the first rebel State grew from the soil. Ask: which two names did the teacher mark imp, and why? 3.1 Who were the Jats and why did they resist? The Jats were primarily an agrarian community of North India, with cultivation as their traditional occupation. Their hostility to the Mughal State stretched back to the reign of Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue policies and the Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed the Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, toward organised resistance. 3.2 How the resistance developed The first organised Jat revolt came in 1669 (teacher's slide: 1669-70), led by the Zamindar Gokla. The torch passed through Rajaram 89-00 to Churaman 95-21, then Badan Singh (1722-55, consolidation), then Surajmal 56-63, each pushing resistance further. Their preferred method was guerrilla warfare: fast, decentralised and hard for a large Mughal army to counter. The Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur, in East Rajasthan, south of Delhi, bordering the Mathura and Agra districts, was formally established by Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721). Like many rebel-state founders (Marathas, Sikhs), Churaman 95-21 turned peasant discontent over high land revenue into political and military power. Note the two names marked imp: Churaman 95-21 = establishment of the Jat kingdom; Surajmal 56-63 = the most powerful. The hostility is about LR (high land revenue) and ending local autonomy. Lohagarh Fort, Bharatpur: the Iron Fort, never conquered, even by the British, built by Maharaja Surajmal (1756-63) 3.3 Surajmal 56-63: the peak Under Maharaja Surajmal 56-63 the Jat State reached its peak. He built a strong, centralised State and forced the Mughal emperor to formally recognise him as an autonomous ruler (within the Mughal Empire). His reforms: 1. He recruited European soldiers to modernise his military. 2. He introduced a Mughal-style revenue system for administrative efficiency. 3. He removed relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism. At its peak the Jat State stretched from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal River to the Ganga, across present-day Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. After Surajmal 56-63's death in 1763 the Jat State collapsed. Panipat 1761: Surajmal 56-63 offered help to the Marathas before the Third Battle of Panipat, but the alliance could not be established because of differences on war strategy and tactics. Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla warfare, but the Maratha commander Sadasiv Rao Bhau disagreed. The Jats still sent essential supplies to the Marathas during the war. On the status row: "the same thing was accepted during Churaman 95-21 Jat" (recognition of an autonomous ruler within the Mughal Empire). On the Panipat row, the Maratha link: Alamgir II 54-59 was a puppet of the Marathas. On Reform 1: Mahadji Scindia 68-94's Campoo = Fauj-i-Hind is the same kind of modernisation (see Chapter 4). On Reform 3: the Mughal family's infighting (R vs R) is the contrast. Map: the Jat State at its peak (orange, Delhi in green) 3.4 Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant? Handout Diagram 1: the Jat Kingdom Though the kingdom was the result of peasant revolts, it was no peasant utopia. Land revenue remained high, and real power rested with Zamindars, not with the ryots. The Jat State replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against.

items.t: 4 · The Afghans: migration and the rise of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45
items.x: Because the Afghans were soldiers for hire, one of them once ruled Delhi himself. Ask: what did Sher Shah 40-45 learn from the Mughals, and what did he build in five years? The Afghans and the rise of Sher Shah Suri Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant? No peasant utopia 4.1 Who were the Afghans and what brought them to North India? Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economic conditions and political instability back home. In the military labour markets of North India they functioned largely as wandering warlords, skilled fighters available to whoever could pay. 4.2 Was there ever a moment when Afghans actually ruled Delhi? The story of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 is the story of all these Afghan migrants compressed into one life. His family, the Suris, a clan of the Pashtun tribe, had migrated from the Sur region of Afghanistan to India during the Lodi Sultanate in the late 15th century. His grandfather had received a small jagir in Sasaram (present-day Bihar) in service of the Lodi Sultans. Sher Shah 40-45, born Farid Khan around 1486 in Sasaram, grew up not in Afghanistan but in Bihar, as a second-generation Indian Afghan, a product of the North Indian military labour market. He served under various masters, rising through ability rather than birth. He served as an administrator under the Afghan governor of Bihar, then briefly under the Mughals after Babur 26-30 defeated the Lodis in 1526. During this Mughal service he closely studied Mughal administrative methods, knowledge he later turned against them. He built his power base in Bihar and Bengal and by 1540 had defeated Humayun 30-40, first reign) at the Battle of Kanauj, driving him into exile in Persia and seizing the throne of Delhi. Handout comparison: compare Suri with the Bangash Pathans of Farrukhabad (same Afghan migrant background, same military-labour-market entry), but a very different ceiling on what they could achieve, partly because the political window available to them was much narrower. The Suri family were Mansabdars in the Delhi Sultanate (Bihar). The Afghan markers on the board timeline: Suris 1540-55; Farrukhabad 1714; Rohilkhand 1737-40; Abdali 1748-61. 4.3 What Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 achieved in five years Administrative hierarchy Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Sub-district (Pargana) Akbar 56-05 later adopted it almost wholesale Grand Trunk Road Upgraded the Uttarapath connecting Bengal to the North-West Frontier Boosts economy and trade Dak Chowki A reliable postal-relay system "Like a relay race" The Rupiya A standardised (by weight and value) silver coin, the basis of Indian currency for centuries Important: the degree of trust between buyer and seller; standardisation needs a central authority Revenue Land surveys and a fair land revenue demand fixed directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman Zamindar Recorded in a Patta (with the ryot) and a Qubuliat (with the government): "head and tail," one document in two copies Handout: Suri was in a sense the first ruler to seriously attempt "administrative reform": streamlining the State machinery to make it efficient and fair. Unfortunately he had only five years. His successors could not hold together what he built. After his death in 1545 the Afghans fragmented again into competing warlord groups. The period 1540 to 1555, the Suri Interregnum, was a brief Afghan interruption of Mughal rule, ending when Humayun 30-40 recaptured Delhi in 1555 after the Battle of Sirhind and briefly restored Mughal authority before his death in 1556. Map: Sher Shah Suri's empire (Encyclopaedia Britannica map Mughal Empire 1526-1707; the green line is the boundary of the Suri empire, running from Bengal across north In Sher Shah Suri's tomb, Sasaram (Bihar): the red-sandstone mausoleum of the five-year Afghan ruler of Delhi, a domed mausoleum in the middle of a lake. The Suri empire's extent is similar to Babur 26-30's (1526-30) and to the Delhi Sultanate (1208-1526).

items.t: 5 · The 18th century: a new surge of Afghan migration
items.x: Because the Mughal State weakened again, a second Afghan wave came. Ask: which two Afghan kingdoms emerged, and which clan founded each? The 18th century brought a new surge of Afghan migration as political instability in their homeland intensified. The progressive weakening of the Mughal State created exactly the opportunity these groups had been waiting for. Two Afghan kingdoms emerged: Farrukhabad (today a district in Uttar Pradesh; Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (also called Rampur, with capital Bareilly; Rohilla Afghans). Map: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand Afghan kingdoms within the Mughal Empire (Article 370-type status): Farrukhabad (Bangash Pathans), 1714-43, Md Khan Bangash. Rohilkhand (Rohillas), 1721-48, Ali Md Khan, with 1737-40 boxed as the period when the Marathas and Nadir Shah weakened the Mughals. Mughal interests: territory does not shrink; military and money. Rebels' interest: dynastic rule over some territory. Factionalism (R vs R): Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother; Farrukhsiyar 13-19 killed Jahandar Shah 12-13. Both kingdoms supported Abdali at Panipat (1761); Awadh annexed both.

Because court politics left vacuums, a warlord with troops could buy a title. Ask: what did Md Khan Bangash get, and who swallowed his son's kingdom? 6.1 How did a Bangash Pathan warlord found a kingdom near Agra? The founding of Farrukhabad shows how factional Mughal court politics created vacuums that outsiders could exploit. It was structurally weak from the start, sitting between powerful neighbours, principally Awadh, which preyed on it whenever it could. Its history is best understood as a sequence across three rulers. Md Khan Bangash (1714-43) A Pathan warlord who backed Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops; rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue assignments near the Ganga; founded Farrukhabad (1714), naming it after the emperor. Died 1743, succeeded by his son Qaim Khan. Qaim Khan (1743-49) In 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 (Nawab of Awadh and Wazir of the emperor) engineered his death in battle; Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered. Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 Retook it in 1750; driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas and Jats; fought beside Abdali at Panipat (1761) to recover it; the EIC annexed it in 1802. The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated. Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19: the handout (section 4.2) says that in 1712-13 Jahandar Shah 12-13 seized power by killing the father of Farrukhsiyar 13-19, and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 avenged this by removing Jahandar Shah 12-13; the teacher's board says Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother. Both are in the class material; the point for answers is Mughal succession violence (R vs R). Md Khan Bangash's gesture (handout): he first founded a town called Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Farrukhabad ("the city of Farrukh") was the diplomatic correction: the classic pattern of a rebel State acknowledging Mughal sovereignty in name while building real autonomy on the ground. Reading the rows: Nawab = a mansabdar rank; the revenue near the Ganga = a Jagir; the Mughal followed the "mid path." After Safdar Jung 39-54's misuse of the Wazir's post, other Mansabdars accused him of misusing his position and he was forced to resign, which was the virtual break of Awadh from the Mughal empire (see Chapter 3). Qaim Khan (handout): the textbook example of the Wazir's loyalty being to his own State, not the Emperor he nominally served; the highest Mughal Mansab had become a tool for personal and regional ambition. 6.2 Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750 onwards Ahmad Khan fought back and retook Farrukhabad in 1750. In 1751-52 the Marathas, specifically Malhar Rao Holkar and Jayappaji Rao Scindia sent by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao 40-61, along with Jats under Surajmal 56-63, drove him out. (Note: Awadh had requested the Marathas and Jats in 1751.) As Abdali's invasion progressed, the Marathas signed a treaty in 1752 that allowed him to return and resume rule, at the price of handing half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 at the Third Battle of Panipat. With the Marathas defeated, he recovered his full dominions, including the half ceded in 1752. Once Abdali left India in 1761, Farrukhabad weakened. In 1802 the EIC annexed Farrukhabad. (The "Ceded Provinces" refers to territories Awadh was forced to hand over under the Subsidiary Alliance of 1801; Farrukhabad was merged into the Ceded Provinces after annexation.) The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated. Flag on Ahmad Khan's dates: the handout's heading reads "Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750-1802", and in the Panipat line-up (Chapter 4) it writes Ahmad Khan 50-82. The slide table reads 1750-1802. The class material is not consistent about the short form (50-71 or 50-82), so remember the anchor dates: retook Farrukhabad 1750; EIC annexed it 1802.

Because Nadir Shah paralysed Delhi in 1739, a slow ground-level builder could finally declare independence. Ask: how did the Mughals respond to what they could not defeat? 7.1 How Afghan mercenaries became rulers The region that became Rohilkhand was originally called Katehr: western Uttar Pradesh, around Bareilly and Moradabad. In the 17th and early 18th century, as Mughal authority weakened, local Zamindars and regional governors in Katehr hired Afghan mercenaries to settle disputes and enforce authority. These Afghan fighters, called Rohillas, became a dominant armed presence. Note: Rohilkhand was formed by settled Afghan mercenaries consolidating power from within the region, already entrenched in Katehr long before Abdali entered India. The word "Rohilla" comes from "Roh," the Afghan homeland, so Rohilkhand means the land of the Rohillas. 7.2 1721: the starting point When Daud Khan, the Afghan commander who had consolidated the mercenary groups, died in 1721, his adopted son and protege Ali Md Khan (1721-48) took over leadership. This is the starting point, not yet an independent State, but the moment one man gained control of a significant armed force. After 1721 he moved methodically: for two decades he consolidated, slowly absorbing lands from the very Zamindars his men had been hired to protect and uniting the scattered Afghan groups under his sole command. 7.3 What finally pushed Ali Md Khan to declare independence? Nadir Shah's devastating invasion of Delhi in 1739. With the Mughal State paralysed, Ali Md Khan stopped paying taxes to Delhi and began ruling Katehr as an independent power, capturing key districts including Bareilly and Moradabad. Handout comparison with Farrukhabad: both Afghan kingdoms used the same window (Mughal paralysis) to convert military presence into territorial control. Md Khan Bangash did it earlier and more formally through Mughal court politics; Ali Md Khan did it through slow ground-level consolidation followed by outright defiance during the 1739 crisis. 7.4 How the Mughals responded Too weak to crush him, the Mughal State fell back on its standard strategy: co-opt what you cannot defeat. In 1740 Emperor Md Shah (1719-48) formally granted Ali Md Khan the title of Subadar. From 1740 Katehr was officially renamed Rohilkhand and functioned as an autonomous State under nominal Mughal sovereignty. (Ali Md Khan took control in 1721 but was officially recognised as Nawab of Rohilkhand by the Mughals in 1740.) The title gave the rebel legitimacy; it gave the Mughals the illusion of control. Both sides understood the fiction. 7.5 How Rohilkhand ended The arc is the same as Farrukhabad: rise on Afghan military power, peak during the Abdali alliance, collapse once that external prop was removed. 1761: under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, Rohilkhand actively supported Abdali at the Third Battle of Panipat. 1761-71: Delhi was effectively under Rohilla influence (the Mughal emperor was in Awadh). 1770: Najib dies; with no Abdali to support since 1761, Rohilkhand weakens. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi and allowed Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 to return home (the Red Fort). 1774: Most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help, because of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), which led to a military alliance. The rest, a small part, became the autonomous State of Rampur with capital Bareilly, legally under Awadh, and from 1801 under the EIC when Awadh gave half of Awadh in the Subsidiary Alliance.

items.t: 8 · Why Abdali came: the immediate trigger
items.x: Because both Afghan kingdoms backed Abdali at Panipat, we ask why he came at all. Ask: why is 'the expulsion of Timur Shah' the answer and Maratha expansion not? Prelims 2010. Abdali's immediate reason for the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) was to avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. In March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah (Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir); the Marathas appointed Adina Beg Khan as Governor of Punjab for an annual tribute of Rs 75 lakh, and on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge. Sabaji Scindia commanded the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar (on the Afghan border) and fiercely defended them against Abdali. The Maratha conquest of Punjab from the Afghans was a direct challenge Abdali could not ignore: that was the immediate trigger. Link to the previous lecture: the practice of auctioning an office (e.g. a governorship) is what the Marathas did with Punjab (Adina Beg Khan paid Rs 75 lakh a year as tribute). The famous phrase marking Maratha reach: "Attock se Cuttack" (Orissa).

items.t: 9 · Synthesis: three Rebel States, one pattern
items.x: Because each story had the same shape, the teacher joins them. Ask: what was the prop in each case, and what happened when it was removed? The Jats From an agrarian base upward: Zamindar-led revolt, then territory, then a reforming ruler (Surajmal 56-63) Farrukhabad From Mughal court politics downward: 12,000 troops for Farrukhsiyar 13-19, then a Nawab title, then a city, then a dynasty Rohilkhand From the ground up over two decades: hired mercenaries, then consolidation, then independence in the 1739 Delhi paralysis The common rule Each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63), and each collapsed once that support was removed How a Rebel State was built (the pattern) Opportunity: the Mughal Empire weakens, factional court politics or paralysis (1739) creates a vacuum Local military power: peasant Zamindars (Jats), Afghan mercenaries (Rohillas), a warlord with troops (Bangash) The middle path: accept Mansabdar status, Mughal sovereignty in name, tribute and troops; get dynastic governorship and a Watan Jagir Dependence: each needed external support to peak (Abdali; Maratha tactical backing) Collapse: support removed (1761 Abdali leaves; 1763 Surajmal 56-63 dies), neighbours annex (Awadh, then the EIC) Founder and year Churaman 95-21, 1695 Md Khan Bangash, 1714 Ali Md Khan, 1721 (recognised 1740) Base Agrarian Zamindars, peasant discontent over LR Pathan warlord with 12,000 troops, court politics Afghan mercenaries hired in Katehr Peak Surajmal 56-63, 1756-63 Ahmad Khan with Abdali, 1761 Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, 1761-71 (Delhi influence) Collapse 1763, Surajmal 56-63 dies 1749 annexed by Awadh; 1802 EIC 1774 Awadh plus EIC; Rampur remains

1486 Farid Khan (Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45) born at Sasaram (around) 1526 Babur 26-30 defeats the Lodis; Suri serves the Mughals 1540 Battle of Kanauj: Sher Shah 40-45 defeats Humayun 30-40, takes Delhi ★ 1545 Sher Shah 40-45 dies; Suri Interregnum (1540-55) continues 1555 Humayun 30-40 retakes Delhi after the Battle of Sirhind 1605 Jahangir 05-27's reign begins (Jat hostility traced from here) 1669 Gokla leads the first organised Jat revolt 1695 Churaman 95-21 founds the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur ★ 1714 Md Khan Bangash founds Farrukhabad ★ 1721 Daud Khan dies; Ali Md Khan takes over Katehr 1722 Badan Singh consolidates the Jat State 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi; Ali Md Khan stops paying taxes 1740 Md Shah grants Ali Md Khan the Subadar title; Rohilkhand ★ 1743 Md Khan Bangash dies; Qaim Khan 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 engineers Qaim Khan's death; Farrukhabad annexed to Awadh 1750 Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 retakes Farrukhabad 1751 Marathas and Jats drive Ahmad Khan out (to 1752) 1756 Surajmal 56-63's reign begins 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 expels Timur Shah from Lahore ★ 1761 Third Panipat: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand back Abdali ★ 1763 Surajmal 56-63 dies; the Jat State collapses 1765 Treaty of Allahabad (Awadh-EIC military alliance) 1770 Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 dies 1771 Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes Delhi 1774 Awadh with EIC help annexes most of Rohilkhand; Rampur remains 1801 Awadh's Subsidiary Alliance; Rampur under the EIC 1802 EIC annexes Farrukhabad 1857 Bangash Pathans join the Revolt

Two bad options and a middle path. When rebels establish their rule in an area, the emperor can fight on and end the rebellion, or lose the territory and let the rebel set up an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts Mansabdar status, the Mughal as emperor, tribute to Delhi and a duty to maintain an army and help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference. Both core interests are met; only the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once, in 1707), stand outside. Three more Rebel States. Apart from the Marathas, the 18th century saw three more: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, Farrukhabad (est. 1714, Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (process began 1721, completed 1737-40, Rohilla Afghans). All three turned local military power into territorial rule as the Mughal Empire weakened, yet none built a large, sustainable empire. The Jats rise from the soil. The Jats were an agrarian community, hostile to the Mughals since Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue and the drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed their Zamindars into organised resistance, mainly by guerrilla warfare. The chain runs Gokla (first revolt, 1669), Rajaram 89-00, Churaman 95-21, who formally founds the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in 1695, and Badan Singh (1722-55), who consolidates it. Surajmal's peak, and the fall. Surajmal 56-63 builds a strong, centralised State and forces the Mughal emperor to recognise him as autonomous. He recruits European soldiers, introduces a Mughal-style revenue system and removes relatives from court posts; the State stretches from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal to the Ganga, with the Iron Fort Lohagarh as his pride. At Panipat 1761 he wanted guerrilla warfare, Sadasiv Rao Bhau did not, yet the Jats still sent supplies. After he dies in 1763 the State collapses: it was no peasant utopia, since land revenue stayed high and power stayed with Zamindars. The Afghan who ruled Delhi. Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economy and instability at home, and worked as wandering warlords in its military labour markets. Farid Khan, born around 1486 at Sasaram in Bihar to the Sur clan, rises through ability, serves the Mughals after 1526 and studies their administration. By 1540, as Sher Shah 40-45, he defeats Humayun 30-40 at Kanauj and seizes Delhi. Five years that mattered (1540-45). Sher Shah 40-45 builds the Suba-Sarkar-Pargana hierarchy (Akbar 56-05 later adopts it), upgrades the Uttarapath into the Grand Trunk Road, sets up the Dak Chowki relay post, issues the standard silver Rupiya and fixes a fair land revenue directly with the peasant, recorded in a Patta and a Qubuliat. After he dies in 1545 the Afghans fragment; the Suri Interregnum (1540-55) ends when Humayun 30-40 retakes Delhi after Sirhind in 1555. Farrukhabad: a warlord and a flattering name. Md Khan Bangash, a Pathan warlord, backs Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops and is rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue near the Ganga; he founds Farrukhabad in 1714, after first naming a town Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed the emperor. His son Qaim Khan is killed in 1749 through the scheme of Safdar Jung 39-54, and Farrukhabad is annexed to Awadh and plundered. Ahmad Khan's see-saw. Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71 retakes Farrukhabad in 1750, is driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas (Holkar and Scindia) and Jats at Awadh's request, and returns by a treaty that hands half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fights beside Abdali 47-72 at Third Panipat and recovers his full dominions. The EIC annexes Farrukhabad in 1802. Rohilkhand: hired guns become rulers. Zamindars of Katehr (around Bareilly and Moradabad) hire Afghan mercenaries, the Rohillas, who grow dominant under Daud Khan. When he dies in 1721 his adopted son Ali Md Khan takes over and spends two decades absorbing lands. In 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi, so Ali stops paying taxes; in 1740 Md Shah 19-48 co-opts him with the Subadar title and Katehr is renamed Rohilkhand. The end of Rohilkhand. Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 backs Abdali at Panipat in 1761 and Delhi is under Rohilla influence until 1771, when Mahadji Scindia 68-94 retakes it. Najib dies in 1770; in 1774 Awadh, with EIC help (allies since the Treaty of Allahabad 1765), annexes most of Rohilkhand. A small remainder becomes the State of Rampur, under the EIC from 1801. Why Abdali came (Prelims 2010). In March 1758 Raghunath Rao 73-74 crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah, Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir. The Marathas made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year, and later Sabaji Scindia held Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border. The immediate reason for Third Panipat was to avenge Timur Shah. One pattern, one prop. The Jats rose from an agrarian base upward, Farrukhabad from court politics downward, Rohilkhand from the ground up over two decades. The common rule: each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghan kingdoms, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal 56-63) and each collapsed once that support was removed: Abdali left in 1761 and Surajmal died in 1763.

items.t: 1 · How did Sikhism begin, and what were its core beliefs?
items.x: Chapter 1 of the story: a peaceful faith with four ideas. Ask: what did Nanak teach that a State could not tolerate? Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539) was a contemporary of Babur 26-30. Sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on four core principles: 1. One supreme and formless God. 2. Direct access to God without rituals or priests. 3. Rejection of the caste system. 4. Emphasis on honest living and selfless service. Guru Nanak undertook four major spiritual journeys (Udasis) over 30 years, covering about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. He finally settled in Kartarpur (present-day Pakistan), where he established the Langar, the free communal kitchen designed to promote equality.

items.t: 2 · When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State?
items.x: Because the Sikhs began to demand a State at Anandpur, the Mughals struck twice. Ask: why does 1606 turn a movement martial? Initially there was no conflict. But as the Sikh population grew and Sikhs began demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla and south of Chamba), an area under the Shivalik Hill Chiefs who were Mughal allies, religious and political tensions built up. First flashpoint, 1606: the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, was executed by Jahangir 05-27. A turning point: a peaceful spiritual movement began its transformation into a martial community. Second flashpoint, 1675: the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, was executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07.

Because two Gurus were killed, the tenth Guru built an army. Ask: why is it compared to NSG or STF? In 1699, at Anandpur, the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, established the Khalsa, a Sikh military organisation created to defend the Sikh Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. The handout compares it to an NSG/STF: its creation marked the formal militarisation of the Sikh community's political ambitions.

items.t: 4 · December 1704 to October 1708: the Sahibzadas and the Guru's death
items.x: Because the Khalsa threatened the Mughal order, the Guru's family paid. Ask: who promised, and who broke the promise? December 1704, Battle of Chamkaur: the Guru's two elder sons, Sahibzada Ajit Singh (aged 18) and Sahibzada Jujhar Singh (aged 14), died in battle. The same month his two younger sons, Sahibzada Zorawar Singh (aged 9) and Sahibzada Fateh Singh (aged 6), were buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, the Mughal Faujdar of Sirhind. (A Faujdar = a district military commander, comparable in local authority to a Superintendent of Police today. Since 2022, 26 December is observed as Veer Bal Divas in memory of the younger Sahibzadas.) 1707: the new emperor Bahadur Shah (1707-12), following the pacifist policy (diplomacy more than war), granted the Guru a high Mansab and promised a Sikh State in and around Anandpur. The promise was never fulfilled. 7 October 1708: Wazir Khan arranged assassins to attack the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib Gurdwara in Nanded, Maharashtra, where he had accompanied Bahadur Shah. The Guru killed the assassins himself but later succumbed to his injuries, dying at the age of 42. No action was taken against Wazir Khan; Anandpur was never given to the Sikhs. Teacher's board: 1707, Aurangzeb 58-07 dies, leading to the Mughal pacifist policy of 1707 (better relations with rivals) 1707: Aurangzeb 58-07 dies, and the Mughal pacifist policy follows: "better relations with rivals." Implementation for the Guru: a very high Mansab [Zat] and Anandpur promised (an Article 370-like status, like Rohilkhand, Jats, Farrukhabad, the Marathas under Shahu 19-49, Mysore, Rajputs). 1708: in Nanded the Guru is killed by men sent by Wazir Khan [Faujdar of Sirhind], who was also responsible for the death of the Guru's four sons. Wazir Khan was not punished by the Mughals; Anandpur was not given. (Compare the same pacifist-policy argument in Chapter 4, section 5.)

items.t: 5 · Why the Guru declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru
items.x: Because a living successor could inflame Jats against Khatris, the Guru chose a Book. Ask: why is a Book neutral? Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) and the Akal Takht, Amritsar: the spiritual and temporal seats of the Sikh community A few days before his death, at Abchal Nagar Sahib, Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 declared that he would be the last living Guru and that all spiritual authority would henceforth be vested in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the holy book he had compiled. The decision was deliberate: to prevent community tensions between the Jat community, which dominated the Khalsa, and the Khatri community of traders, to which all ten Gurus had belonged. By vesting authority in the holy book rather than a human successor, the question of community dominance was permanently closed. The Guru Granth Sahib Ji was installed at the Akal Takht in the Golden Temple complex, Amritsar. From the Akal Takht the Gurus issued Hukumnamas (formal orders) and Sikh warriors took blessings before going into battle against the Mughals. The 19th-century sects of Nirankaris and Namdharis believe in a living Guru, which has historically led to serious conflicts within the community. Teacher's board: Guru Gobind Singh declared himself the last Guru and all (spiritual) authority was vested in the Guru Granth Sahib (two parts: the Holy Book; the Guru it The Guru Granth Sahib has two aspects: the Holy Book and the Guru itself. Disrespect = Beadbi (very sensitive today also). Jats dominated the Khalsa; Khatris were the men of money (merchants, moneylenders, ijaradars) ([*Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari in Punjab and Bengal]); all the Gurus were Khatris. The teacher's ink places Banda Bahadur 08-15's small state "in and around Patiala", which takes revenge by executing Wazir Khan.

items.t: 6 · Banda Bahadur 08-15: the first Sikh State, and why it collapsed
items.x: Because the Guru was dead, Banda took revenge and built a State. Ask: what makes a State real (coins, officials, seal)? From 1708 the rebellion was carried forward by Banda Bahadur 08-15. He defeated and killed Wazir Khan at the Battle of Chappar Chiri on 10 May 1710, which also led to the conquest of Sirhind. He established a Sikh State over territories between the River Ravi and the River Jamuna, with its own coins, its own officials and its own seal for administrative orders (the teacher's ink: full independence). Farrukhsiyar 13-19 appointed Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress this Sikh State. By 1715 Banda Bahadur 08-15 was defeated; captured and executed in Delhi in 1716 by Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Flag on the territory: the handout places Banda's State between the Ravi and the Jamuna; the teacher's ink on the board says "a small state in and around Patiala." Both appear in the class material; the handout's wording is the answer-writing one. Why his State fell (three reasons): 1. Khatri traders turned against him. Constant warfare hurt trade, and the commercial class needs decisive victors and political stability to function. 2. Divide and rule. Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari (the revenue-farming system) in Punjab specifically to co-opt Khatri traders with business opportunities. Both Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered Mansabs to Khatri traders, who switched sides. (Note: this further increased the number of Mansabdars, adding to the Jagirdari Crisis; see Chapter 2.) 3. Hindu Jat zamindars switched sides. Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721), for instance, went over to the Mughals after they recognised his Jat Kingdom, granting him conditional dynastic autonomy in exchange for loyalty. Teacher's board: why Banda Bahadur 08-15 lost? Khatris stopped supporting him [Z = money]; Churaman Jat ditto [guns and military], co-opted by accepting a Jat kingdom wit Khatris stopped supporting him (money); Churaman 95-21 Jat likewise (guns / military), co-opted by accepting a Jat kingdom within the Mughal empire. The Khatris wanted peace because trade was hurt by constant wars, so they chose the stronger side. Banda Bahadur 08-15 was not a Guru, so he lacked the Gurus' authority. Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari in Punjab and Bengal (a business opportunity), and Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 made Khatris Mansabdars. The general rule (double-starred): when a personality weakens, power leaves (downward or sideways), and factionalism rises (Khatris against Banda Bahadur 08-15).

items.t: 7 · What kept the Sikh State alive: the Misl confederacy
items.x: Because Banda fell but the Mughals were weak, power spread to Misl chiefs. Ask: is a confederacy strength or weakness? The defeat of Banda Bahadur 08-15 did not end the Sikh State. The Mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab, and power became decentralised among Misl Chiefs. Misls are kinship-based clans. They united during wars, particularly against Afghan invasions, but otherwise operated independently. Whenever a Misl conquered territory, the lands were distributed among its members in proportion to their military and monetary contribution. Even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share of land. By 1770 there were 12 major Misls in Punjab, with the Dal Khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the Misl chiefs: a confederacy structure with a weak centre and strong constituent units. Takeaway (handout): compare it to the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, where a nominal centre held together largely autonomous regional chiefs. Decentralisation was both a source of resilience and, ultimately, a vulnerability. Teacher's board: misl confederacy The death of Banda Bahadur 08-15 left no strong centre, so power decentralised to the misl chiefs. Polity structure: a Confederacy (of misls); fragmented. The board's sketch shows one big circle (Punjab) with about a dozen circles inside (misls), "roughly 40-60 misls" (the handout's formal count is 12 major Misls by 1770). The Dal Khalsa = the assembly of misl chiefs: e.g. on Abdali's 1748 invasion the Dal Khalsa will meet and prepare a joint defence, e.g. Manupur 1748, where Abdali was defeated (see Chapter 4). Teacher's board: fragmented polity PYQ PYQ (UPSC Mains): "By the mid-18th century India was a spectre of fragmented polity." State PCS FYQ: "By 1715 Punjab was a spectre of fragmented polity." In today's language this is a weak centre, as with coalition governments at the Centre: factionalism, instability, shorter tenures, a weak PM. Teacher's board: nature of power "It is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality." The board's wave diagram shows power cycling between centralised and fragmented; the teacher marks "today" at a trough and links it to (PSIR) terms: multi-polar world, balance of power, fragmented world order, confederalism.

Because power gathers in a strong personality, Ranjit Singh 01-39 unifies the Misls. Ask: which crisis became his opportunity? Maharaja Ranjit Singh (01-39): a painted portrait of a white-bearded man in a turban with a jewel, yellow coat, seated holding a sword Ranjit Singh 01-39 of the Sukerchakia Misl played a crucial role in defeating Zaman Shah's third Afghan invasion of 1799 (the slide reads: he rose during Zaman Shah's Afghan invasions of 1796-1799). This gave him the platform to establish dominance over the other Misls, and he was coronated King (Maharaja) of the Sikh State in 1801. The other Misl chiefs were reduced to tribute-paying vassals, retaining conditional control of their lands in return for loyalty and tribute to the King (the teacher's ink: lands held as Jagirs, not Watan). Zaman Shah (Abdali's successor) invaded: "crisis = opportunity." The Sukerchakia misl of Ranjit Singh 01-39 emerged the most powerful. 1801: coronation. 1809: the Treaty of Amritsar made the Sutlej the border with the Company State (British India) and brought a military alliance with the EIC. The Misl chiefs' lands: Jagirs, not Watan. 8.1 Territorial expansion: rapid and systematic Handout Diagram 3: Ranjit Singh's expansion and administration 1. 1801: conquered Lahore (handout list); the slides place the capture of Lahore in 1799 from the Bhangi Misl. 2. 1808: conquered Jammu from the Dogras (the handout adds: in 1819 he returned Jammu to the Dogras but within the Sikh Empire: the Dogras became vassals; the slide adds: Jammu later granted as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820, and his son Gulab Singh formally made Raja of Jammu in 1822). 3. 1809: the handout lists "conquered the whole of Punjab" as the third step; the slide reads: "signed the Treaty of Amritsar ... secured his eastern frontier." Flags on the Ranjit Singh 01-39 dates: the handout gives Lahore 1801 and Jammu returned to the Dogras in 1819; the slides give Lahore 1799 (captured from the Bhangi Misl) and Jammu given as a jagir to Kishore Singh in 1820 and Gulab Singh made Raja in 1822. Also, the handout says Zaman Shah's third invasion of 1799, the slide says the invasions of 1796-1799. For answers, anchor on: coronation 1801; Treaty of Amritsar 1809; Multan 1818; Kashmir 1819; Peshawar 1834; Tripartite Treaty 1838.

Because he now borders the EIC, he settles the frontier. Ask: what did he gain, and which way did he then expand? In 1809 Ranjit Singh 01-39 signed the Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC, represented by Charles Metcalfe, the EIC's Resident in the Delhi court. (Recall that the Scindias had been removed from Delhi in 1803 and the EIC had set up indirect rule there through a British Resident.) Four outcomes: 1. The EIC recognised Ranjit Singh 01-39 as the sovereign ruler of Punjab. 2. It led to a military alliance (later link to the EIC's Policy of Ring Fence). 3. The Sutlej River was fixed as the border between the Sikh State and the Company State. 4. Ranjit Singh 01-39 was free to expand on his side of the Sutlej without British interference. Map of Punjab (districts, rivers Ravi, Beas, Sutlej; Amritsar, Gurdaspur, Hoshiarpur, Jalandhar, Kapurthala, Nawanshahr, Rupnagar, Chandigarh, Firozpur, Moga, Faridkot, L On the Punjab map: north of the Sutlej = Ranjit Singh 01-39 (RJ 01-39); south of the Sutlej = the EIC.

items.t: 10 · How far did Ranjit Singh 01-39 expand after 1809?
items.x: Because the east was secured, he turned west and north. Ask: which conquest completed what the Marathas left unfinished? With his eastern border secured, Ranjit Singh 01-39 turned west and north: 1. 1818: removed the Afghans from Multan. 2. 1819: conquered Kashmir. (Recall that Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 captured Punjab and Kashmir; Punjab was taken back by the Marathas in 1758 but not Kashmir; Ranjit Singh 01-39 completed what the Marathas left unfinished.) 3. 1834: conquered Peshawar (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, bordering Afghanistan along the Durand Line). Peshawar was conquered by Hari Singh Nalwa, whose reputation was so fearsome that Afghan mothers used his name to frighten unruly children: "If you don't stop crying, Haria Ragle will turn up." 10.1 The 1838 Tripartite Treaty In 1838 Ranjit Singh 01-39 signed the Tripartite Treaty between the Sikh State, the EIC and Shah Shuja of Afghanistan. The design: to establish British indirect rule in Afghanistan through Shah Shuja as a puppet ruler. The aim: to create a buffer of Afghanistan and Punjab against the feared Russian invasion of British India from the north-west. British fear of Russia: the chain drawn on the board is Russia, then Afghanistan, then the Khyber Pass, then the Sikh State, then the Company State (British India). Afghanistan and Punjab are the buffer. The 1838 Tripartite Treaty

items.t: 11 · What kind of State did Ranjit Singh 01-39 build?
items.x: Last scene: how did he hold it together? Ask: which four groups did he balance, and what did the Kardar do? How power was built Coercion, diplomacy and careful balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles such as the Dogras (similar to the successor States) Character Militarily strong and economically prosperous Revenue policy Fair for the masses; trade flourished; a strong State delivered law and order Land Only 40% of land under the Jagirdari system; from the rest revenue went directly to the King Kardar Main income source LR collected by Kardars, the chief administrative officer at the Taluqa (district) level: revenue collector, local magistrate (judge), police chief and customs officer Ijaradari Relied on Ijaradari: instead of a fixed cash salary a Kardar often acted as an Ijaradar, but it was ensured the ryot was not oppressed by very high LR Village autonomy State authority stopped at the village level; local chiefs and clans respected (connects to the Mahalwari Settlement in Punjab, where even the British respected village autonomy) Secular cabinet Fakir Azizuddin (Muslim) as Foreign Minister; Dewan Dina Nath (Hindu) as Finance Minister Culturally broad Sahajdhari (non-Khalsa) Sikhs included; they do not keep the five Ks How Chapter 6 feeds UPSC. The chapter carries no mapped UPSC Prelims questions (1995-2025). It feeds two Mains answers, where Sikh-State facts are a supporting strand: Mains 2014: why were so many empire-shaking battles fought at Panipat? (see Chapter 4) and Mains 2017: the spectre of a fragmented polity in mid-18th-century India (the Misl confederacy is your Punjab example). From Guru Nanak to Ranjit Singh 01-39 Faith: Guru Nanak's formless God, anti-caste, Langar Two flashpoints: 1606 Arjan Dev, 1675 Teg Bahadur: a peaceful movement turns martial 1699 Khalsa: a military organisation for a Sikh State at Anandpur 1704-08: Sahibzadas killed, the promise of Anandpur broken, the Guru killed at Nanded; Guru Granth Sahib declared final Guru 1708-15 Banda Bahadur 08-15: a first Sikh State (Ravi to Jamuna) that falls when Khatris and Jats defect 1715-1801 Misls: confederacy of 12 major Misls with the Dal Khalsa 1801-39 Ranjit Singh 01-39: unified Sikh State, treaty with the EIC, expansion west and north Commercial class Khatri traders turned against him (trade hurt, co-opted by Ijaradari and Mansabs) Khatri traders balanced among the pillars of his State Landed groups Jat zamindars switched (Churaman 95-21 recognised) Misl chiefs as tribute-paying vassals; Dogras and local chiefs respected Centre No Guru authority; Mughals' Governor of Lahore sent against him Strong king: coronation 1801, treaty with the EIC 1809 Outcome Captured 1715, executed 1716 Prosperous State, expansion to Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar
