A peaceful faith. Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), a contemporary of Babur 26-30, teaches four things: one formless God, direct access without rituals or priests, no caste, honest living and selfless service. He makes four Udasis over 30 years (about 30,000 km), then settles at Kartarpur and starts the Langar, a free kitchen for equality. Territory, and the first blow (1606). The teacher says a State is an organisation with a territory motive, and until the Sikhs wanted territory there was no dispute. They begin demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla, south of Chamba), land held by Shivalik hill chiefs who are Mughal allies. In 1606 Jahangir 05-27 executes the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, and a peaceful movement starts turning martial. The Khalsa (1675-1699). In 1675 Aurangzeb 58-07 has the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, executed in Delhi. In 1699 the 10th Guru, Gobind Singh 76-08, founds the Khalsa at Anandpur: a Sikh military organisation, something like an NSG or STF, to defend the Panth and struggle for a Sikh State. Its identity is the five Ks. The Sahibzadas and a broken promise (1704-1707). In December 1704 the two elder sons, Ajit Singh (18) and Jujhar Singh (14), die at Chamkaur. The same month the two younger, Zorawar Singh (9) and Fateh Singh (6), are buried alive in a wall on the orders of Wazir Khan, Faujdar of Sirhind. In 1707 Bahadur Shah 07-12, on a pacifist policy, gives the Guru a high Mansab and promises Anandpur, but never keeps it. Nanded and the Book (1708). On 7 October 1708 Wazir Khan's assassins strike the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib in Nanded; he kills them but dies of his injuries at 42, and Wazir Khan is not punished. A few days before, he had declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru, to stop Jat versus Khatri tension: Jats dominated the Khalsa and all ten Gurus were Khatri traders. The Book was installed at the Akal Takht. Banda Bahadur 08-15's State. From 1708 Banda Bahadur 08-15 carries on. On 10 May 1710 at Chappar Chiri he kills Wazir Khan and takes Sirhind. His State between the Ravi and the Jamuna has its own coins, officials and seal, which the teacher reads as full independence. Farrukhsiyar 13-19 sends Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore to crush it. Why it fell (1715-1716). The Khatri traders, hurt by constant war, turned away. Jahandar Shah 12-13 brought Ijaradari to Punjab to co-opt them, and he and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 offered them Mansabs. Hindu Jat zamindars switched too: Churaman 95-21 went over when the Mughals recognised his Jat Kingdom. Banda Bahadur 08-15 was also not a Guru. He was defeated in 1715 and executed in 1716. The Misl confederacy. The Mughals are too weak to take Punjab back, so power spreads to Misl chiefs: kinship clans that unite in wars, especially against Afghan invasions, and otherwise act alone. Conquered land is shared by contribution. By 1770 there are 12 major Misls with the Dal Khalsa at the centre; at Manupur 1748 it prepares a joint defence and Abdali is defeated. This is a weak centre, a fragmented polity, like the Maratha Confederacy. Ranjit Singh 01-39 centralises. Zaman Shah's invasions are a crisis that becomes an opportunity for Ranjit Singh 01-39 of the Sukerchakia Misl, who takes Lahore from the Bhangi Misl and is crowned Maharaja in 1801. The other Misl chiefs become tribute-paying vassals holding Jagirs, not Watan. The handout dates Lahore to 1801, the slides to 1799. Treaties and conquests (1809-1838). In 1809 Charles Metcalfe, the EIC's Resident at Delhi, signs the Treaty of Amritsar: Ranjit Singh 01-39 is recognised as sovereign, there is a military alliance, the Sutlej is the border, and he is free to expand on his side. He then takes Multan (1818), Kashmir (1819) and Peshawar (1834, Hari Singh Nalwa). The 1838 Tripartite Treaty with Shah Shuja makes Afghanistan and Punjab a buffer against feared Russian invasion. A balanced, secular State. Ranjit Singh 01-39 built power by coercion, diplomacy and balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles such as the Dogras. Only 40% of land was Jagirdari; the rest paid the King directly, collected by Kardars (collector, magistrate, police chief, customs officer). Village autonomy was respected, Fakir Azizuddin was Foreign Minister, Dewan Dina Nath Finance Minister, and Sahajdhari Sikhs were included.

Prelims 2001 Which Indian ruler established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? (d) Tipu 82-99 Sultan: embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, with new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. The distractors were Haider Ali 61-82, Mir Qasim 60-63 and Shah Alam II 60-06 Mysore: Tipu 82-99's innovations

Story so far: nothing yet. These three States stood outside the middle path of Mughal rule. Ask: which is Rajput, which southern, which grew from Vijayanagar? The teacher's note beside the title: [Part of the Vijayanagar empire, 1336-1646]. (Mysore's roots are in the Vijayanagar Empire; see section 6.) These are the third class of regional States from Chapter 3: Already Autonomous States, where even when the Mughal was powerful he did not rule. The Rajputs were brought into the Mughal system by Akbar 56-05 but kept their home territories; Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire; Mysore grew out of the Vijayanagar world.

Because Rajputana had no single centre and fighting all clans was costly, Akbar made a deal. Ask: what did each side get? Akbar 56-05 and the Rajputs 16th-century Rajputana No single central power; roughly 20 major Rajput clans, each controlling its own territory (in modern IR terms a multi-polar world: many power centres, no single dominant one) Akbar 56-05's approach Defeating all would be expensive and uncertain, so he co-opted the more powerful Rajput chiefs Mansabdars The chosen chiefs became ranked nobles with military and administrative responsibilities Vatan Jagirs Their home territories were recognised as Vatan Jagirs: the land remained theirs but within the Mughal framework Obligations Accepted the Mughal Emperor as sovereign, paid tributes, contributed troops Hindu bloc As a group they formed the Hindu bloc within the Mansabdari system (about 15% of all Mansabdars) In return Akbar 56-05 helped them subdue the smaller Rajput chiefs Result A partial consolidation of power The board's sketch: 20 clans numbered 1 to 20, with a few strong ones (Mewar, Marwar) swallowing the smaller: a partial (Centralization). The whole of Rajputana was never under one king (the crossed-out triangle/pyramid).

items.t: 2 · Rajputs against Aurangzeb 58-07, and the Marathas
items.x: Because the bargain rested on balance, Mewar's growth upset it. Ask: why did the 1680 revolt collapse? The 1680 Rajput revolt Mewar expands: under Raj Singh, aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states Aurangzeb 58-07 is uneasy: he did not want one Rajput power to dominate all Rajputana and rival the Mughals 1680, the trigger: a child comes to the throne in Marwar (astride the Delhi/Agra to Ahmedabad trade route); Aurangzeb 58-07 interferes in the succession Marwar and Mewar revolt The rebellion collapses: the other Rajput chiefs refuse to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them Rajputana after Aurangzeb 58-07: Marathas, then the EIC Handout Diagram 1 (Rajputs): 16th century Rajputana with about 20 major clans and no single centre (multi-polar world); Akbar co-opts powerful Rajput chiefs, who help sub This arrangement held through most of the 17th century. Trouble came under Aurangzeb 58-07. Mewar, under Raj Singh, had been expanding aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states; Aurangzeb 58-07 grew uneasy, not wanting one Rajput power to dominate Rajputana and rival the Mughal State. 1680: a child came to the throne in Marwar, a kingdom astride the important trade route connecting Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad. Aurangzeb 58-07 interfered in the succession: the trigger. Marwar and Mewar both revolted, but the revolt failed. The other Rajput chiefs refused to join, fearing that if the revolt succeeded Mewar would dominate them. After Aurangzeb 58-07's death in 1707 the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms. The most prominent figure was Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber, who ruled Jaipur and remained a powerful Mansabdar in Delhi, but on his own conditions. From 1751 the Marathas began regular raids into Rajputana, extracting tribute and interfering in succession disputes, but could never fully conquer the region. After the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the EIC replaced the Marathas as the regional power and signed Subordinate Alliances (also called Subsidiary Alliances) with the Rajput states. Subordinate Alliance is like World History's Protectorate: the Indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered control of foreign policy and defence to the EIC, which stationed its own troops, paid for by the Indian ruler. Under suzerainty = loss of external sovereign functions plus loss of symbolic sovereignty. The teacher's ink: "will do in future" (the Subsidiary Alliance is taken up in Chapter 11).

Because after 1707 the Rajputs acted on their own terms, one of them is worth knowing in detail. Ask: what are his four roles? "Sawai" A title (1.25 times more able than any contemporary ruler) conferred by Aurangzeb 58-07 Four roles at once Mughal Mansabdar, regional state-builder, astronomer and town planner Subedar Held the Subedari of Malwa (1729-37) and Agra (the teacher's ink: Governor) Hurda conference, 1734 A conference of Rajput rulers at Hurda to forge a united front against the Marathas; it collapsed due to internal Rajput rivalries Treaty of Bhopal 1738: Malwa annexed by the Marathas (the teacher: Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 = the Mughal Governor of Malwa) Jaipur founded, 1727 Designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya on Vastu Shastra principles, grid-pattern layout; the first planned city of modern India; Sawai Ram Singh painted it pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales Social reform Tried to curb dowry and excessive marriage expenditure among Rajputs; limited success Last Yajnas The last Indian ruler to perform the Ashvamedha and Vajapeya Yajnas: a conscious assertion of Hindu Chakravartin status as Mughal authority collapsed The teacher flags "astronomer and town planner" (arrows to Prelims), and marks Jaipur 1727, Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, grid-pattern layout, the first planned city, and the pink colour of 1876 for memorising. 3.1 The Jantar Mantars and astronomy Five observatories (Jantar Mantars) were built at Delhi (1724), Jaipur (1734), Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi. Jaipur's is the largest: a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2010). The Samrat Yantra there, the largest sundial in the world, could measure local time to an accuracy of 2 seconds. Astronomical tables tell where a celestial body (sun, moon, planet, star) will be at any given date and time. The existing tables, the Zij-i-Ulugh Begi (Islamic) and the Siddhantic (Hindu), had accumulated errors over centuries. The Jantar Mantars generated fresh observational data to correct them in the form of the Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (1733), dedicated to Muhammad Shah 19-48. He also sent a scientific delegation to Portugal (1730) and commissioned Sanskrit astronomical works. He chose stone instruments over brass for greater accuracy: Samrat Yantra Sundial for time Jai Prakash Yantra Celestial mapper Ram Yantra Altitude meter for the Sun's position

Because the Mughals never reached the far south, a small State could build itself on trade. Ask: where did the trade money go? Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire. The Mughal State simply never expanded far enough south to include it. By the 1740s, Marthanda Varma 29-58 had built a strong, centralised State by subjugating local chiefs across the region, and a European-style military: modern weapons, trained soldiers. Takeaway: Travancore established a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues were reinvested into the military, irrigation works and transport infrastructure: a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity. 4.1 Colachel 1741 and the fall of the Dutch Since 1663 The Dutch East India Company's Malabar headquarters at Cochin (central Kerala), captured from the Portuguese 1741 Battle of Colachel: a landmark in the history of Kerala; Marthanda Varma 29-58's army crushed the Dutch East India Company Effect Terminal: it permanently ended Dutch political and military ambitions in Kerala, reducing them to mere merchants in Cochin 1759 Battle of Bedara (also called Battle of Chinsura): the British EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in India 1795 Final expulsion from South Asia by the British (Ceylon / Sri Lanka)

items.t: 5 · Travancore against Mysore and the EIC
items.x: Because the military declined after Marthanda Varma, the neighbours and then the Company moved in. Ask: which year did Malabar go? Under Rama Varma 58-98 Travancore became a centre of art and scholarship, but military strength declined. The consequences were quick: in 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 of Mysore annexed Malabar and Calicut. (Malabar was the heart of the spice trade: pepper, cardamom, ginger. Whoever controlled Malabar's ports controlled a significant share of Indian Ocean commerce, which is why both Mysore and the British were so interested.) After 1798 Travancore came steadily under British influence. Travancore's loss of independence 1805 Nair mutiny: troops unpaid Travancore seeks British help In return it signs the Subsidiary Alliance (1805): independence effectively ends Anger: heavy financial burden and interference in internal affairs; Velu Thampi Dalawa leads resistance 1809 revolt: against the British Resident, Kundara Proclamation calls the people to rise Suppressed: Velu Thampi, seeing no escape, takes his own life A light note: Shashi Tharoor is from the Nair community. Dalawa meant Prime Minister and Chief of the Armed Forces, but books may use Dewan for the PM of a State subordinated by the British; as Dewan he was Head of all administration (revenue, civil, police, criminal justice), since the military was with the British. The handout adds: this was one of the earliest organised resistance movements by an Indian ruler against the Subsidiary Alliance system, and a directly tested topic in UPSC.

items.t: 6 · Mysore: from Vijayanagar to Haider Ali 61-82
items.x: Because Vijayanagar broke at Talikota, Mysore became autonomous, and a strongman took it over. Ask: how did Haider Ali rise? Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646). The Empire's effective power was shattered at the Battle of Talikota (also called Rakkasa-Tangadi) in 1565, when a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated Vijayanagar. The dynasty lingered until 1646, but 1565 marks the operational end of Vijayanagar as a major power. After Vijayanagar's decline Mysore gradually became autonomous under the Wodeyar dynasty. Under Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar (1672-1704) it was militarily powerful and centrally governed. By 1761 the Wodeyars had been reduced to figureheads by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj. Haider Ali 61-82 ended that. He began as a junior military officer, his early career made possible partly because the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts. Capable, ambitious and strategic, in 1761 he overthrew NanjRaj and seized effective power, keeping the Wodeyar as a nominal head of State. Pattern alert at the 18th century: the king becomes a puppet as personality weakens. Recall the Peshwa and Chhatrapati relationship (Chapter 4). 6.1 Haider Ali 61-82's military machine Haider Ali 61-82 took French assistance for military training, technology transfer and organisational reform. The army was now on a European model, organised into Risalas (regiments): Each Risala's commander was directly appointed by the King, ensuring personal loyalty upward. Each unit had a clear chain of command. Each was self-sufficient: its own weapons, transport and supplies (recall the Campoo system of Scindia, Chapter 4). Result: a fast, efficient military with regiments capable of independent action. He then spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars (local chiefs and landlords who controlled land, the wealth of temples and had their own armed men, the real rulers of the countryside since the Vijayanagar era) and the Deshmukhs (revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars). Non-State power was systematically dismantled. 6.2 How Mysore funded this machine: Military Fiscalism Khalisa land expanded More revenue went directly to the State treasury Jagirdari minimised Maximised State income, reducing the nobles' independent economic power Direct collection Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries; State officials collected taxes and got salaries (far smaller than commissions) Detailed field surveys Assessed LR by soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access and past production trends; prevented over-assessment Investing in agriculture Canals repaired and built; cash crops promoted; sericulture introduced Boosted tax collection More peasant income meant a larger tax base; even enemies admitted Mysore's population was among the most prosperous These policies are called Military Fiscalism: the systematic generation of State wealth as a foundation for military power. (The handout's analogy: replacing a commission-based agent with a salaried employee; the State kept far more of the revenue.) Khalisa land = land whose revenue went directly to the State treasury. Jagirdari land = land whose revenue was assigned to nobles or commanders.

items.t: 7 · Tipu 82-99 Sultan (1782-99): innovations and why he still lost
items.x: Because his father built the machine, Tipu took it abroad and also overreached. Ask: which innovation answers Prelims 2001? Modern navy and trading company: a government-owned trading company modelled on the EIC, trading in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk and cardamom, with 30 trading centres inside and outside India, including Muscat, Oman. (Before the age of machines a "factory" meant a warehouse or trading depot, not a production facility; a trading settlement meant warehouses, homes, offices and sometimes a fort. Details in Chapter 8.) Iron-cased rocket artillery: developed by Haider Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99, 100% indigenous, range 2 km; the iron cylinder casings did not burst and could take high pressure compared with cardboard-cased rockets (fireworks), which existed for centuries in India and China. The British studied them closely: William Congreve's rockets, deployed in the early 19th century, drew directly from Tipu 82-99's designs. 1785: Tipu 82-99 formally declared independence from both the Wodeyars and the Mughal Emperor, and requested a sanad from the Khalifa recognising him as independent of Mughal authority. Modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. 7.1 Tipu 82-99 and Revolutionary France In the 1790s Tipu 82-99 sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British. Since 1789 the French Revolution had set France on a collision course with the monarchies of Europe, including Britain (the 23-year wars, 1792-1815). In 1798 Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East, partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea. Tipu 82-99 exchanged communications with Napoleon and planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore (a symbol of the French Revolution), and joined the Jacobin Club. The alliance did not materialise into military support. The British were alarmed, and it became a reason for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. Prelims 2001: who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? Answer (d): Tipu 82-99 Sultan. He set up modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. The Jacobin membership and Tree of Liberty marked him in British eyes as an ideological adversary, not merely a military one. 7.2 Why Mysore lost Mysore's long-term ambition was to dominate all of South India and control its international trade (Vijayanagar 2.0). But constant warfare against neighbouring Indian powers and the EIC drained the State's resources faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish them. The ambition was real; the capacity, ultimately, was not enough. 1766: Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, triggering the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), as the EIC feared losing coastal trade access through Malabar. Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. The Fourth (1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam; Mysore's power was broken. Flag on Travancore: the handout's section 7 says that in 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 "had invaded Travancore and annexed Malabar and Calicut", while the same chapter (section 4) says he annexed Malabar and Calicut, and the teacher's bracket on the slide adds "could not successfully invade Travancore." Use the slide's wording: Malabar and Calicut were annexed; Travancore was not successfully invaded. Mysore's rise and fall Handout Diagram 3: Mysore's rise and the ambition-versus-capacity collapse 1761 Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj; the Wodeyar stays nominal French-assisted Risalas: self-sufficient regiments under commanders loyal to the King Military Fiscalism: Khalisa expanded, Deshmukhs removed, surveys, canals, sericulture: wealth for war Tipu 82-99: navy, government trading company, iron-cased rockets, 1785 independence, modern embassies, French link Overreach: ambition to dominate all South India (Vijayanagar 2.0); constant war drains the State faster than fiscalism refills it 1799: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu 82-99 dies at Seringapatam; Mysore's power broken Relation to the Mughals Co-opted by Akbar 56-05: Mansabdars with Vatan Jagirs; Hindu bloc (15%) Never part of the Mughal Empire Part of Vijayanagar, then autonomous under the Wodeyars Key figure Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 Marthanda Varma 29-58 Haider Ali 61-82, Tipu 82-99 Strength Astronomy, Jaipur, politics on own terms Trade monopoly, centralised State, Colachel 1741 Risalas, Military Fiscalism, rockets, trade company End Subordinate Alliances after 1803-05 Subsidiary Alliance 1805; revolt 1809 Four wars; Tipu 82-99 dies 1799

1336 Vijayanagar Empire begins (to 1646) 1565 Battle of Talikota: Deccan Sultanates defeat Vijayanagar ★ 1663 Dutch take Cochin from the Portuguese 1672 Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar (to 1704) makes Mysore powerful 1680 Marwar and Mewar revolt; it collapses ★ 1699 Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber (rule 1699-1743) 1724 Delhi Jantar Mantar built 1727 Jaipur founded ★ 1729 Marthanda Varma 29-58 begins (1729-58); Jai Singh 99-43 Subedar of Malwa (to 1737) 1733 Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi 1734 Hurda conference; Jaipur Jantar Mantar 1738 Treaty of Bhopal: Malwa passes to the Marathas 1741 Battle of Colachel: Travancore crushes the Dutch ★ 1751 Maratha raids on Rajputana begin 1759 Battle of Bedara (Chinsura): EIC defeats the Dutch in Bengal 1761 Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj ★ 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 annexes Malabar and Calicut 1767 First Anglo-Mysore War (to 1769) 1785 Tipu 82-99 declares independence; Khalifa sanad request 1795 Final Dutch expulsion from South Asia (Ceylon) 1798 Travancore comes under British influence 1799 Fourth Anglo-Mysore War: Tipu 82-99 dies at Seringapatam ★ 1805 Nair mutiny; Travancore signs Subsidiary Alliance ★ 1809 Velu Thampi revolt and Kundara Proclamation ★

Outside the middle path. These are the third class of regional States from Chapter 3: Already Autonomous States, where even when the Mughal was powerful he did not rule. The Rajputs were brought into the Mughal system but kept their homes, Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire, and Mysore grew out of the Vijayanagar world. Akbar's Rajput bargain. Rajputana had no single centre, only roughly 20 major clans (a multi-polar world). Defeating them all would be expensive and uncertain, so Akbar 56-05 co-opted the powerful chiefs as Mansabdars with Vatan Jagirs, and in return they accepted the Emperor, paid tribute and sent troops. They formed a Hindu bloc of about 15% of the Mansabdars, and Akbar helped them subdue smaller chiefs: a partial consolidation. 1680. Mewar under Raj Singh began expanding aggressively, and Aurangzeb 58-07 grew uneasy at one Rajput power dominating Rajputana. In 1680 a child came to the throne of Marwar, which lay astride the trade route from Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad, and Aurangzeb interfered. Marwar and Mewar revolted, but the other chiefs refused to join for fear of Mewar, and the revolt collapsed. Own terms, then new masters. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms, most prominently Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber. From 1751 the Marathas began regular raids for tribute but never fully conquered the region. After the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the EIC replaced them and signed Subordinate Alliances: the ruler keeps his throne but surrenders foreign policy and defence. Four hats. Sawai means 1.25 times more able than any contemporary ruler, a title from Aurangzeb 58-07. Jai Singh was a Mughal Mansabdar, state-builder, astronomer and town planner, Subedar of Malwa (1729-37) and Agra. His Hurda conference of 1734 collapsed, and the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) gave Malwa to the Marathas. He founded Jaipur in 1727 (Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, Vastu Shastra, grid, the first planned city of modern India), and was the last Indian ruler to perform the Ashvamedha and Vajapeya Yajnas. Stone and sky. Five Jantar Mantars stand at Delhi (1724), Jaipur (1734), Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi; Jaipur's is the largest, a UNESCO site (2010), and its Samrat Yantra measures time to 2 seconds. The old tables (Zij-i-Ulugh Begi, Siddhantic) had accumulated errors, so fresh observations gave the Zij-i-Muhammad Shahi (1733), dedicated to Muhammad Shah 19-48, and a delegation went to Portugal (1730). The Samrat, Jai Prakash and Ram Yantras were stone, not brass, for accuracy. Travancore builds on trade. Marthanda Varma 29-58 subjugated local chiefs, built a centralised State and a European-style military, and held a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues went into the military, irrigation works and transport. In 1741 his army crushed the Dutch East India Company at Colachel, leaving them as mere merchants in Cochin; Bedara (1759) and the 1795 expulsion finished the Dutch. Malabar slips, the Company arrives. Under Rama Varma 58-98 Travancore became a centre of art and scholarship but its military declined. In 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, the heart of the spice trade. After 1798 British influence grew; in 1805 the Nair troops mutinied over unpaid salaries and Travancore signed a Subsidiary Alliance. In 1809 Velu Thampi Dalawa issued the Kundara Proclamation, and when it was suppressed he took his own life. From Vijayanagar to Haider Ali. Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646), which Deccan Sultanates shattered at Talikota in 1565. The Wodeyars then made Mysore autonomous, and Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar made it militarily powerful. By 1761 a corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj, had made the Wodeyars figureheads, and Haider Ali 61-82, a junior officer, overthrew him and kept the Wodeyar as nominal head. The machine and the money. With French help Haider Ali 61-82 built Risalas on a European model and spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars and Deshmukhs. To pay for it Mysore practised Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded, Jagirdari minimised, Deshmukhs removed so State officials collected directly, field surveys, canals, cash crops and sericulture. Tipu looks abroad. Tipu 82-99 ran a government-owned trading company with 30 centres including Muscat, and used indigenous iron-cased rockets (range 2 km) that inspired Congreve's. In 1785 he declared independence and asked the Khalifa for a sanad; he set up embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt (Prelims 2001). He also planted a Tree of Liberty and joined the Jacobin Club, but the French alliance gave no military support. Why Mysore lost. Mysore wanted to dominate all of South India and its trade (Vijayanagar 2.0), but constant war drained the State faster than Military Fiscalism could refill it. The 1766 annexation of Malabar and Calicut triggered the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), and four wars (1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam.

Prelims 2021 Where St Francis Xavier died Shangchuan Island (off China), 1552, not Goa. His body was brought to Goa (Basilica of Bom Jesus) 4.6 Religious intolerance Prelims 2022 The claim that the Dutch received land from the Gajapati dynasty Incorrect. The Gajapatis (15th-century Odisha) had declined long before the Dutch arrived 6. The Dutch VOC

Story so far: this is a Prelims chapter, and the teacher says UPSC asks three things. Ask: where, who, roughly when, and which came first? Very important chapter (Prelims). The teacher's board (slide 22) says what UPSC asks: (1) where and who set up a factory or fort, (2) a rough idea of when, (3) chronology (first-order: which came first). So learn the tables T1, T2, T3 and T5 as place + who + rough year + order. The handout for Chapter 8 ends with an index for the next chapter (Carnatic Wars). That belongs to Chapter 9. Two Prelims traps are inside this chapter: St Francis Xavier died at Shangchuan Island, not Goa (Prelims 2021) and the Dutch did not get land from the Gajapati dynasty (Prelims 2022). Both are flagged where they occur. Lecture 10 covers Sections 1 to 4 of the handout (up to the decline of the Portuguese). Lecture 11 adds ink on the tables and on the Dutch, English, Danes, Surat and Roe sections. Lecture 12 (slides 1 to 55) covers Sections 12 to 19 and then the Chapter 8 PYQs (section 21). Sections 5 to 9 are mostly handout text.

items.t: 1 · Asia, the economic power of the world
items.x: Because Europe wanted what only Asia made, the whole chapter starts with goods and profit, not conquest. Ask: who carried the goods before the Europeans? Sec 1 Asia: Economic Power of the World Three main attractions Indonesia (Java and Sumatra) for spices; India for textiles (plus Malabar for spices); China for silk and tea Routes China: land route (the Silk Route). India and Indonesia: a mix of land and sea, through the Middle East and the Arabian Sea Who controlled trade Arab traders dominated the Arabian Sea leg. Then Italian merchants of Genoa and Venice carried goods across the Mediterranean into Europe. Both earned enormous profits at each handoff The teacher marked "islands" over Indonesia and sketched the trade as two funnels (the Mediterranean Sea and the Arabian Sea) meeting at a point, with the "new route" arrow going round the Cape of Good Hope (CoGH) from Europe (Portugal). Beside the Arabian Sea part he wrote "The empire of Arabs and Ottoman." Silk and Spice Trade Routes map of Europe, Asia and Africa Medieval European trade routes map: Hanseatic, Venetian, Genoese, Venetian and Genoese, and overland or river routes (legend) Who gained: the teacher's board on "no political control" If there was no political control (no colonialism or imperialism), the trade was good for India. [1757: colonialism began; Goa is an exception.] The idea (marked imp): Europeans came to India to purchase Indian FINISHED GOODS; there was competition among Europeans for these goods and competition between Arabs and Europeans. So this was good for: exports of India; forex for India; strength of Indian kingdoms; India getting a BETTER PRICE (boxed); Indian merchants; Indian artisans. Teacher's board: trade flow diagram Teacher's board: IF no political control (colonialism or imperialism; note: 1757 colonialism began, Goa an exception) Flow of goods on the teacher's board Ryots and artisans (villages) produce Indian merchant (city, town) collects and sells inside Indian territory: domestic trade Coastal area: goods meet Arabs / Europeans: international trade Europeans pay export duty (tax) to the Indian ruler OUT OF INDIA Europe was not wealthy; spices and the 800% profit Sec 1 continued Europe was not wealthy Eastern goods were luxuries only the rich could afford. A common European could not afford Indian cotton or Chinese silk. The profit came from supplying Europe's wealthy classes, and Genoa and Venice guarded this position zealously Spices held a special place Until the 1600s European food was as spiced as Indian food. Spices preserved and made palatable the meat stored through winter (no industrial refrigerator: clove and pepper did the job) Profit was staggering Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold in Europe at 800% profit; by the 1600s, 1 kg of clove cost the equivalent of 1 kg of gold Beside the table: "6 months = average journey time from EU to India." And on trade: a buyer gives Gold or Silver to the seller, but this will deplete the forex reserves of a country. A side note in brackets on the slide: [Savings Bank A/c: 4%; 6-7%] (a comparison of rates of return; the handout does not explain it). The handout's aside: had the present been the 1650s, most of us would have been "spitting gold" as children, with the cloves our mothers tucked into rice that we picked out and pushed to the side of the plate. (memory hook for clove = gold) Forex versus domestic currency, and the triangle Teacher's board: Forex versus Domestic Currency Used in the international market; a country buying from another country; import-export transactions Within the borders of a state, domestic transactions must be done (ideally) in domestic currency Till 1971: Gold. 1971 onwards: the Dollar replaced Gold  The EIC triangle trade (teacher's triangle) (1) Buy goods: the EIC buys goods (cloth) from India (2) Sell Indian goods: the EIC sells Indian goods to Indonesia (3) Sell goods: Indonesian goods (spices) come back to the EIC (4) The EIC sells Indonesian goods to the rest of Europe for profit Shift over time: as European incomes rose in the 17th and 18th centuries and spices became more widely available, Indian cotton textiles became the most sought-after commodity from the East. But in the beginning it was spice that started everything. "As people came out of poverty / as the size of the middle class expanded, demand increased" (incomes rose: underlined).

items.t: 2 · The Ottoman blockade (1453) and the Age of Discovery
items.x: Because the land road closed in 1453, Europe had to find a sea road. Ask: which two powers led, and which inventions made the voyage possible? 1453: interruption The Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople (today's Istanbul) and blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia. European traders needed a new way east Age of Discovery (16th century) This necessity became the engine of one of history's great turning points. European powers, led initially by Portugal and Spain, sent ships into the Atlantic searching for a direct sea route to the East What the era gave (1) Better use of the astrolabe (location) and the magnetic compass (direction) What the era gave (2) The system of latitudes and longitudes and the modern world map What the era gave (3) Geography as a formal discipline What the era gave (4) The invention of the Caravel: a ship able to sail at an angle against the wind The teacher's correction on the word "blockaded": it is "effectively" blockaded, not literally. The Ottomans demanded a share of the profits on trade, making trade unviable for Europeans. His sketch: a ship with a wind arrow from the upper left, sailing at an angle to it, towards a destination. The Caravel, sailing at an angle against the wind

Because two powers claimed the same ocean, a Pope drew a line. Ask: which side of the line is Brazil, and why? Rivalry and mediator Portugal and Spain competed over who owned the new sea routes and lands. Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 The line An imaginary line in the Atlantic Ocean, about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands East Lands EAST of the line went to Portugal West Lands WEST of the line went to Spain Why Brazil is Portuguese Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so it became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas; the rest of the continent became Spanish Map of north-west Africa and the Atlantic with southern Europe (Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania, Senegal, Mali) Period map of the Treaty of Tordesillas, anno 1494: a vertical line through the Atlantic, two kings pointing (Spain on the west side, Portugal on the east side), South Am [1492: Columbus reached Central America] (the Spanish went west). The Portuguese went east round the Cape of Good Hope to the "East Indies", where mid-east, India, China, Indonesia and South East Asia are all "the East." Brazil = the only Portugal colony (in the Americas). The handout defines the East Indies as all lands east of the Cape of Good Hope. Tordesillas, 1494 Portugal and Spain compete over new sea routes and lands Pope Alexander VI mediates Line ~1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands East of the line: Portugal West of the line: Spain Brazil's eastern tip falls on the Portuguese side: the only Portuguese colony in the Americas

Because Tordesillas gave them the east, the Portuguese reached India first. Ask: how did a State, not a company, run the trade? 4.0 · Da Gama at Calicut (1498) Sec 4 Portuguese Arrive in India Da Gama at Calicut (1498) Armed with the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) and backed by the Portuguese Crown, Vasco Da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode, Kerala) in 1498, sailing round the Cape of Good Hope, the southernmost point of Africa He traded and left Received permission to trade from the Zamorin of Calicut but faced heavy opposition from Arab traders. No factory or permanent settlement on this voyage The handout adds: the Cape was named "Cape of Good Hope" by Portugal's King John II, as it represented hope of finally finding a sea route to India. The teacher wrote "NOT COCHIN" beside Calicut: Da Gama landed at Calicut (1498), and the first permanent factory was at Cochin (1500), not his landing place. Photo: Vasco da Gama monument at Kappad Beach (Calicut), a stone relief portrait with a ship's wheel and anchor sculpture and the sea behind, where he first landed in Ind Why trade, not empire? (the teacher's board) Primary purpose of the Europeans = Trade, not empire building. But empire building did take place in the Americas (weak states), while India had strong states (land powers, i.e. strong armies). And the board adds: resources from mining (gold, silver) are an extra plus; if empire building is possible, there are greater trade profits (+) and they can get land revenue (LR) and other taxes. With political control, as government in any territory you can export goods to the home country at a low price. Why South India was vulnerable (handout): when the Portuguese arrived, the Mughal Empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist in India. South India was divided between the Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, without a unified central naval power. This fragmentation let the Portuguese dominate trade and some territory in the 16th century. Character of the Portuguese approach: part commerce, part conquest, part coercion. Printed map of the west coast of India (Kathiawar to Cape Comorin) with European settlement dates: Diu (1535, Portuguese), Surat (1612, British), Daman (1558, P), Bassein Learn the west coast from north to south: Diu, Surat, Daman, Bombay, Goa, Mahe, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore. Calicut = a small kingdom; Cochin = a small kingdom on the northern border of Travancore. The dates printed on this map differ from some dates in the handout text (for example Goa 1610 on the map against 1510 in the text; Bombay 1638 on the map against 1668 in the handout). Use the handout text and tables (T1) for exam dates; the map is for locating places and showing who came where. 4.1 · Structure of trade: a State enterprise Unlike the private joint-stock companies the British and Dutch later set up, Portuguese trade was a State enterprise called the Estado da India, directly controlled by the Portuguese Crown through its official administration. The Portuguese government was the trader. [Like a PSU / Govt]. The English EIC and the Dutch VOC were private companies. The teacher's side note: the French EIC was initially a private company; later taken over by the French Govt. Depot, Factory, Settlement In this period a "factory" did not mean a manufacturing unit. It was a trading post: warehouses for storing goods, offices for trade, homes for company employees, and often a fort for protection. The word comes from "factor," a merchant agent; the factory was where factors worked. 4.1 Depot vs Factory vs Settlement (table) 4.1 Portuguese Trade Was a State Enterprise [Think bus depot] for a depot ("for going out of India": goods waiting for the ship). A factory is also called a trading post; its function is the "Office." A settlement has multiple factories and warehouses and "collects LR (land revenue) and consumes LR." Don't confuse "LEJ" here: a depot has no (L)egislative, (E)xecutive, (J)udicial jurisdiction; a settlement has sovereign territorial rights: L E J. [Taxes can be charged only by the Ruler / Govt.] Farman, Parwana, Nishan Teacher's board: Farman (Govt order or notification) branches into three: Imperial or Royal = issued by the King or Emperor; Local or Parwana = by the Governor of a Provi The handout defines these when discussing the Danes: Farman (Imperial Decree by the Mughal Emperor), Nishan (Princely Decree by a Prince of the Royal Blood), Parwana (Provincial Decree or Order by a Provincial Governor). Teacher's board: UPSC Prelims asks (1) where and who set up a factory or fort, (2) a rough idea of the time of setting up of the factory or fort, (3) chronology (1st ORDE UPSC Prelims: where / who set up a factory or fort; a rough idea of the time; chronology (1st order). 4.2 · Early factories, the first fort and the aggression (1498-1503) Because Da Gama left no factory, the next steps matter: 98, 00, 02, 03. Ask: where is the first permanent factory, and where the first fort? 4.2 Early Factories, 1st Fort Manuel (1503) and Aggression (1498-1503) Early Portuguese moves, 1498 to 1503 1498: Da Gama at Calicut; trade permission from the Zamorin; no factory 1500, Cabral: first Portuguese factory, Calicut (permission of the Samoothiri/Zamorin); destroyed by Arab merchants (about 50 Portuguese killed) Cabral bombards Calicut (the Zamorin would not evict the Arabs) and sails south 1500: first PERMANENT factory, Cochin (protection of the Raja of Cochin) 1502, Da Gama's 2nd voyage: bombards Calicut, massacres innocent fishermen; aims: avenge Cabral, subdue the Zamorin, expel Arab rivals 1503: Fort Manuel, Cochin (Albuquerque 09-15, then a naval commander): first European fort in India Cochin = first capital of Portuguese India until the HQ shifted to Goa in 1530 The teacher sketched Zamorin, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore along a slanted line, and marked (1st - 1498) next to Da Gama's second voyage. "Notice the nature of the Portuguese" (the violence). Under Albuquerque 09-15: 1504-15. [Goa annexed in 1510] with an arrow to 1530 (HQ shift). The 2nd voyage disrupted the Arab-Venetian domination of the trade; Europe could now trade directly with India (Portugal a player in the Indian Ocean trade). In the handout, the second voyage marked the forcible integration of Indian Ocean trade into the European mercantilist framework. Albuquerque 09-15's years are written as 09-15 beside his name in the handout, to tell him apart from Almeida 05-09 (05-09); in 1503 he was not yet Governor. 4.3 · Blue Water Policy and the Cartaz System (Almeida 05-09, 1505-09) Because India's kingdoms had armies and Portugal had ships, the Blue Water Policy followed. Ask: what was a Cartaz, and what did Diu 1509 settle? 4.3 Blue Water Policy and Cartaz System (Almeida 1505-09) 1st Governor Francisco de Almeida 05-09 was the 1st Governor of the Portuguese Estado da India (Viceroy in common usage, but the legal title was Governador) Blue Water Policy Emphasis on NAVAL supremacy rather than territorial conquest. Since India had powerful land-based States, the Portuguese chose to dominate oceans and maritime trade routes. The objective: a monopolistic trading regime without extensive territorial expansion Why South India was vulnerable No Mughal Empire yet (1526-1858); South India divided between Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, with no unified central naval power Their approach Commerce, coercion in trade, and some (boxed) conquest: Goa 1510 Blue Water = oceans and seas. The decision to focus on the blue waters was expected, since the primary goal of the Age of Discovery (16th c) was trade. Goa 1510 = the exception to this Blue Water policy. Almeida 05-09 was the "CEO of the company in India"; from 1510+ the Governor = CEO + CM of Goa. WHY: they had a better navy, the goal was oceanic trade, and Indian armies were strong (so land conquest was hard); the south was also weak since Talikota 1565 (the note is partly unclear on the slide). Teacher's board: Military, Navy versus Territorial Army Territorial army was strong for Indian kingdoms. Europe's navy was usually greater than the Indian powers' navy (Marathas and Travancore had good navies, and books talk about it). Land-locked states focus on the territorial army; states with a coast focus on the territorial army plus a Navy, in budget and technology. (Examples on the board: Portugal, Dutch, French, British, Spain.) Teacher's board: CARTAZ (circled) analogy Cartaz = a toll booth on the sea. On land a car on a highway pays at a TOLL booth; in the oceans a ship on a trade route pays Cartaz fees. 4.3 (contd) Not a battle for Diu as a territory, but for the domination of the Arabian Sea. The coalition was "all stakeholders of the old routes": Arabs (Egypt), Indian (Gujarat, Zamorin), military ships from the Ottoman. 1502: Arabs and the Zamorin defeated in India; 1509: top player of the Arabian Sea. The teacher also notes that only under Akbar 56-05 was the coastal area added to the Mughal state. The handout: the coalition's scale shows how seriously the established trading powers of the Old World viewed the Portuguese threat; Venice's trade was being destroyed by Portuguese dominance of the Indian Ocean. 4.4 · Afonso de Albuquerque 09-15 (2nd Governor, 1509-15) 4.4 Afonso de Albuquerque (2nd Governor, 1509-15) Imprisonment and release Albuquerque 09-15 arrived (back in India in 1508) with the King's orders to take over leadership, but Almeida 05-09 did not trust him and arrested him. After the Battle of Diu (1509) a new fleet confirmed the King's orders; he was released and became the 2nd Governor Territorial transformation Turned the Portuguese presence from a purely trading enterprise into a territorial colonial State: annexed Goa (1510) from the Sultan of Bijapur, for better control of the Arabian Sea. Goa 1510 = a notable exception to the Blue Water Policy (a rare land conquest) Luso-Indian policy Encouraged intermarriage between Portuguese settlers and Indian women (mixed ancestry). A substantial share of the women were war widows or captured women, often forced without consent. Greater political stability Administrative and religious Integrated local elites into the administration, attempted to regulate practices such as Sati, and promoted Christianity as a tool of political control The teacher marked [Babur 26-30 not in India] (Babur 26-30 had not yet arrived in 1510). On the Luso-Indian policy: via increased numbers (the Portuguese population grows), like Mughal "more mansabdars" (co-opted). On the elites: "co-opted". Two ways to power: (1) fight all, defeat all, remove all; or (2) co-opt (e.g. Babur 26-30, Akbar 56-05, H...). Co-opt is underlined. The handout says the textbooks often call him "Viceroy," but his legal title was Governador, the formal administrative office that ruled Portuguese territory in India. The same applies to Almeida 05-09. Teacher's board: Religion = Soft Power Teacher's board: Abolition of Sati, or any social reform, can therefore be of 2 intents: (1) Conversion, by weakening the bond of people with their religion, by abolishin Religion = Soft Power. Conversion reduces opposition to the political power of the (Christian) Portuguese and gives a narrative of brotherhood: social power (success at conversion) increases political power. Abolition of Sati (or any social reform) can have two intents: (1) Conversion, by weakening the people's bond with their religion (abolishing, making fun of, or targeting the legitimacy of rituals); (2) Noble intent: reform or women's empowerment. 4.5 · Peak under Nuno da Cunha 29-38 (Governor 1529-38) Capital shifted to Goa (1530) Nuno da Cunha 29-38 officially shifted the HQ (capital) from Cochin to Goa in 1530 (Goa annexed 1510). The Portuguese dominated the Indian Ocean trade for nearly a century Western-coast consolidation Acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, securing strategic ports and trade routes [1613: the EIC's Surat factory, after defeating the Portuguese] marks the end of the "nearly a century." 4.6 · Religious intolerance: Inquisition and Francis Xavier Because conversion was a political tool, intolerance bred a backlash. Ask: where did Xavier die, and where was he buried? Most aggressive power Among the most religiously aggressive of all European powers in India; Jesuit missionary activity generated widespread resistance Slavery and forced conversions The administration was marked by the slave trade (including the Hughli settlement in Bengal) and forced conversions Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) A brutal colonial church court to investigate and punish heresy (beliefs contradicting church doctrine) and violently enforce Portuguese cultural and religious orthodoxy; deep socio-religious backlash St Francis Xavier In India from 1542, died 1552; spearheaded mass Catholic conversions in coastal India and laid the ideological groundwork for the Goa Inquisition Prelims trap (2021): St Francis Xavier did NOT die in Goa. He died on Shangchuan Island (off China) in 1552 while trying to enter mainland China. His body was later brought to Goa and is preserved in the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa. The question tested the place of death, not of burial. The teacher's arrow shows Xavier "led" to the Inquisition (and a dotted line from the Inquisition back to Xavier). Photo: the 'Breast Ripper', an iron torture device of the Portuguese Inquisition, hanging on a wall; used on women who refused to convert. Map: slave trade from Africa to the Americas 1650-1860 The slide map on the slave trade (1650-1860) is a teacher's add-on beside the Portuguese slave trade; it counts about 10 to 15 million enslaved people taken from western Africa to the Americas, mostly to the West Indies, Central America and South America (Brazil about 5 million). 4.7 · Portuguese contribution: New World crops The Portuguese introduced these New World crops that permanently transformed Indian agriculture and cuisine: tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple, guava. Cocoa and rubber are also New World plants, but reached India only in the British period, not through the Portuguese. Encyclopaedia Britannica map: The Columbian Exchange The Columbian Exchange: European exploration of the Americas in the 15th and 16th centuries brought the Old and New Worlds into contact. Plants, animals and microbes from Europe, Asia and Africa went to the Americas, and many others went from the Americas to Europe, Asia and Africa. 4.8 · Why did the Portuguese decline? i) Political Strong regional powers rose in Persia, Egypt and North India; especially the rise of the Marathas directly threatened the Portuguese (1739: Marathas defeated the Portuguese); teacher: Konkan coast: Marathas ii) Religious backlash Jesuit activity and the brutality of the Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) produced deep local resistance iii) Economic and administrative decay Corruption, inefficiency, decline in discipline, and employees' piracy and illicit trade (teacher: "personal trade") eroded the institutions iv) External competition The English and Dutch, with superior naval technology, joint-stock finance and more disciplined commercial organisation, displaced them v) Imperial overextension Focus diverted to Brazil (far more lucrative) plus lack of support from Lisbon (the Govt) starved the Estado da India Takeaway: the Portuguese set the stage for all later European expansion in India: colonial administration centred in Goa, armed maritime trade, and religious conversion as a tool of political control became patterns the British would study, adapt and eventually supersede. He sketched the coast with Calicut above, Cochin below. 1502, Da Gama's 2nd voyage: "To avenge the Calicut factory (??)" and "= the Arabian Sea can be used by the Portuguese." 1503: "Cochin = HQ/Capital from 1505 till 1530." 1505-09, Battle of Diu (1509): an arrow "=> Arabian Sea domination." 1509-15, Albuquerque 09-15, "territorial State": a circled T "= Goa": Goa was the territorial State, not just trade posts. 1530: a triangle sketch with Goa marked, and a date range beside it that is partly unclear ("1336-1646", check your notebook). items.t: 5 · How the Dutch and English broke the Portuguese-Spanish monopoly
items.x: Because the Portuguese-Spanish hold had to break, the 1588 Armada defeat opened the sea. Ask: why did the Dutch and English go to Indonesia first? By the second half of the 16th century two new naval powers had emerged: Britain and the Dutch Republic (Netherlands). Both wanted to break the strict monopoly held by Spain and Portugal over European international trade and to achieve freedom of navigation in the oceans. 1588: the British Navy defeated the Spanish Armada ("Invincible Armada") in the Atlantic, severely weakening Spanish-Portuguese naval supremacy. By 1580 Portugal had entered a political union with Spain, so defeating Spain also opened trade routes Portugal had controlled. With the Armada defeated, British and Dutch ships could travel safely to Asia via the Cape of Good Hope. First priority for both: Indonesia (the spice trade of the East Indies). India came later, for a commercial reason: the people of the spice islands had little interest in English or Dutch goods but readily accepted Indian cotton textiles. To buy spices in Indonesia you first needed cloth from India. The handout's clarification: the Netherlands, Holland and "the Dutch Republic" all refer to the same country. "Dutch" is the adjective; "Holland" is technically a region within the Netherlands but is often used as a general name. The trilateral (triangle) trade: England → India → Indonesia → England. This is the commercial logic that shifted the EIC's focus from Indonesia to the Indian subcontinent. (Compare the teacher's triangle in section 1.) Board, slide 2: why the monopoly had to be broken. "End the rival's monopoly (e.g. 1502, Da Gama in coastal Malabar) -> a multi-player domain -> establish your own monopoly (requires additional resources), i.e. the Battle of Diu 1509 -> Arabian Sea." Two challenges for the British and the Dutch in trading with the East Indies: (1) How to reach India, China, Indonesia: Spain and Portugal dominate the routes and oceans. (2) How to purchase goods from India: the Portuguese dominate the Indian coastline and the Indian international market. In a small table on the right: "1588: end of monopoly over routes" (the second row was left empty). Board, slide 4: who dominated world oceanic trade, by period. 1500s: Portugal vs Spain. 1600s: Dutch vs British. 1700s-1815: British vs French, with the arrow "-> Britain = top naval power." 1870-1945: British + French vs Germany. 1945-91: US vs USSR. 2000s+: US vs China. (The teacher drew smiley faces on the Dutch-British and British-French periods.) Slide 5 ink (this section). After "freedom of navigation" he added "in oceans and of TRADE." Underlined: Armada, Atlantic, British and Dutch. Above "Armada": "Naval Fleet." In the trilateral-trade row he struck out both "England" words and wrote "EIC", so the triangle is EIC -> India -> Indonesia -> EIC. Board, slide 6 (left): the EIC's triangle. Indonesia at the top, India bottom right, the EIC bottom left. Arrows: the EIC buys goods from India; sells Indian goods to Indonesia; buys Indonesian goods. Board, slide 6 (right): CHARTER, State and Company. Charter = founding document, issued by the State (Monarchy or Parliament), granting special powers and rights to a company. State = an organisation with a territorial (circled T) motive (defend, annex), so it has a military and may wage war. A State rules a territory, so coins, currency and taxation are with the State; the circled L, E, J powers are also with the State (my reading: legislative, executive, judicial). Company = an organisation with a profit motive for its shareholders, and it requires property. Teacher's board (Lecture 11 slide 2): end a rival's monopoly, then set up your own (Battle of Diu 1509); two challenges for the British and the Dutch: reaching the East I Teacher's board (slide 4): domination of world oceanic trade Teacher's board (slide 6): the EIC triangle (Indonesia, India, EIC) and, on the right, Charter, State versus Company: territorial motive and the power to wage war for a S

Because the VOC had capital and a Charter, it beat the Portuguese in the south. Ask: why is the VOC the first joint-stock company? 1602: the Dutch East India Company (VOC, Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) was established by a Charter issued by the Dutch Parliament, by merging six smaller Dutch companies that had been competing for eastern trade. Takeaway (handout): the VOC was the world's first multinational company, and the first to issue publicly tradable stocks and shares on a formal exchange: the world's first joint-stock company. An ordinary person could become a part-owner by buying shares, without a say in management: the ancestor of the BSE, NSE, NYSE and the modern shareholder economy. Charter powers: the right to wage war, sign treaties, acquire territory, build forts and mint its own currency: powers that ordinarily belong to a State, showing how European powers saw companies as an extension of State power. The first Dutch expedition (1595) went to the East Indies (Indonesia), not India. Dutch settlements in India: Masulipatnam (Northern Sarkars) 1605 (first factory), Pulicat (Carnatic) 1610, Surat (Gujarat) 1616, Bimilipatam (Golconda) 1641, Karikal (near Pondicherry) 1645, Chinsura (Bengal) 1653, later Kasimbazar, Baranagore, Patna, Balasore, Nagapatnam, Agra, Cochin (where they captured the Portuguese fort in 1663). At its peak in 1669 the VOC was the richest private company in the world: 150 merchant vessels, 40 warships, an army of 10,000 soldiers, 50,000 employees; over its life 5,000 voyages from the Netherlands to the East Indies. 1799: bankrupt and dissolved; possessions taken over by the Dutch government as the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), a Dutch colony until independence in 1945 after World War II. Prelims 2022 trap: the Gajapati dynasty and the Dutch. The claim that the Dutch received land grants from the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha is INCORRECT. The Gajapatis were a 15th-century dynasty centred in Odisha whose power had declined well before the Dutch arrived. Do not confuse later local rulers of the Odisha coast with the Gajapati dynasty itself. Ink on the VOC slides (Lecture 11, slides 7 to 11). Underlined: the VOC's name, six smaller Dutch companies, the first publicly tradable stocks, the Charter powers (war, treaties, territory, forts, own currency), Masulipatnam (1605), Chinsura (1653) and the capture of the Portuguese fort at Cochin in 1663. Margin notes: "CHARTER = founding document"; "Much larger capital (Rs) for the company"; "Dutch want to be a big buyer of eastern goods ... a big company => deep pockets, i.e. more buying power." Beside the first factory: "[* Last time: 1st FACTORY 1500 by the Portuguese]" (the Portuguese Cochin factory, 1500, remains the first European factory). Board (slide 8): to make the VOC a big company with deep pockets and buying power: (1) merger of six companies, (2) joint-stock company (raise Rs from the public). Beside Masulipatnam in Andhra: a note on the Northern Sarkars and "5 districts"; the sign between them is unclear (= or not equal), so check your notebook. Why the VOC fell (slide 9): "Bankrupt because of tough competition by the English EIC, plus war defeat during the French Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804) and the Napoleonic War (1804-15)." Priority ticks on Table T2 (slide 10): the teacher ticked 1602, 1605, 1653, 1663 and 1741. Colachel (1741): "South Travancore;" under Marthanda Varma 29-58: 29-58 and "ended (Dutch) political ambitions" (the next words, about trade conflict, are unclear). 1759, Bedara/Chinsura: "British vs Dutch." Kew Letters (slide 11). Beside the 1795 row he wrote "[SYLLABUS X]": not in the syllabus. His board explanation: "France vs the rest of Europe (1792-1815); France will attack all assets, e.g. companies like the VOC. 1795: France removed the then government in the Netherlands and brought its puppet to power. The earlier ruler then wrote letters to different Dutch establishments across the world to give temporary control to the British." items.t: 7 · The English EIC and the Royal Charter of 1600
items.x: Because the EIC lived on a licence, its Charter shaped its fate. Ask: who gave the Charter, and what did it give? The English East India Company was formed on 31 December 1600: its founding document was a Royal Charter issued by Queen Elizabeth I 58-03. A Royal Charter is essentially a licence granted by the Monarch. If it was not renewed, the company would legally cease to exist. This shaped the EIC's relationship with the British State for the next two and a half centuries: its survival depended on the goodwill of whoever held power in Britain. The EIC was the 4th joint-stock company in England, formed by pooling money from 215 London merchants ("merchant adventurers") who wanted to challenge Dutch dominance in European trade with the East. The stated goal was trade with the East, not empire-building or colonialism. Britain or England? In 1600 it was England (not Britain) that granted the Charter. England and Scotland united in 1707 to create the Kingdom of Great Britain; in 1801 Ireland was added, creating the United Kingdom. Before 1707 "British" technically means English. What the Royal Charter of 1600 gave the EIC 1. A monopoly over England's trade with the East Indies for 15 years. 2. The right to carry gold (foreign exchange) out of England to purchase eastern goods. 3. Management by a body of private people: a Governor, a Deputy Governor and 24 members, which later evolved into the Board or Court of Directors. The handout's forex aside: for a State, forex is the currency that matters in international trade; domestic currency works only within a country's borders (like a household's internal reward system for children, valid only inside the home). Until 1971, Gold was forex, until the Dollar took over. (Same idea as the teacher's board in section 1.) Ink on the 1600 Charter slides (slides 12 to 16). Board, slide 12: the EIC = joint-stock company; special rights and powers via a Charter (31 Dec 1600); Dutch competition. Slide 13: he underlined founding document, Royal Charter and Elizabeth I 58-03. Board, slide 14: why is the VOC (1602) called the first joint-stock company when the English EIC (1600) was also one? "Answer: in 1600 the EIC was not a proper joint-stock company. It operated on a per-VOYAGE system: before each journey to the East Indies the EIC gathered Rs from the public; brought and sold goods in Europe at a profit and shared all the profits; for the next journey, repeated. It is later that the EIC became a proper joint-stock company, i.e. one with permanent capital." Board, slide 15: a proper joint-stock company "does not usually give back all profits; it gives dividends." A pie of the profit: Retain, Re-invest, assets, Dividends. Slide 16, what the Charter gave: the teacher's correction. Underlined: England's trade, for 15 years, right to carry gold, out of England, private people, Court (of Directors). "WRONG = monopoly over trade with India with the EIC. CORRECT = monopoly over England's (or British) trade with the East Indies, with the EIC." A line from Grant 2 to "forex is controlled by the State." Under Grant 3: "BoD/CoD = EIC's top decision-making body = not any government organisation." Teacher's board (slide 14): why the VOC (1602) is called the first joint-stock company: the EIC of 1600 worked on a per-voyage system (collect money, sell goods, share al Teacher's board (slide 15): a proper joint-stock company gives dividends rather than all profits; pie of Retain, Re-invest, assets, Dividends.

items.t: 8 · Charters until 1793: the EIC's changing legal character
items.x: Because the Charter was renewed again and again, the ladder tells the story of its power. Ask: which Charter made it a quasi-State? The EIC's legal existence depended on Charter renewal, and the Charters also tell the shift of power in Britain from the Monarch to Parliament. 1601-03, the first voyage (James Lancaster): the fleet sailed not to India but to Indonesia, consistent with the EIC's original priority of the spice trade. They reached Java and Sumatra, where they set up the very first EIC factory. On the way Lancaster's fleet looted a Portuguese ship, the Sao Tome, in the Strait of Malacca (a cargo of textiles and spices). William Dalrymple and others note that the EIC's first major profit came not from trade but from outright piracy. Shareholders got substantial dividends; the fleet returned in 1603. 1609, James I 03-25: the original 15-year monopoly became a perpetual monopoly. 1657, Cromwell 51-60's Charter: Context: Charles I 25-49 tried to levy taxes without Parliament's consent, which triggered the English Civil War (1642-51). The Parliamentarians (largely Protestant) defeated the Royalists; Charles I 25-49 was beheaded in 1649; England became a Republic under Oliver Cromwell 51-60 (the handout writes his years as 51-60). After Cromwell 51-60's death in 1658 his son briefly took over, but the experiment proved autocratic and unpopular. In 1660 the Monarchy was restored under Charles II 60-85. Cromwell 51-60 issued a new Charter in 1657, declaring the previous Royal Charter invalid, and reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company. Earlier, money was raised voyage by voyage (pool, voyage, profits, fund dissolved); from 1657 one continuous unified capital fund, giving a stable financial foundation. 1661, Charles II 60-85's Charter (after the Restoration) was arguably the most consequential legally: it turned the EIC from a commercial trading body into a quasi-State power. It gave the right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, and exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over settlements in India. (The right to mint its own money came in 1676.) From 1793 Parliament takes over: the British Parliament begins passing Acts for the renewal of the EIC's Charter, mirroring the democratisation of Britain (power moving from Crown to elected representatives). Indian constitutional history and British political history are inseparable threads. Takeaway (1661): the 1600 EIC was a merchant association with a trade monopoly; the 1661 EIC had the legal powers of a State within its territories. A trading company had, through successive Charters, accumulated the powers of a sovereign. Ink on the charter timeline (Lecture 11, slides 17 to 22). Slide 17, context he wrote at the top: "1642-51 English Civil War -> King Charles I 25-49 beheaded. 1651-60 Republic under Cromwell 51-60. 1660 Restoration of the Monarchy under King Charles II 60-85." 1657 box: "per-voyage system ended." 1793 box: "1st time the Charter was issued by P (Parliament)." Priority marks on the six boxes: 1600 = circled "imp"; 1609 = "not imp"; 1657 = "not imp"; 1661 = circled and underlined "imp"; 1676 = "not imp"; 1793 = circled "imp". So learn 1600, 1661 and 1793 first; 1609, 1657 and 1676 are the lower-priority years. Slide 20, the 1661 Charter: next to "quasi-State power" he wrote "semi" (semi-State). Beside civil and criminal jurisdiction he wrote "[Ruling Power]." Underlined: forts, troops, war and peace, 1676 (mint), and "legal powers of a State." Board, slide 21: how a company became an empire-builder. "Any company or citizen of a State must follow (a) the law of the home country and (b) the law of the foreign country where it operates. A State's powers: territorial jurisdiction (circled T) and subject jurisdiction." "The EIC built an empire in India, and the EIC = a Company (empire = 'Company State'). Legally possible because of the 1661 Charter, which gave the EIC State-like powers: war and peace, army, and (a circled letter plus 'er', unclear: possibly 'over') ..." Slide 22: underlined Acts and democratisation of Britain. Board: "WORDS: 'Charter ACT' (ACT circled) -> tells me it is made by L (circled: Legislature)." After 1793, an Act of Parliament (not a monarch's charter) renews the EIC. Lecture 11 slide 17: EIC Charter evolution 1600-1793 Teacher's board (slide 21): a company follows home-country law and foreign-country law; the State has territorial and subject jurisdiction; the EIC built an empire becaus EIC's legal character: from merchants to a State within a State Handout Diagram 2: EIC Charter evolution 1600 Elizabeth I 58-03: 15-year East Indies monopoly; 215 London merchants; 4th English joint-stock company 1609 James I 03-25: perpetual monopoly 1642-51 English Civil War; Charles I 25-49 beheaded 1649; Cromwell 51-60's Republic 1657 Cromwell 51-60: permanent joint-stock company (one continuous capital fund) 1660 Restoration; Charles II 60-85 on the throne 1661 Charles II 60-85: forts, troops, war and peace, civil and criminal jurisdiction (mint 1676) 1793 onwards: Parliament renews the Charters 8.7 · Why couldn't Indian merchants dominate the new trade routes? Because the Europeans had navies and Indian merchants did not, the new routes went to the Europeans. Ask: what three things did Indian merchants lack? (i) Naval power Indian merchants lacked armed ocean-going fleets to break European domination of the trade routes (ii) Capital VOC (1602) and EIC (1600, by 1657) had moved to permanent joint-stock structures and could pool the huge sums needed for bulk trade (iii) State backing The Mughal State after Akbar 56-05 did not focus on a navy and focused on territorial expansion, investing in the territorial army Ink on 8.7 (slide 23). Above "armed ocean-going fleets" he wrote "MILITARY NAVY" and underlined it. After (ii): "[Gathering Rupee from masses.]" Underlined: did not focus on a navy and territorial army. Board: "Navy" splits into "Merchant" and "Military." Then: "Modern capitalism absent in INDIA. [Why? The State = an organisation with a territorial (T) motive.]" Lecture 11 slide 23: why Indian merchants could not dominate the new routes

Because the Danes came late and weak, they stayed on the margins. Ask: which post did they use as HQ, and which one became famous? Established 1616, out of envy of Dutch and English profits. Its Charter was issued by King Christian IV 88-48 of Denmark-Norway, granting a 12-year monopoly on trade between Denmark-Norway and the East Indies. The Danes were never in the same league: weaker finance, limited military capacity. The first Danish company ended around 1650; a second Danish EIC was set up in 1670 but wound down gradually, selling all its Indian mainland settlements to the British EIC by 1845. Danish settlements in India 1. 1620: Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu: first factory; first fort: Fort Dansborg; official administrative HQ of Danish India from 1620 until 1845. 2. 1624: Pondicherry (brief): under Roland Crappe; a short-lived factory, abandoned for lack of resources, long before the French arrived. 3. 1625: Masulipatnam (Andhra Pradesh); Pipli and Balasore (Odisha). 4. 1755: Serampore (Srirampur / Frederiksnagore), Hooghly district, Bengal: a parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan 40-56. Tranquebar remained the HQ, but Serampore became the most commercially successful and culturally significant Danish post. Colonial powers in Tranquebar, Serampore and the Nicobar Islands (the Nicobars were sold separately to the British in 1868; today part of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands UT). 1799-1800: Serampore Mission Press, associated with Baptist missionaries including William Carey: translated the Bible into Indian vernacular languages, ran schools, and made an immense contribution to early printing and education in Bengal. Their architectural legacy at Tranquebar and Serampore and their missionary work (not forced conversions) are the most visible Danish traces. Ink on the Danes (slides 24 and 25). Boxed at the top: "[Denmark]" and "[not Dutch / Holland / Netherlands]." His order of arrival beside "Established 1616": "Portugal (1500); EIC 1600; VOC 1602; Danish 1616." Underlined: 1616, the Charter of Christian IV 88-48, the 12-year monopoly, 1620-1845 (HQ), Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu, Serampore (Frederiksnagore), most commercially successful and culturally significant, William Carey and the Baptist missionaries, early printing and education, "not forced conversions", Serampore Mission Press (1799-1800). Note under the Tranquebar row: "[* From 1717, ... 17-27, Bengal = successor State]" (one word is unclear; the reign code 17-27 is as he wrote it). items.t: 10 · How the EIC broke Portuguese dominance: Hawkins, Swally and Surat
items.x: Because the EIC wanted Surat, it first had to beat Portugal. Ask: what is the difference between 1612 and 1613? 1608: the EIC decided to set up a factory at Surat, then the most important port on India's west coast and firmly within Portuguese-dominated territory. It sent Captain William Hawkins to the court of Jahangir 05-27. Jahangir 05-27 first gave Hawkins a Mansab (rank of 400) and a Jagir, but Hawkins was ultimately expelled from the Mughal court due to persistent Portuguese pressure. The lesson: Portugal had to be defeated militarily before the EIC could establish itself on the west coast. 1612, Battle of Swally (Suvali): Captain Thomas Best led a small EIC armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the Portuguese. The Mughal State had its own reason to welcome this: Mughal ships traded in the Arabian Sea but were perpetually vulnerable to Portuguese piracy, a source of humiliation for a great land power. Impressed by English sea capability, Jahangir 05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613, giving the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat. 1612 versus 1613: 1612 = the Battle of Swally (military victory) and the local Mughal governor's temporary permission/parwana; 1613 = the legally permanent establishment, when Jahangir 05-27 ratified the local agreement with an imperial farman. Breaking Portuguese dominance on the west coast 1608: EIC wants a Surat factory; sends Captain William Hawkins to Jahangir 05-27 Hawkins gets a Mansab (400) and Jagir but is expelled under Portuguese pressure Lesson: defeat Portugal militarily first 1612: Battle of Swally: Captain Thomas Best defeats the Portuguese Mughals welcome it: their ships were vulnerable to Portuguese piracy 1613: Jahangir 05-27's Royal Farman: permanent factory at Surat Ink on Hawkins, Swally and Surat (slides 27 to 29). Slide 27: "Jahangir 05-27" at the top; "imp" above the 1612 Battle of Swally; underlined 1612, Captain Thomas Best, Suvali and rank 400. The 1613 Royal Farman heading is circled. Box 1: "FACTORY" splits into "Warehouse" and "Home, offices for staff." In the lesson box: "Began attacking Mughal ships" (the Portuguese). Box 3: "ESTADO DA INDIA (sad face) vs EIC (happy face)," and "FOR TRADE [not the territory (T) of Surat]": the EIC wanted trade rights, not Surat as territory. Board, slide 28: why the EIC's army stayed small until Bengal. "A company = an organisation with a PROFIT motive (of the shareholder), e.g. the EIC had an army of about 500-800 men. If it spent Rupees on an army, it would go against that goal (sad face). If the army came from its own Rupee, it would be small, to meet the core interests of trade." Starred: "1757: free Rupee of Bengal" -> "Large army," "i.e. why Plassey 1757, imp." (Plassey 1757 is marked important.) Board, slide 29: Britain's national interest and the EIC. "Britain's national interest = the EIC's interest." Roe = "a government person working for the EIC's benefit." Four points: (1) Britain's trade with the East Indies = the EIC's trade; (2) the EIC has a monopoly over Britain's trade with the East Indies; (3) via the EIC, Britain can dominate WORLD trade. His lesson: "Put companies to act as agents of the State in geopolitics, e.g. the USA's use of companies for implementing sanctions on Russia" (marked "imp"). Lecture 11 slide 27: how the EIC broke Portuguese dominance Teacher's board (slide 28): a company has a profit motive, so the EIC's army was small (about 500-800 men) until the free Rupee of Bengal after 1757; "Plassey 1757 imp".
