items.t: 11 · The Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)
items.x: Because one factory was not enough, England sent an ambassador. Ask: what did Roe's Farman of 1618 give? England wanted liberal trading rights across the entire Mughal Empire, so King James I 03-25 sent Thomas Roe as formal ambassador to Jahangir 05-27's court. Roe arrived at Surat in 1615 and stayed until 1619. Jahangir 05-27 refused a formal treaty between equals (a trading company was no sovereign equal). Through sustained diplomacy and personal rapport Roe got a series of privileges and a Royal Farman (1618) allowing the EIC to set up factories throughout the Mughal Empire with liberal trading rights: lower customs duties and ease of doing business. 1616-19: new factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach (Bharuch). With Surat they formed the Surat Presidency (1618): the EIC's first administrative Presidency in India, coordinating English trade on the west coast until the later shift to Bombay (1687). Portuguese enraged; naval conflicts continued. 1631-32: Shahjahan 27-58 ordered his Bengal governor Qasim Khan to defeat the Portuguese and eject them from Hugli, because they were misusing their trade privileges with piracy and the slave trade from their Bengal base. Roe's account, The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to the Court of the Great Mogul, is one of the most important primary sources on the Mughal Empire of this period (court administration, wealth, politics, daily life). Ink on Roe (slides 30 and 31). Top right: "Ambassador, i.e. British Resident in Jahangir 05-27's court" (starred). Underlined: the title of Roe's memoir, Royal Farman (1618), the right to establish factories across the Empire plus lower duties and ease of business ("= LIBERAL TRADING RIGHTS"), and Surat Presidency (1618). Under Surat Presidency: "HQ (e.g. Cochin 1505-1530, HQ of Portugal; Tranquebar, HQ of the Danes 1620)": a Presidency was the EIC's regional HQ, like those earlier HQs. Slide 31: "27-58" (Shah Jahan's reign code) written above the Hugli row; underlined Hugli action (1631-32) and slave trade.

Because a royal wedding settled a debt of trade and war, Bombay changed hands. Ask: what did England get, and what did it promise? The treaty, signed at Whitehall, London, marked the marriage of King Charles II 60-85 of England and Princess Catherine of Braganza of Portugal. 1. Portugal paid a dowry of 500,000 pounds in cash. 2. England received Bombay and Tangier (Morocco). 3. Trade and military cooperation, with England agreeing to protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Result: a continued Portuguese presence in Goa, Daman and Diu under English protection, lasting until 1961, when independent India took over these territories militarily, after a people's movement. 1668: the British Crown transferred Bombay to the EIC at an annual rent of 10 pounds: the start of Bombay's journey from a Portuguese dowry to the commercial capital of British India. Ink on the 1661 Treaty (slides 32 and 33). Under the title: "Restoration of MONARCHY 1660." Underlined: Whitehall, King Charles II 60-85, Princess Catherine of Braganza, dowry and 500,000 pounds in cash, Bombay and Tangier (in Morocco), military cooperation, protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Beside Term 3: "[Goa, Daman and Diu]." A rough map: EU at the top, Africa below, and Morocco circled (Tangier). Board, slide 33: two ways to deal with a rival. (1) "End your rival 100% (destroy)": "Power = 100." (2) (V2) "Thrash the rival and lessen his power permanently; huge anxiety in the rival about survival; instead of (1), convert the rival into your puppet or a junior permanent friend," "non-threatening, never big enough." Result: "Power = 100 + 90" (the second number is partly unclear). The slide follows the 1661 treaty, but the board does not name the countries. Lecture 11 slide 32: the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661 Teacher's board (slide 33): two strategies against a rival: destroy it 100% (power = 100), or thrash it and make it a puppet or junior permanent friend (power = 100 + 90) Board, Lecture 12 slide 2: who beat whom, and why the EIC won. Top row: Portuguese -> "British vs Portuguese" plus "Dutch vs Portuguese" -> the two winners meet in "British vs Dutch" -> "By 1650s" (underlined). Then a grid of South Asia and South East Asia. MAJOR: British in South Asia, Dutch in South East Asia. Minor presence: Dutch in South Asia (a bracket under the Dutch reads Indonesia) and British in South East Asia (bracket: Singapore, Malaya). The brackets sit where the teacher drew them; the grid matches the Treaty of Breda terms in section 13. Result: how the EIC won the competition. "For INTERNATIONAL TRADE (boxed) [not T (circled)] of India, i.e. who will BUY Indian GOODS." Then, bracketed and starred: "PRIMARY purpose of empire = TRADE." Why this matters: the rivals were fighting over who would buy Indian goods, not over land (T = territory). The same idea is on the Lecture 10 board for Surat ("for trade, not the territory of Surat"). items.t: 13 · The Dutch: rise, dominance and fall in Asia
items.x: Because the Dutch chased the Portuguese out, they became the richest company, then lost it. Ask: what are the dates that mark the fall? 1623, the Amboyna Massacre: the Dutch killed English traders in the spice islands, a brutal episode that ended English ambitions in Indonesia; the Dutch had effectively removed both the English and the Portuguese from Indonesia. 1658: the Dutch removed the Portuguese from Ceylon. Anglo-Dutch wars 1654-67, settled in the Treaty of Breda (1667): (1) the British leave Indonesia to the Dutch; (2) the Dutch leave the English alone in India; (3) both keep minor presences in each other's primary domains. Cochin: captured from the Portuguese in 1663, held as HQ of Dutch Malabar (not the overall HQ). Ink on slide 3. Above the table, "Java, Sumatra" with a tick pointing down: the Dutch zone is Indonesia. Under the 1623 row: "INDONESIAN TRADE" (the label for the Amboyna Massacre row). Underlined: Indonesia, Anglo-Dutch rivalry, "settled" (the Treaty of Breda settled it), Pulicat 1610-1690, Nagapattinam 1690-1795 and 1759 Bedara (Chinsura). Marthanda Varma 29-58 is written 29-58. Lecture 12 slide 3: Dutch rise, dominance and fall Board, slide 4: the coast zones. A V-shaped peninsula. West side, top to bottom: Gujarat (circle), Konkan, Malabar. East side: Bengal (circle at the top), Coromandel. The next slide places the Dutch locations on this map. Lecture 12 slide 4, teacher's board: V-shaped peninsula with Gujarat, Konkan and Malabar on the west side and Bengal and Coromandel on the east side. Ink on slide 5 (Dutch locations). Underlined: Masulipatnam, "First Dutch factory," Geldria, "First Dutch fort," "Main HQ" (Pulicat) and Nagapattinam, "Main HQ" (Nagapattinam). A dotted arrow runs from Main HQ at Pulicat down to Main HQ at Nagapattinam: the main HQ moved (1690). Fort Gustavus (Chinsura) has only a dotted underline. Side sketch of the peninsula: top part "N. Sarkars (5 districts) (Andhra)" (the number is partly legible); "Golconda (1687), annexation by A 58-07" (Aurangzeb 58-07 annexed Golconda in 1687); and, from the lower part, "1336-1646" (Vijayanagara, whose permission gave Pulicat). Reading: Masulipatnam lay in the Northern Sarkars, under Golconda; Pulicat lay in the Vijayanagara zone. Lecture 12 slide 5: Dutch locations and HQ roles Exam trap: Cochin was NOT the overall Dutch HQ; it was only the Dutch Malabar regional HQ. Overall main HQ: Pulicat (1610-90), then Nagapattinam (1690-1795). (The handout dates Chinsura's Fort Gustavus as 1655-1795, while section 6 and Table T2 list the Chinsura factory as 1653.) Board, slide 3 (right margin): the HQ example. "e.g. Amazon India: # India HQ: Bengaluru; # Regional HQ: Gurgaon (North)," with an arrow to the HQ rows. Reason: a company has one main HQ and smaller regional HQs. Read it as: Pulicat, then Nagapattinam = main HQ (like Bengaluru); Cochin = only the Malabar regional HQ (like Gurgaon for the north). This is why "Cochin = overall HQ" is the trap. Two decisive military defeats 1. 1741, Battle of Colachel: Marthanda Varma 29-58 of Travancore decisively defeated the Dutch, ending their political power in Kerala (see Chapter 7); the Dutch kept Fort Cochin till 1795. 2. 1759, Battle of Bedara (also Battle of Chinsura): the British EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in India. Sketch beside the Decline row (slide 3): an oval with Cochin at the top, Travancore along the side and Colachel at the bottom, with a dot at Cochin and a dot at Colachel. Marthanda Varma 29-58 of Travancore (29-58) beat the Dutch at Colachel in the south, while the Dutch still held Cochin in the north of Kerala.

Because France overthrew the Dutch government at home, the Dutch colonies fell to Britain. Ask: what were the Kew Letters? 1795, during the French Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804) leading into the Napoleonic Wars (1804-15): the French army invaded the Netherlands, overthrew the Dutch government and set up a puppet State, the Batavian Republic, controlled by France. Britain declared all Dutch overseas colonies enemy territory. The exiled Dutch leader Prince William V 51-95 had fled to London and issued the "Kew Letters": orders telling Dutch colonial governors to hand over their territories to the British "for safekeeping," so France could not seize them. The British used this as their legal basis to take over the remaining Dutch posts. By 1795 the British occupied the remaining Dutch settlements in South Asia: Cochin (Kerala), Chinsura (Bengal), Pulicat and Tuticorin (Coromandel), and the coastal regions of Ceylon (Trincomalee and Colombo). The teacher marked the Kew Letters "[SYLLABUS X]" (Lecture 11, slide 11): not in the syllabus. Read this section for the story of the Dutch fall, not as an exam topic. Ink on slide 6. Under the title: "NOT imp FROM exam - FOR UNDERSTANDING." This is the same call as the Lecture 11 mark "SYLLABUS X" above: read the Kew Letters for the story, do not memorise them. He also inserted "over" so that the line reads "hand over their territories," and wrote "Kew = place near London."

items.t: 15 · Why Ceylon did not become part of British India: the Crown Colony
items.x: Because Ceylon was too important for a company to run, Britain took it directly. Ask: who ruled India, and who ruled Ceylon? 1795-96: the British captured the Dutch areas of Ceylon and gave administration to the EIC, through the Madras Presidency. Treaty of Amiens, 1802: a peace treaty in Europe between Britain and France along with its Dutch ally, the Batavian Republic. The Dutch formally and permanently ceded the coastal regions of Ceylon to Britain. The British government decided Ceylon was too strategically important to be run by a trading company: it removed the EIC's administration entirely and declared Ceylon a British Crown Colony, ruled directly by an appointed British Governor, separate from the EIC's Indian empire. Takeaway: India was a colony ruled by the EIC (a commercial entity with State-like powers); Ceylon was a Crown Colony where the British State itself governed directly. Ink on slide 7 (Crown Colony). The words "Crown Colony" in the title are boxed, with "(not imp) BUT concept" and below it "imp: Meaning." So: the Ceylon story is not important for the exam, but the meaning of "Crown Colony" is. Board: British Colonies, RULED BY -> "EIC" = Company's Colony; "Br State" (boxed) = Crown Colony. Under the Amiens panel: "Rule = Doing L, E, J on a T" (L, E, J and T each circled): to rule is to do the Legislative, Executive and Judicial work on a Territory (LEJ as in section 4.1). Underlined in the last panel: "ruled directly" and "by the British State." Lecture 12 slide 7: why Ceylon became a Crown Colony

Because an EIC trade base had to be run, it became a Presidency. Ask: what does a Presidency become after annexations? A Presidency was a regional headquarters of EIC trade. A settlement got Presidency status when it had grown large enough with significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings and a fort. Initially small coastal towns; as the EIC annexed surrounding territories the towns grew into cities and the Presidencies expanded into provinces of British India (governed directly by the British). The Presidencies were named after the major forts built within them. Board, slide 9: Presidency = HQ, and the years. Left: "Presidency = ? (HQ)" (HQ circled). "Surat 1613 Factory" -> "Br: 1st Presidency = Surat (1618)" (Surat underlined); then "shift to Bombay: 1687 (year?)." Right: "Bombay with EIC: since 1668"; "Bombay = Presidency = HQ = 1687" (Western HQ), with a "20 yrs" bracket between 1668 and 1687; "Calcutta settlement 1690" -> "Presidency = 1699" (East India); "Madraspatnam (village): ___" -> "Presidency 1652" (South). Order of the Presidencies: Surat 1618, Madras 1652, Bombay 1687, Calcutta 1699, one for the west, south, west again (after the shift) and east. The board gives the first year of each pair: 1652 (London order; 1653 implemented) and 1699 (1699/1700 in the handout). Learn both years as in the handout. Lecture 12 slide 9, teacher's board: Presidency = HQ Slide 10 (board only): a sketch of a building with the sign "Amazon" (the top line is hard to read) standing on an "empty PLOT." The slide has no other words. It continues the Amazon (HQ versus regional HQ) example from slide 3. Ink on slide 11 (factory to province). "factory" and "fort" are underlined. Under Growth: "To Settlement" -> Settlement splits into Town and Rule/Admin (POLITICAL). Under Presidency: "In Beginning, Presidency = BIG TOWN or CITY"; "Madras, Bombay, Calcutta = TRADE HQs (REGIONAL HQs)." A yellow arrow joins "trade" to "province of British India," and an arc is labelled "annexations of Large T" (T = territory). Province box: Bombay  Reason: a Presidency began as a trading city (a trade HQ). When the EIC annexed large territories, it became a province: the arrows run from the Maratha lands into Bombay, from Mysore, Hyderabad and the Carnatic into Madras, and from the Bengal Suba into Calcutta. Lecture 12 slide 11: from factory to province Board, slide 12: the word "investment." For an industrialist the word has the usual meaning ("this you know"). For a merchant or trader it means: (1) purchased GOODS (boxed; an arrow marked PRIMARY) and (2) associated godowns etc. So when the EIC speaks of its "investment" in India, the primary meaning is money spent on buying Indian goods. (Compare the slide 2 board: primary purpose = trade.) Lecture 12 slide 12, teacher's board: the word investment

items.t: 17 · How each of the three Presidencies came to be
items.x: Because each Presidency grew from a different coastal base, each has its own story. Ask: which came first, and which was named after which fort? 17.1 · Madras Presidency (from 1652/1653) The EIC's first factory in India was a temporary one at Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in the Northern Sarkars (Andhra Pradesh) in 1611. (Northern Sarkars = the northern coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh, outside Mughal direct control.) 1639: the EIC, led by Francis Day, purchased land at the village of Madraspatanam from Hindu Nayakas (provincial governors of the Vijayanagara Empire, 1336-1646) and built Fort St George (1639-44): the first fort built by the EIC in India and the anchor of the first permanent settlement. 1690: the EIC purchased a fort at Cuddalore (south of Madras) from the Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram 89-00 and named it Fort Saint David. Its history: partly built by the Dutch from 1608; construction halted due to Portuguese pressure on the Vijayanagara Empire; a Hindu merchant eventually completed it. In 1677 Shivaji 74-80 conquered the nearby Jinji fort and region including Cuddalore before it passed to the EIC. The Madras Presidency was formally established as the Presidency of Fort St George in 1652, on the orders of the Court of Directors in London; because of the ship travel time, it was implemented in India in 1653. (Both dates appear in sources: the London order versus the on-ground implementation.) Ink on slide 13 (Madras). Top right: "FACTORY = warehouses + home and office + MAY be a [FORT]" (FORT boxed; "home and office" is hard to read): a factory may or may not have a fort. Underlined: 1st EIC factory, temporary, Masulipatnam, 1611, 1639, Madraspatanam, Hindu Nayakas (Vijayanagara governors), Fort St George (1639-1644) and Presidency of Fort St George (1652). Under Vijayanagara: "1336-1646" (the dynasty's span). Ink on slide 15 (Fort St David). Under the 1690 row: "After death of Sambhaji 80-89, Rajaram 89-00 left Svarajya, shifted to e.g. Jinji in Carnatic": the Maratha Chhatrapati who sold the fort had moved to Jinji in the Carnatic. Beside "Layered build": "not imp" (the Dutch, Portuguese and Hindu merchant history of the fort is not needed). Board: a large oval = Madras Presidency, cut by a diagonal with two dots, Madras and Cuddalore: "2 FORTS in Madras Presidency: Madras and Cuddalore." Lecture 12 slide 13: how Madras and Bombay Presidencies came to be Lecture 12 slide 15: Fort St David at Cuddalore 17.2 · Bombay Presidency (1687) From 1613 to 1687 Surat was the EIC's main trade centre on the west coast. The shift happened because of the growing power of the Marathas in Gujarat, making Surat increasingly risky. Bombay, a cluster of seven islands, offered a more defensible location. Charles II 60-85 received Bombay in 1661 as part of the Portuguese dowry and transferred it to the EIC in 1668 at 10 pounds per annum. The Bombay Presidency was established in 1687, replacing Surat as the western HQ. Bombay Castle (Casa da Orta) was originally built by the Portuguese and expanded by the EIC through the 18th century. Ink on slide 13 (Bombay). Right margin: "1st permanent FACTORY = Surat 1613" and, beside "replacing Surat," "PRESIDENCY 1618" (the last digit is slightly unclear; it matches the Surat Presidency of 1618 in Table T5). Also "1534-1661: Portugal" (Portugal held Bombay from the 1534 Bassein deal to the 1661 dowry). Left margin: "FORT" with a line to "Bombay Castle (Casa Da Orta)": the fort was originally Portuguese. Underlined: Charles II 60-85, Bombay in 1661, dowry, 1668 at 10 pounds per annum rent, Bombay Presidency, in 1687. 17.3 · Calcutta Presidency (from 1699/1700) The EIC's Bengal presence began with a factory at Hugli in 1651, permitted by a nishan from Shah Shuja, the Mughal governor of Bengal and son of Shahjahan 27-58. 1690: the EIC founded a settlement at the village of Sutanuti: the Calcutta establishment. The Calcutta Presidency was formally established in 1699/1700 as the Presidency of Fort William, with its own Governor. Through the 18th century the EIC developed Calcutta Port; Calcutta came to account for 60% of all EIC trade from India. 1800: Fort William College was established by Wellesley 98-05 for training EIC civil servants. 1870: the Calcutta Port Act created the Calcutta Port Commissioners and Port Trust, the first formal legal authority governing the port. Covered later (in the chapter on the Battle of Plassey): Child's War, the 1690 pardon and 1691 Farman, and the 1717 Farman. Ink on slide 14 (Calcutta). "27-58" after Shah Jahan. After "Calcutta establishment": "[3 villages: Sutanuti, Gobindapur, Kolikata]." Left: "famous for Textile" with an arrow to the "Bengal = 60%" line. Bracket on the right: "if EIC bought Rs 100 goods from India, then bought Rs 60 goods from Bengal." Under Fort William College: "Training of EIC officers"; under Wellesley 98-05 the teacher wrote the full years out as a check. Board, slide 14 (right margin): what a Presidency and a Governor are. "Presidency = Regional HQ of EIC TRADE" (TRADE underlined); "Governor = Regional Manager." Then a line with the word "annexations" and an arrow down: "Presidency = Province"; "Governor = Ruler / CM / Subadar / Nazim." Reason: before annexations the Governor only managed trade in a region; after annexations he ruled a province like a Mughal Subadar or Nazim (or a modern Chief Minister). Lecture 12 slide 14: Calcutta Presidency

items.t: 19 · The French in India and the story of Pondicherry
items.x: Because the French came last, they had Pondicherry rather than a long run. Ask: who was the real founder of French power in India? The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was founded in 1664 by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under King Louis XIV 43-15; great-grandfather of Louis XVI, overthrown in the French Revolution of 1789). It started as a private company but was later nationalised, making it in today's terms a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU). Ink on slide 19. Beside the title: "# Bengal: Chandernagore" and "# Pondicherry = MAJOR HQ 1674" (Pondicherry, MAJOR HQ and 1674 underlined). So: the French main HQ = Pondicherry (1674); their Bengal base = Chandernagore. Yellow underlines: the 1664 company, King Louis XIV 43-15, "a private company," "later nationalised," Pondicherry (acquired 1674, Sultan of Bijapur, and Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General). Lecture 12 slide 19: French East India Company and Pondicherry French settlements in India (handout list) 1. 1668, Surat: first factory, on a farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667. 2. 1669, Masulipatnam: farman from the Sultan of Golconda (1518-1687). 3. 1673, Chandarnagar: permission from Shaista Khan 64-88, Mughal governor of Bengal; financial crunch delayed it: a settlement only in 1690-92. 4. 1674, Pondicherry: acquired from Sikandar Adil Shah (1672-86) of Bijapur and his local governor Sher Khan Lodi. Developed as a city by Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General 1701-06, earlier Governor), the real founder of French power in India: centralised French administration with Pondicherry as capital (1701) and built Fort Louis. 5. 1723, Yanam: permission from Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, also called Asaf Jah I. 6. 1724, Mahe (Malabar coast): acquired from the Nair ruler Vazhunnavar in 1721; trade settlement built 1724-25 after overcoming a rebellion; named after Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46, who came with a fleet from Mauritius. 7. 1739, Karaikal: granted by Pratap Singh 39-63, Maratha ruler of Tanjore, as a reward for French help in a succession dispute. (The Thanjavur Maratha dynasty was founded not by Shivaji 74-80 directly but by his half-brother Venkoji (Ekoji) in 1674, defeating the Nayaka rulers of Madurai.) 8. 1721, Mauritius a French colony, but proper control only by 1735 under Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46 (Governor 1735-46). He came again with a fleet in 1746 and helped Dupleix 42-54 capture Madras in the 1st Carnatic War (1746-48). 9. 1949: a referendum in Chandernagore merged it into India; the rest stayed under French control until 1954. Ink on slide 20 (French acquisitions). Underlined: Surat, "farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667," Chandarnagar, Pondicherry, Sultan of Bijapur, "capital 1701," "Fort Louis built," Yanam, "Mahe on the Malabar coast" and Karaikal. A tick stands beside 1674 (Pondicherry is the key row). The 1721/1735 Mauritius row has a cross beside it (no reason is written; treat it as low priority). Ink on slide 21. "East" is underlined in the first three rows (Puducherry, Karaikal, Yanam), and a bracket closes after Mahe. So three districts are on the East coast and Mahe is the odd one out (West coast, Arabian Sea). An empty V-shaped peninsula is drawn under the table; nothing is marked on it. Pondicherry's occupation history (mnemonic PDa-FDu-BFBF to India). Pondicherry is synonymous with the French, but they were not the first there: Portuguese (16th century) → Danes (briefly in 1624) → French (1674) → Dutch (captured briefly in 1693) → British. The English captured Pondicherry in 1761 and restored it to the French via the Treaty of Paris (1763); the British captured it again (for example in 1793) before finally returning it to the French in 1814. It remained French until transferred to India in 1954.

items.t: 20 · Who came when: a master comparison

Why Asia? Asia was the economic power of the world: Indonesia gave spices, India textiles, China silk and tea. Arabs and the merchants of Genoa and Venice carried them to a Europe that was not wealthy, and each handoff made huge profit. Da Gama's 1498 cargo sold at 800% profit, and in the 1600s a kilogram of clove cost the equivalent of a kilogram of gold. The road closes. In 1453 the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople and (the teacher corrects it to 'effectively') blockaded the land routes between Europe and Asia. Necessity drove the Age of Discovery, led first by Portugal and Spain. The era gave the astrolabe, the magnetic compass, latitudes and longitudes, geography as a discipline and the caravel, a ship that could sail at an angle against the wind. The line. Pope Alexander VI mediated the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. An imaginary line in the Atlantic, about 1,185 miles west of the Cape Verde Islands, gave lands to the east to Portugal and lands to the west to Spain. Brazil's eastern tip fell on the Portuguese side, so Brazil became the only Portuguese colony in the Americas. Calicut and Cochin. Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 and got permission to trade from the Zamorin, but faced Arab opposition and left without a factory. In 1500 Cabral set up the first factory at Calicut, which Arab merchants destroyed, and then the first permanent factory at Cochin under the Raja of Cochin's protection. In 1502 Da Gama bombarded Calicut, and in 1503 Albuquerque built Fort Manuel at Cochin, the first European fort in India. Blue water, then Goa. Almeida 05-09, the first Governor, chose naval supremacy over territory (the Blue Water Policy) and forced every non-Portuguese ship to buy a Cartaz. In 1509 he beat a coalition of Gujarat, Mamluk Egypt and the Zamorin at Diu. Albuquerque 09-15 took Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur in 1510, a rare land conquest, and Nuno da Cunha 29-38 moved the HQ to Goa in 1530 and acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535). The fall of the Portuguese. The Goa Inquisition (1560-1812) and forced conversions bred resistance. St Francis Xavier, who spearheaded conversions, died on Shangchuan Island in 1552, not Goa. The causes of decline were political (the Marathas), religious backlash, corruption and personal trade, the English and Dutch, and overextension with Brazil as the priority. The companies arrive. After the English beat the Spanish Armada in 1588, British and Dutch ships could sail to Asia. The VOC was founded in 1602 by merging six companies and was the first joint-stock company with tradable shares. It reached Masulipatnam in 1605 and took Cochin in 1663. It was beaten at Colachel in 1741 by Marthanda Varma 29-58 and at Bedara in 1759, lost its posts through the Kew Letters of 1795 and was dissolved in 1799. A licence that became power. The English EIC began on 31 December 1600 under a Royal Charter of Elizabeth I 58-03, a 15-year monopoly pooled from 215 London merchants. James I 03-25 made it perpetual in 1609 and Cromwell 51-60 made it a permanent joint-stock company in 1657. The 1661 Charter of Charles II 60-85 gave it forts, troops, war and peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction, so it became a quasi-State. Surat, Swally and Roe. In 1608 Hawkins went to Jahangir 05-27's court for a Surat factory but was expelled under Portuguese pressure. The lesson was to defeat Portugal first, and in 1612 Thomas Best won the Battle of Swally. Jahangir then issued a Royal Farman in 1613 for a permanent factory at Surat, and Thomas Roe (1615-19) won the Farman of 1618 for liberal trading rights across the Mughal Empire. Presidencies. In 1661 Catherine of Braganza's dowry gave England Bombay and Tangier and 500,000 pounds, and in 1668 the Crown gave Bombay to the EIC for 10 pounds a year. The EIC's first Presidency was Surat (1618), then Madras (1652/1653), Bombay (1687) and Calcutta (1699/1700), each named after its fort. Each began as a trade HQ and grew into a province of British India. Danes, French and the order. The Danes (company 1616, Tranquebar 1620, Serampore 1755) sold their mainland posts to Britain by 1845. The French company (1664) opened at Surat in 1668 and acquired Pondicherry in 1674, which Francois Martin 01-06 made the capital in 1701. Pondicherry's occupiers ran Portuguese, Danes, French, Dutch, English, then India in 1954, so the order of arrival is a favourite Prelims test.

Prelims 1995 (Lecture 13, slides 23 and 24) Which pair is correctly matched? (a) Battle of Buxar: Mir Jafar 57-60 vs Clive 57-67; (b) Battle of Wandiwash: French vs East India Company; (c) Battle of Chilianwala: Dalhousie 48-56 vs Marathas; (d) Battle of Kharda: Nizam vs East India Company (b). Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the EIC, the decisive battle of the 3rd Carnatic War; the British under Eyre Coote beat the French under Count de Lally. Traps: Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63 (with Awadh and Shah Alam II 60-06), not Mir Jafar 57-60; Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh War); Kharda (1795) = Nizam vs the Marathas Section 6.2 Prelims 1996 (Lecture 13, slides 25 and 26) Who were the first European to initiate the policy of taking part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories? (a) Clive 57-67 (b) Dupleix 42-54 (c) Albuquerque 09-15 (d) Warren Hastings 73-85 (b) Dupleix 42-54. He invented the model of empire building in the 2nd Carnatic War (backing Muzaffar Jung 50-51 and Chanda Sahib 49-52). Clive 57-67 and Warren Hastings 73-85 used and refined the model; Albuquerque 09-15 belongs to an earlier era of direct conquest (Goa 1510) Section 5.1 Mains (teacher's board, Lecture 13, slide 9) "Model of empire building (in India) by trading companies was founded by the French and implemented by the British. Analyse." Founded by French = the 2nd Carnatic War (Dupleix 42-54's four steps). Implemented by British = future topics (Plassey, Subsidiary Alliance) Section 5.1 (the model) and Section 6.5

Story so far: one question runs through the chapter: how did a company that existed for profit end up ruling India? Ask: what do the teacher's board codes CW, (T), AWoS and MJ stand for? This chapter asks one question: how did a company that existed for profit end up ruling India? Sections 1 and 2 give the frame (the Charter of 1661, wars for trade versus wars for territory, the Anglo-Mughal War). Sections 3 to 6 are the three Carnatic Wars. The teacher's short codes on the board: CW = Carnatic War (1st, 2nd, 3rd); (T) = territory; AWoS = Austrian War of Succession; Fr eic and Eng eic = the French and English East India Companies; MJ = Muzaffar Jung 50-51; Hyd = Hyderabad. The handout for Chapter 9 ends with an index for the next chapter (Plassey and Buxar). That belongs to Chapter 10. Teacher's board: where the Carnatic Wars sit in the EIC's conquest of India The big picture on the board. The Carnatic Wars (1746-63) come first; then the EIC takes the Indian States one by one: Bengal by the Battle of Plassey 1757, Awadh by the Battle of Buxar 1764, Mysore by 4 Anglo-Mysore wars, the Marathas by 3 Anglo-Maratha wars [1775-82, 1803-05, 1817-19], the Sikhs by 2 Anglo-Sikh wars. On the right he lists the three classes of regional States from Chapter 3: SS (Successor States): Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad; Rebel States: Marathas, Jats, Sikhs, Farukhabad, Rohilkhand; AAs (Already Autonomous States): Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore. The legend at the bottom right (an empty circle leading to Diplomacy, then Domination) seems to say: the circled States (Hyderabad, Jats, Farukhabad and Rohilkhand, Rajputs and Travancore) came under the EIC through diplomacy, while the uncircled ones (Bengal, Awadh, Marathas, Sikhs, Mysore) are exactly the ones in the war list on the left. Check this board against your notebook. (1) The board writes the Anglo-Mysore wars as [1766-69, 80-84, 90-92, 99], while Chapter 7 gives the first war as 1767-69. (2) The Anglo-Sikh wars are written [1844, 1849] as they appear on the board; the detailed dates come in a later chapter.

items.t: 1 · How did a trading company become a State?
items.x: Chapter 1 of the story: a profit-making firm with State-like powers. Because the 1661 Charter gave forts, troops and courts, the Company could wage war. Ask: under which two conditions did wars for territory happen? How Did a Trading Company Become a State? Company purpose: companies exist to make profit for shareholders, the EIC was no different, but in India it became a Company Sta Companies exist to make profit for their shareholders. The EIC was no different. But what the EIC became in India went far beyond a trading enterprise. It became a Company State that, by 1857, controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. This chapter deals with Empire Building by the EIC. On the slide the teacher struck out "controlled" and wrote "RULED": by 1857 the EIC ruled 63% of the territory and 78% of the population. His fork explains the numbers: India = British India (63% of territory, 78% of population) + 565 Princely States (37% of territory, 22% of population). 1.1 The 1661 Charter 1661 Charter (teacher's ink: Charles II 60-85) The right to build forts  The right to command troops  The right to make war and peace  The right to exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India 1676 The right to mint its own money The teacher underlined forts, troops, war, peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction: these are State-like powers in the hands of a company. The same charter sits in the EIC charters table of Chapter 8. 1.2 Two kinds of wars: for trade and for territory The wars the EIC fought in India fall into two broad categories. Wars for trade: fought to protect or expand trade. Wars for territory: fought for empire building. These were different in nature and in motivation. The board's tree. The EIC was not formed for territory (T). Its goal was trade with the East Indies (not just India). So its wars were of two kinds. (1) For trade: either defensive, to protect present trade (the Carnatic Wars), or offensive, to expand trade (the Battle of Suvali 1612, from Chapter 8). (2) For territory: only in two situations, given below. Note the point for this chapter: the Carnatic Wars were wars for trade, even though they ended up laying the base for territory. Wars for territory happened under two specific conditions. 1. When the Governor or Governor-General in India was personally ambitious: an empire builder by temperament. Britain was far away. Communication was slow. These men had enough operational freedom to pursue wars that London might not have formally approved. 2. At times the EIC Army put pressure for wars. Any army has a structural interest in war: war brings a bigger defence budget, prestige, promotions and political relevance to the military. Teacher's board (no typed text): why the EIC fought wars The EIC Army was no different. Robert Clive 57-67 Governor of Bengal Presidency, in two stints: 1757-60 and 1765-67 Richard Wellesley 98-05 1798-1805 Francis Hastings 13-23 1813-23 Dalhousie 48-56 1848-56 The EIC Army's self-reinforcing war cycle (condition 2) Overhype threats: the army routinely overhyped threats to the borders; war brings budget, prestige, promotions Pressure to expand: overhyped threats create pressure for territorial expansion New borders: expansion always creates new borders New threats: new borders bring new neighbours, and so new threats, fictional or real Back to the start: the new threats are overhyped again; a self-reinforcing cycle The board gives the army's vested interest in wars as three kinds of power: economic power (a bigger defence budget, written "Def BD"), political power (a larger army) and social power. The handout's present-day parallel: think of how the Pakistan Army today has eaten Pakistan from within by putting its vested interests above the national interest, while the Indian Army has consistently done the opposite.

items.t: 2 · Wars for trade: the Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90)
items.x: Because Aurangzeb 58-07's wars and Bengal's customs disputes hurt trade, the Company picked a fight and lost. Ask: why did Aurangzeb 58-07 not expel it? Wars for Trade: Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90) The Anglo-Mughal War of 1686-90 was fought in Bengal and the Arabian Sea. It was the first significant military clash between the EIC and an Indian power. It is also called Child's War, after two men: Josiah Child: Chairman of the Court of Directors of the EIC in London. John Child: Governor of Bombay and the "General" of all EIC forces in India. The reasons were two-fold: Aurangzeb 58-07's constant warfare was disrupting EIC trade (problems in sourcing goods from the hinterland). Ongoing disputes with the Nawab of Bengal over bribes and heavy customs duties levied on the EIC. Child's War, 1686 to 1691 The EIC seizes Hugli It escalates: attacks Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea Aurangzeb 58-07's military crushes the EIC in both Bombay and Bengal By 1690 the Company surrenders February 1690: Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons the EIC in return for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation 1691 Farman: old privileges restored and duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year The starred box on the slide: "1651: the 1st EIC factory in Bengal, in Hughli." That is why Hugli is the place the EIC seizes in this war. 2.1 Why did Aurangzeb 58-07 not abolish the Company and expel the British? Because the EIC was economically useful. Its trade brought forex/gold into India, and Aurangzeb 58-07 needed them for war. With Aurangzeb 58-07's own constant warfare disrupting domestic trade, the EIC's export business was, ironically, even more valuable to the Indian economy. Indian bankers earned interest by lending money to the Company for the purchase of goods. Indian merchants, artisans and ryots all participated in and benefited from this trade ecosystem. 2.2 The 1691 Farman The 1691 Farman was technically a Parwana, because it was issued by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman. (For Farman, Parwana and Nishan see Chapter 8.) It was issued under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval. It restored the EIC's old privileges and gave it the right to duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum. Anglo-Mughal War (contd.): the 1691 Farman (technically a Parwana by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman), under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval, restored old privi The Company had been defeated militarily, yet it got this privilege, because of the benefits of European trade with India. Why give duty-free trade to a defeated company? The board's flow answers it. Ryots and artisans sell to the Indian merchant; the Indian merchant sells to the EIC; Indian bankers give loans to the EIC. Everyone in the chain earns. The money the EIC saves on duty will be used to buy more Indian goods, which means more exports. The starred aside: "TODAY we don't tax exports" (the same logic: a State gains more from exports than from taxing them).

items.t: 3 · The Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63): why the French, and why three wars
items.x: Because the rival in India was now France, three wars followed. Ask: which two wars were global spillovers, and which one was factionalism? Teacher's board (no typed text): the 3 Carnatic Wars To understand why conquest by the EIC began in Bengal, one must first understand what was happening in South India, and why the French were there. Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 was the Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742-54. Dupleix 42-54 had personal ambitions of empire building and of dominating the international trade of South India. He would become the template for everything that followed. By 1740, French EIC trade was roughly half the value of British EIC trade. The board's frame for all three wars. The reason was the international trade of India: "who will dominate the purchase of goods." The main players were the British EIC versus the French EIC. The 1st and 3rd wars were a result or a part of some international war (Britain versus France). The 2nd was caused by factionalism in Hyderabad and Carnatic: "R vs R" (rival against rival), with the French behind one rival and the British behind the other. Royal armies (British and French) took part in the 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 ONLY. Result: 3 divided by 2 = 1.5 each: the French won the 1st war and the 1st phase of the 2nd; the British won the 2nd phase of the 2nd and the 3rd. After 1756-63 the French were limited to Chandernagore and Pondicherry (the full list of five posts is in section 6.4). 3.1 Reasons for the Carnatic Wars The EIC-French contest in India had two overlapping reasons. 1. European rivalry. Two global wars spilled into India. As the two nations fought, their respective companies also entered into hostilities in India. 2. Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad contributed to the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54). The strategy was simple: put your chosen candidates in power to gain strategic influence. 1st Carnatic War 1746-48 The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) spilled into India Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746) Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) French 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54 Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad (factionalism) Ambur (1749); Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751) Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Phase 1: French. Phase 2: British 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) spilled into India Battle of Wandiwash (1760) Treaty of Paris (1763) British Under the Dupleix 42-54 row the teacher wrote "42-54, 1742-54: not in 3CW 1756-63." Remember it as a check: Dupleix 42-54 was recalled in 1754, so he took no part in the 3rd Carnatic War (he comes back in section 6.2 as "Dupleix 42-54 not here"). On the right: "How a company can build an empire: the first to show it was the French, Dupleix 42-54." The handout's heading for this section is printed as "Carnatic Wars (17456-48, 49-54, 56-63)". It is a typing slip for 1746-48.

items.t: 4 · The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) and the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)
items.x: Because the Austrian war reached India, Dupleix 42-54 took Madras and met the Nawab's cavalry. Ask: who sent the 10,000 cavalry, and what did Adyar prove? 4.1 Reason The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) was the Indian chapter of the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48). In that war Britain and France, along with their respective allies, fought each other across Europe, America and India, each wanting its preferred candidate on the Austrian throne. 4.2 Events during the war From Madras to Adyar, 1746 Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George in Madras; the EIC is defeated The Nawab of Carnatic, Anwaruddin 44-49, intervenes: he expected the French to hand over the fort to the Nawab as promised Dupleix 42-54 refuses Anwaruddin 44-49 sends an army of 10,000 cavalry Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746): about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroy the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry The battle was fought on the north bank of the River Adyar. The French force was roughly 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers. It completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. What happened here changed the nature of power in India. Who sent the 10,000 cavalry? The slide's compressed wording ("Dupleix 42-54 refused and sent 10,000 cavalry") can be misread. The handout is clear: Anwaruddin 44-49, the Nawab, sent the army of 10,000 cavalry against the French. The handout's Diagram 1 (section 7) adds one name the text does not give: "La Bourdonnais 35-46 takes Fort St George, Madras." The handout text and the slide credit the capture to Dupleix 42-54 (the Governor-General). La Bourdonnais 35-46 and Madras appear in Chapter 8. 4.3 Why the French won: three advantages of European warfare The French won due to three critical advantages that would define European military superiority in India across all the wars to come. 1. Superior artillery Light, mobile European cannon that could be repositioned rapidly on the battlefield, against which massed cavalry had no answer (link: like the small bronze cannons of Babur 26-30, spelt Babar 26-30 in this handout) 2. Tactical discipline European-trained infantry fought in coordinated formations, including infantry squares that could hold ground against cavalry charges from any direction 3. Regular cash salaries Unlike Indian armies, where soldiers were often not paid regularly, European-trained sepoys received regular wages. This created a professional, reliable fighting force with no incentive to desert between campaigns French-Trained Sepoys: the New Model Force On the three-advantages slide (Lecture 12, slide 69) the teacher underlined "light, mobile European cannon", "Babur 26-30", "formations", "infantry squares" and "small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery." He labelled the photograph "Infantry Square" and traced its corner: the men face outward on every side, so a cavalry charge from any direction meets a wall of muskets. On the Adyar slide he boxed the words "Turning Point" and wrote under it: "Indian kings wanted European help in modernising their military." Takeaway (Adyar 1746). This was not just a military victory. For the first time it was proven conclusively that a small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional Indian army. The psychological impact was enormous: it gave Europeans the confidence to start interfering directly in Indian political disputes, which is exactly what Dupleix 42-54 proceeded to do. The Indian royal elites also wanted to use the military service of the Europeans in their internal and external disputes. The Wagner Group analogy (handout). Have you heard of the Wagner Group? It is a company which sells military service to the Russian State. In a way the French were now the Wagner Group of India: a company whose army could be hired by Indian rulers. The teacher develops this on the board in section 5.1. 4.4 Consequence: the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) However, in North America, which was more strategically important to France, Britain had won. So in the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748), which ended the War of the Austrian Succession, both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in America and India. Madras went back to the EIC. For Dupleix 42-54 this was deeply frustrating: his victories in India were traded away at a negotiating table in Europe. Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748) But he was not done. His next opportunity came almost immediately, in the form of succession disputes: one in Hyderabad, one in Carnatic. The board's reasoning for the treaty. "The French won in India BUT the British won in the Americas." The two countries valued different places: Britain's main interest = India; France's main interest = the Americas, especially North and Central America. So France gave back Madras to recover what it had lost in America. Three results he lists: (1) no change in territory; (2) European infantry is far greater than Indian cavalry (the lesson of Adyar stays even though Madras is returned); (3) "Dupleix 42-54 KAT gaya" (Hindi: he was cut out, left empty-handed).

items.t: 5 · The 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): how Dupleix 42-54 invented the blueprint for empire in India
items.x: Because Aix-La-Chapelle returned Madras, Dupleix 42-54 found new quarrels. Ask: which four claimants, and which side moved first? 5.0 The succession disputes that triggered the war In Carnatic: Anwaruddin 44-49 had been appointed Nawab of Carnatic by the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1744. (The slide adds: he then became autonomous of the Nizam.) On his death a succession dispute began between: his son Md Ali 52-95 Wallajah (Md Ali 52-95), and; Chanda Sahib 49-52, the son-in-law of the earlier Nawab Dost Ali Khan 32-40 (1732-40). In Hyderabad: Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 died in 1748. The rivals for the throne were: his son Nasir Jung 48-50, and; his grandson Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (the slide adds: grandson from a daughter). Teacher's board (no typed text): "2nd CW 1749-54 Dupleix 42-54 backed Muzaffar Jung 50-51 in Hyderabad and Chanda Sahib 49-52 in Carnatic. He wanted his chosen candidates in power for economic/trade and political influence. An anxious EIC backed the opposing sides: Nasir Jung 48-50 in Hyderabad and Md Ali 52-95 in Carnatic. Carnatic Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan 32-40) Md Ali 52-95 (son of Anwaruddin 44-49) Hyderabad Muzaffar Jung 50-51 (grandson of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) Nasir Jung 48-50 (son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48) Mnemonics from the handout and the board. French side: "MuzaFFrance" (the board writes MUZAFRANCE) for Muzaffar Jung 50-51; and for Chanda Sahib 49-52: "Paris and the moon (Chanda) are symbols of romance" (board: Moon = Romance, Paris = city of romance). British side: "Nasir Hussain: England captain, cricket" for Nasir Jung 48-50; and "Jinnah, pro-British" written beside Md Ali 52-95 (the same first names as Jinnah's). The circled numbers (1) on the French EIC and (2) on the English EIC show the order: the French interfered first, the EIC only reacted. Why did the EIC react at all? The board's reasoning: "Fear of the British = if the French EIC is able to put its favourite in power, then loss of trade for the EIC." On the slide he adds what Dupleix 42-54 wanted: (a) empire building and (b) a monopoly of the international trade of South India. He also notes that Anwaruddin 44-49 wanted his son Md Ali 52-95 to be Nawab. Teacher's board (no typed text): a sketch map of Carnatic Learn the map by the board's code "MWP": on the coast from north to south come Madras (HQ of the EIC), Wandiwash (the battle of the 3rd Carnatic War) and Pondicherry (HQ of the French EIC). Arcot, inland, is the capital of Carnatic. Hyderabad lies north of the River Krishna, and the Northern Sarkars run along the coast further up. In the 2nd Carnatic War "all gathered in Carnatic": Nasir Jung 48-50 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 also arrived in Carnatic. The war has two phases: the French EIC smiles in the 1st phase (till 1751); the English EIC smiles in the 2nd phase. 5.1 Phase 1: French victory (1749-51) Phase 1 of the 2nd Carnatic War Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 is killed Chanda Sahib 49-52 is declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot By December 1750: Nasir Jung 48-50 is also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is declared Nizam Muzaffar Jung 50-51 marches toward Hyderabad, accompanied by Bussy's army February 1751, Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass: Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool; the Nawab of Kurnool is also killed Bussy reaches Hyderabad and installs Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 was killed. Chanda Sahib 49-52 was declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot. (The slide notes: Ambur is 190 km west of Chennai; the teacher added "towards Bengaluru.") By December 1750, Nasir Jung 48-50 was also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 was declared Nizam. Bussy was the junior of Dupleix 42-54. Accompanied by Bussy's army, Muzaffar Jung 50-51 began marching toward Hyderabad. But he was killed in February 1751 at the Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool, who felt cheated as he was not given the territory promised to him for his support. The Nawab of Kurnool was also killed. (The slide's aside on the pass: "unlucky lol.") Bussy now reached Hyderabad and installed Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam. He was a son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 and an uncle of the recently killed Muzaffar Jung 50-51. Beside the Hyderabad row the teacher starred: "Asaf Jahi dynasty, by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 [Asaf Jah I]." All the Hyderabad claimants here (Nasir Jung 48-50, Muzaffar Jung 50-51, Salabat Jung 51-62) belong to this one family; see Chapter 3. Teacher's board (no typed text): the Wagner Group analogy The Wagner Group board. The Wagner Group is a company that sells a service for money, and the service is military service. In the same way Muzaffar Jung 50-51 ("MJ") and Chanda Sahib 49-52 hired the French EIC, like a Wagner Group, to become rulers. So the death of MJ was a blot on the military reputation of the French EIC: a firm that sells protection cannot let its client be killed. That is why Bussy created terror on the way to Hyderabad, as a general message: "don't mess with the French EIC," and then made Salabat Jung 51-62 the Nizam. The gains from Phase 1 Dupleix 42-54's Gains from Phase 1 Hyderabad: the resident Bussy was made the French resident and agent at the Nizam's court, wielding real political influence Hyderabad: the army A French army was stationed for the Nizam's protection, and Hyderabad was to pay for it Hyderabad: the payment The payment was the Northern Sarkars region (present-day Andhra Pradesh): Bussy administered it on behalf of the Nizam and kept its revenues as payment for the French army Hyderabad: cash 2,00,000 pounds for the French EIC from the Nizam Hyderabad: personal Bussy extracted personal jagirs in Masulipatnam and Yanam Carnatic: title Dupleix 42-54 declared himself Nawab of all lands between the River Krishna and Cape Comorin (= Carnatic), with Chanda Sahib 49-52 as his Deputy Nawab of Arcot Carnatic: personal Dupleix 42-54 extracted a personal jagir of Rs 1 lakh per annum in Villianallur near Pondicherry In the Northern Sarkars Bussy's methods were brutal: terror and massacre of civilians for land revenue extraction. In Andhra folklore this terror is preserved in the word "boochi" (meaning ghost, or the feared), derived from Bussy's name. The teacher's notes on the gains slide. He wrote "Fr eic's" above the title: these are the French EIC's gains, not only Dupleix 42-54's. (1) "Hyderabad under French military domination" (the army stationed there). (2) "THINK: the French are selling a military service" (Hyderabad pays for the army, the Wagner idea again). (3) "In a way Salabat Jung 51-62 = a puppet of the French EIC." (4) Plus: "the French can counter any anti-French decision via supervision" (that is what a resident sitting in the court is for). His triangle sketch fixes the geography: Carnatic = the land from the River Krishna (top) down to Kanya Kumari or Cape Comorin (the tip). The notebook page adds two things. (1) Dupleix 42-54 got 80 villages as the Jagirdari of Villianallur, worth Rs 1 lakh. (2) In red: "today, for inflation, = 3 crore rupees per annum," to show how large a personal income this was. The two circled places on the map, Yanam and Masulipatnam, are Bussy's personal jagirs. Two things to check on the notebook page. (1) Its title dates the 2nd Carnatic War "1750-54"; the handout and every slide give 1749-54. (2) The red bracket is written "x 300%", but Rs 1 lakh becomes Rs 3 crore only when multiplied by 300 times; take the point (a very large income), not the arithmetic. Teacher's board (no typed text) THINK: why do Company men build empires? As an employee of the French EIC a man gets only a salary. BUT empire building now brings him personal jagirs plus cash. So the personal interest of these empire-builder employees drives the wars. And this holds for every company: the French EIC, the English EIC, the Estado da India and the Dutch VOC. (This is condition 1 of section 1.2: the personally ambitious Governor.) Takeaway: Dupleix 42-54 had just invented the model of empire building in India. Put your candidate in power, station your army at his expense, extract territory as payment, and sit in the court as the real power behind the throne. This is exactly the model the British EIC would refine and use with devastating effect for the next century. (The handout's aside: "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54" would be the thoughts of the EIC.) Dupleix 42-54's model of empire building (later copied and refined by the EIC) 1. Succession dispute = opportunity: interfere and bring your favourite claimant into power 2. Extract gains, military domination: station your army in the Indian State and make the State pay for this army 3. Extract gains, territory as payment: take land as payment for the army 4. Puppet State: station your Resident in the Indian King's court, who establishes his indirect rule On the model slide (Lecture 13, slide 10) the teacher wrote "FACTIONALISM (R vs R)" above step 1: the opening is always a quarrel between two rivals. Beside step 2 he wrote "Free of cost domination": the Indian State itself pays for the army that dominates it. He underlined "Resident in the Indian King's court" and "Indirect Rule" in step 4. Teacher's board (no typed text), headed "FYQ-M" (underlined; the first letter is unclear, probably PYQ-M) The Mains question on the board: "Model of empire building (in India) by trading companies was founded by the French and implemented by the British. Analyse." The teacher split the answer into two parts: "founded by French" = the 2nd Carnatic War (this section: the four steps above, with Hyderabad and Carnatic as the examples); "implemented by British" = future topics (Plassey and Buxar in Chapter 10, the Subsidiary Alliance in Chapter 11). Prelims 1996: the first European to take part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories = (b) Dupleix 42-54. He invented the model: back a candidate, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment, sit in court as the real power. It was first used in the 2nd Carnatic War (backing Muzaffar Jung 50-51 and Chanda Sahib 49-52). Clive 57-67 came later: he used and refined the model in Bengal (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764) but did not invent it. Albuquerque 09-15 was a 16th-century Portuguese conqueror (took Goa 1510): an earlier era of direct conquest, not the "back-a-claimant" model. Warren Hastings 73-85 was a later EIC Governor-General: a refiner, not the originator. 5.2 Phase 2: the EIC bounces back The EIC decided to fight back by supporting Md Ali 52-95 (Carnatic), who was holding out in Trichinopoly. Dupleix 42-54 got obsessed with eliminating any future challenge to his power. Hence he made the critical mistake of leaving the capital Arcot unguarded and focusing on Trichinopoly. Robert Clive 57-67, operating from Madras with a small force of roughly 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys, took over Arcot (the slide dates it: Arcot 1751). He then defended it against a massive counter-siege for 53 days. The capital was now with the British! Clive 57-67 became a celebrated figure back in Britain. The French government in Paris, anxious to honour the 1748 treaty and preserve its more lucrative American possessions, refused to help Dupleix 42-54. By 1754 the French had lost the 2nd Carnatic War. Phase 2: how the capital was lost Md Ali 52-95 holds out in Trichinopoly, backed by the EIC Dupleix 42-54's critical mistake: he focuses on Trichinopoly and leaves the capital Arcot unguarded Clive 57-67 takes Arcot (1751) from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys He defends it through a 53-day counter-siege Paris refuses to help Dupleix 42-54: it wants to honour the 1748 treaty and keep its American possessions By 1754 the French have lost the 2nd Carnatic War On the slide the teacher underlined only two phrases: "1748 treaty" and "refused to help Dupleix 42-54." That is the real reason for the defeat: France chose America over India again, exactly as in 1748. 5.3 The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Dupleix 42-54 was recalled to France, replaced by Godeheu, on account of the high war expenditure. He died in poverty in France in 1763, abandoned by the State he had served. The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) was a middle path: 1. Hyderabad French influence remained in Hyderabad: (1) Bussy as agent, (2) the French army in Hyderabad, (3) the Northern Sarkars with the French French 2. Factories French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic were retained  3. Carnatic Md Ali 52-95 became Nawab of Carnatic: hence EIC influence in Carnatic British Chanda Sahib 49-52, having escaped to Tanjore (present-day Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu), was beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, the Maratha Raja of Thanjavur: an old rival. Maratha rule in Tanjore had begun in 1674 when Venkoji (also known as Ekoji), half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80, conquered the region. Why was a winning Governor-General recalled? The teacher's bracket: "Company = an organisation with a profit motive." High war expenditure eats profit, so the company removes the man who causes it. Beside the Factories row he repeats the definition from Chapter 8: "Factory = warehouses + homes + offices + maybe a fort." His two smileys read the treaty as a split: the French smile in Hyderabad, the British smile in Carnatic. Teacher's board (no typed text): how wars end The board's theory of treaties (marked "imp factors"). War is expensive for both, the losing party and the victorious party, so both want an end to the war. The victor will agree to end the war if it has achieved its war aims, that is, the core goal of the war. For the EIC the core motive was trade, so it could settle once its trade was safe (the two branches read Hyderabad and Carnatic, each with a smiley, matching the treaty slide's split). When a treaty is negotiated, the important factors are the power differential between the two sides and their ability, economic and military. Apply this to all three treaties: 1748 (the bracket recalls the Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 and the 1st Carnatic War 1746-48), 1754 and 1763.

Because royal armies now joined the Companies, the contest turned decisive. Ask: why did France lose, and why did the EIC win all three wars? 6.1 Reason The 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) was once again a European conflict brought to Indian shores: the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), fought across Europe, the Americas, Africa and India. French side: Count de Lally (of the French State, not the French EIC) arrived from France with the Royal military and led the French alongside Bussy of the French EIC. British side: Eyre Coote (of the British State, not the EIC) arrived from Britain with the Royal military and led the British alongside Robert Clive 57-67 of the EIC. The board's recap before the 3rd war. Of the three Carnatic Wars (1746-63), wars 1 and 3 come from "IR" (international relations: Britain against France), war 2 from factionalism. What is new in war 3: the Royal militaries (French and British) joined the armies of the French EIC and the English EIC. So the line-up is [EIC + Britain] versus [French EIC + France]. On the typed slide he wrote "had impacts" above "a European conflict on Indian shores" and underlined Count de Lally, Eyre Coote and royal military on both sides. Teacher's board (no typed text) 6.2 Why did France lose the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)? Handout map (also Lecture 13, slide 16): a close-up of the Coromandel Coast from an old printed map The most decisive battle was the Battle of Wandiwash (1760). (The handout's memory line: "where the French were washed away.") After that the French lost everywhere, including Pondicherry itself, their headquarters officially since 1701, with Fort Louis. The chain slides add: Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760, and the Siege of Pondicherry came in 1761. The three pointer lines on the map mark the same three coastal places as the board's "MWP": Madras (the British base), Wandiwash (between the two) and Pondicherry (the French base). Wandiwash lies between the two headquarters, which is why the decisive battle was there. Prelims 1995: UPSC asked "match the battle to who fought it" by jumbling correct pairs. The correct pairs are: Battle of Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63 (with Awadh and Shah Alam II 60-06); Battle of Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh War); Battle of Kharda (1795) = Nizam of Hyderabad vs the Marathas; Battle of Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the East India Company. The answer was (b). The trap in (a): Mir Jafar 57-60 was the EIC's man at Plassey 1757, not its enemy at Buxar. France lost for four reasons. Wandiwash (1760): Why France Lost the 3rd War 1. Tactical mistake Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic. Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Bengal and took over the Northern Sarkars in 1759 2. Poor leadership Lally was despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, which demoralised the army 3. Financial weakness French soldiers went unpaid for months. The French EIC had spent heavily in the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) and the first two Carnatic Wars without commensurate gains. In contrast, Britain had been profiting from eastern trade since 1600. British capitalism was mature; feudalism in France ended only after the French Revolution of 1789, while the Industrial Revolution had begun in Britain (1750-1850) 4. Superior British navy This gave Britain decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic. Britain's navy was able to dominate the Coromandel coast The sketch for the tactical mistake. Step (1): Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars and goes down to Carnatic to help Lally. Step (2): from Bengal, Clive 57-67 comes down into the now unguarded Northern Sarkars (1759). Under "Poor leadership" the teacher wrote "Dupleix 42-54 not here": the one able French leader had been recalled in 1754, so France fought this war with Lally. On financial weakness. The "earlier wars" that drained the French EIC are the Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 [the 1st Carnatic War 1746-48] and the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54. His note on the second: "Hyderabad gains, BUT STILL higher war expenditure": even the winning phase cost more than it earned. For the navy point he wrote Carnatic over Coromandel Coast: Carnatic is the land along the Coromandel coast, so whoever commands the sea commands the war there. Teacher's board (no typed text): "if you want to see [CAPITALISM] in SOCIETY" (Capitalism boxed), with three bullets: "wake up at 4am and sit in BALCONY (facing a main ro What does "British capitalism was mature" mean? The board's picture. If you want to see capitalism in a society: wake up at 4 am and sit in a balcony facing a main road. People are already at work. In a capitalist society people at the mass level have a belief that they can become rich by working hard. Bombay never sleeps, because the city provides opportunities to earn 24x7. The French Revolution of 1789 ended feudalism, and only then did capitalism come to France (but note: merchants existed in France before 1789 too). Britain had this money-making society earlier, so it could pay for its wars. 6.3 Why did the EIC win the Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63)? 1. France starved Dupleix 42-54 of reinforcements To preserve its gains from the 1748 Treaty (Aix-La-Chapelle) 2. Leadership French: the recall of Dupleix 42-54 after the 2nd Carnatic War hurt the chances of French victory; Lally displayed poor leadership in the 3rd Carnatic War. British: Robert Clive 57-67 and Eyre Coote displayed good leadership 3. Superior British navy British naval dominance of the coast 4. Finances The EIC was a private joint-stock firm with deep capital; it had accumulated wealth, along with huge monetary gains after Plassey 1757. The French EIC was a State PSU with weak finances. The French economy was weak compared to Britain, which was the world's top economy of the time. Past war expenditure without any formidable gains hurt French capabilities, e.g. Lally's troops went unpaid (the slide adds: unpaid for months, so low morale) 5. Tactical mistakes Leaving Arcot (the capital of Carnatic) unguarded in the 2nd Carnatic War and leaving the Northern Sarkars unguarded in the 3rd Carnatic War Above the slide's title the teacher wrote "all (3)": this table answers "Why the EIC won all 3 Carnatic Wars," while section 6.2 answers only the 3rd war. For a Mains answer, use 6.3 for the whole contest and 6.2 for Wandiwash. The handout numbers these factors 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 (the number 2 is printed twice). There are five factors; they are renumbered 1 to 5 here. 6.4 The Treaty of Paris (1763) Under the Treaty of Paris (1763): France lost all gains made in India since 1749 and was restricted to its pre-1749 position. France retained only five small trading posts: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam and Chandernagore. France was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases. P Pondicherry East coast M Mahe West coast (teacher: Malabar) K Karaikal East coast Y Yanam East coast C Chandernagore East (teacher: Bengal) The slide's mnemonic "PM KYC (Yojana)" is underlined by the teacher: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore. Only Mahe is on the west coast (Malabar); Chandernagore is in Bengal. He replaced "trading posts" with "trading CENTRES." At the top he lined up the three treaties to learn in order: 1748 Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle, 1754 Treaty of Pondicherry, 1763 Treaty of Paris. In 1769 the French EIC was abolished by France. This signifies that the French government had given up on its ambitions of dominating the international trade of India. The abolition of the French EIC does not mean other French traders could not trade in India, just that the French State was not interested in running a government company for it. After successfully countering the Portuguese by 1612, the Dutch by the 1650s and the French by 1763, the British EIC now had a monopoly over India's international trade. Under the British monopoly row the teacher wrote "NOT (T)": in 1763 the EIC has a monopoly over trade, not territory. What was decided was only "who will buy Indian goods, who will dominate exports from India." This fits the board in section 1.2: the Carnatic Wars were wars for trade. 6.5 Link with Plassey, and what came later Takeaway: link with the Battle of Plassey (1757). The 3rd Carnatic War brought large numbers of British Royal military troops to India, and it was this military strength, and Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy, that made Plassey possible. Without Carnatic there may not have been a Plassey, which led to Empire Building by the EIC. From a global war to Plassey (teacher's flow) Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) 3rd Carnatic War British Royal military in India Confidence of Clive 57-67 for accepting Jafar's offer: Plassey 1757 Carnatic Wars: Legacy and After Later: In the Treaty of Hyderabad (1766), Hyderabad formally ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually and protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Hyderabad became the 1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC, in 1798. Mysore signed in 1799 and Travancore in 1805, while Carnatic was annexed in 1801. Thus the Carnatic Wars, though fought for the international trade of India, laid the foundation of British domination of South India. Under "Domination of South India" the teacher wrote "3rd CW + 3.5 decades": that is, from the end of the 3rd Carnatic War (1763) it took about three and a half decades to reach the first Subsidiary Alliance (Hyderabad, 1798). He underlined each item of that row: Hyderabad 1798, Mysore 1799, Travancore 1805, Carnatic annexed 1801. "Jafar's offer" in his flow is Mir Jafar 57-60's deal with Clive 57-67, the story of Chapter 10.

items.t: 7 · Diagram 1: the Carnatic Wars in one chain
items.x: Last scene: the whole chain on one page. Ask: can you retell it from the Austrian war of 1740 to the Treaty of Paris in 1763? How to read Diagram 1. In the printed figure the arrows of the middle row run from the Treaty of Pondicherry box to Arcot and then to the 2nd Carnatic War box, which is the reverse of the time order. Read the middle row from left to right instead: 2nd Carnatic War (Ambur 1749), then Arcot 1751, then the Treaty of Pondicherry 1754. The class slides (Lecture 12, slides 66 and 67) show the same chain in the correct order, as below. The Carnatic Wars: the chain, 1740 to 1763 Austrian War of Succession (1740-48): Anglo-French rivalry in Europe spills into India 1st Carnatic War (1746-48): Battle of Adyar/St Thome 1746; the French crush the Nawab's cavalry Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748): ends the Austrian War; Madras returned to the EIC 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54): Ambur 1749; Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Salabat Jung 51-62 installed; Dupleix 42-54 invents the empire model Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751): 53-day defence; Md Ali 52-95 (Wallajah) prevails Treaty of Pondicherry (1754): Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu; French momentum broken 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63): Seven Years' Global War; de Lally versus Eyre Coote Wandiwash (22 January 1760): decisive EIC victory over the French Siege of Pondicherry (1761), then Treaty of Paris (1763): French power in India permanently broken

1600 Britain profiting from eastern trade since this year 1612 Portuguese countered by the EIC (Battle of Suvali: an offensive war for trade) 1650s Dutch countered by the EIC 1651 First EIC factory in Bengal, at Hugli (teacher's note) 1661 Charter: right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, civil and criminal jurisdiction ★ 1674 Maratha rule in Tanjore begins under Venkoji (Ekoji), half-brother of Shivaji 74-80 1676 EIC gets the right to mint its own money 1686 Anglo-Mughal War (Child's War) begins, to 1690 ★ 1690 February: Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons the EIC for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation 1691 Farman (technically a Parwana): duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year ★ 1701 Pondicherry the French headquarters officially, with Fort Louis 1732 Dost Ali Khan 32-40 Nawab of Carnatic (to 1740) 1740 War of the Austrian Succession (to 1748); French EIC trade about half of British EIC trade 1742 Dupleix 42-54 becomes Governor-General of the French EIC (to 1754) ★ 1744 Anwaruddin 44-49 appointed Nawab of Carnatic by the Nizam of Hyderabad 1746 1st Carnatic War (to 1748); Fort St George captured; Battle of Adyar/St Thome ★ 1748 Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle: Madras returned to the EIC; Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 dies ★ 1749 2nd Carnatic War (to 1754); Battle of Ambur: Anwaruddin 44-49 killed, Chanda Sahib 49-52 Nawab ★ 1750 December: Nasir Jung 48-50 killed; Muzaffar Jung 50-51 declared Nizam 1751 February: Muzaffar Jung 50-51 killed at Lakkireddipalli Pass; Salabat Jung 51-62 installed; Clive 57-67 takes Arcot (53-day defence) ★ 1754 Treaty of Pondicherry; Dupleix 42-54 recalled, replaced by Godeheu ★ 1756 3rd Carnatic War and the Seven Years' Global War (both to 1763) ★ 1757 Battle of Plassey, made possible by the Royal troops of the 3rd Carnatic War 1759 Clive 57-67 takes the Northern Sarkars after Bussy leaves them 1760 22 January: Battle of Wandiwash, Eyre Coote defeats Lally ★ 1761 Siege of Pondicherry 1763 Treaty of Paris: France back to its pre-1749 position, five posts only; Dupleix 42-54 dies in poverty ★ 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: Northern Sarkars ceded to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year 1769 French EIC abolished by France 1798 Hyderabad: first Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance ★ 1799 Mysore signs the Subsidiary Alliance 1801 Carnatic annexed 1805 Travancore signs the Subsidiary Alliance 1857 EIC controls 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population

A shop that became a State. Companies exist for profit, and the EIC was no different, yet by 1857 it ruled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. The 1661 Charter had given it forts, troops, war and peace and courts, and 1676 its own mint. Its wars were for trade (defensive, like the Carnatic Wars) or for territory, when a Governor was personally ambitious or the EIC Army pushed for war. Child's War (1686-90). Aurangzeb 58-07's wars and quarrels over bribes and customs in Bengal pushed the EIC to seize Hugli and attack Mughal ships. Aurangzeb 58-07 crushed it in Bombay and Bengal, the Company surrendered by 1690, and in February 1690 he pardoned it for Rs 1.5 lakh. The 1691 Farman, technically a Parwana, gave duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year, because the EIC brought forex and gold and fed bankers, merchants, artisans and ryots. Enter Dupleix. Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 is Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742 to 1754, with personal ambitions of empire and of dominating South India's trade; by 1740 French trade is about half of the British. The three Carnatic Wars are 1746-48, 1749-54 and 1756-63: the 1st and 3rd are global wars spilling into India, and the 2nd is factionalism, R versus R. Adyar, 1746. The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) reaches India, and Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George at Madras. Anwaruddin 44-49, Nawab of Carnatic, expected the fort and, when Dupleix 42-54 refused, sent 10,000 cavalry; at Adyar about 700 French-trained sepoys and 300 French soldiers destroyed them with light cannon, infantry squares and regular pay. It was a turning point: Indian kings now wanted European help to modernise their armies. Aix-La-Chapelle, 1748. The treaty ended the Austrian war and returned possessions in America and India, so Madras went back to the EIC. The French had won in India but the British in the Americas, and Britain's main interest was India while France's was the Americas. Nothing changed in territory, European infantry stayed far greater than Indian cavalry, and Dupleix 42-54 was left empty-handed. Two quarrels, four claimants. In Carnatic, Md Ali 52-95 (son of Anwaruddin 44-49) faces Chanda Sahib 49-52 (son-in-law of Dost Ali Khan 32-40). In Hyderabad, after Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 dies in 1748, his son Nasir Jung 48-50 faces his grandson Muzaffar Jung 50-51. The French move first for Chanda Sahib 49-52 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51, and the anxious EIC reacts for Md Ali 52-95 and Nasir Jung 48-50, fearing lost trade. Phase 1: the French kingmaker. At Ambur in 1749 Anwaruddin 44-49 dies and Chanda Sahib 49-52 is made Nawab; by December 1750 Nasir Jung 48-50 is dead and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is Nizam. Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed in February 1751 at Lakkireddipalli Pass, so Bussy installs Salabat Jung 51-62. The French gain a resident and an army at Hyderabad, paid for with the Northern Sarkars, 2,00,000 pounds and jagirs, and Dupleix 42-54 styles himself Nawab from the Krishna to Cape Comorin. His four steps are a model: a succession dispute, an army at the State's cost, territory as payment, a Resident. Phase 2: Arcot, 1751. Dupleix 42-54 fixes on Trichinopoly, where Md Ali 52-95 holds out, and leaves Arcot unguarded, so Clive 57-67 takes it from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys and holds it for 53 days. Paris, wanting to honour the 1748 treaty and keep America, refuses to help. By the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) Dupleix 42-54 is recalled, Godeheu replaces him, the French keep Hyderabad influence and Md Ali 52-95 becomes Nawab of Carnatic; Chanda Sahib 49-52 is beheaded at Tanjore by Pratap Singh 39-63. The 3rd war and Wandiwash. The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) brings royal armies for the first time: Count de Lally with Bussy for France, Eyre Coote with Clive 57-67 for Britain. Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars to help Lally, so Clive 57-67 takes them in 1759, and Lally's rude conduct and unpaid soldiers weaken the French, who also face a superior British navy. Eyre Coote wins the decisive battle of Wandiwash on 22 January 1760 and Pondicherry falls in 1761. Paris, 1763. France loses all gains since 1749, keeps five posts (Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore) and may not keep a strong army or fortify its bases; in 1769 the French EIC is abolished. Having countered the Portuguese by 1612 and the Dutch by the 1650s, the British EIC now has a monopoly over India's international trade. It won all three wars because France starved Dupleix 42-54, had weaker leadership and a weaker navy, and could not match a private joint-stock firm with deep capital. From Carnatic to Plassey. The 3rd war brought large royal military forces to India, and that strength plus Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey 1757 possible.
