Story so far: one man, three roads (Lapse, War, Lieu), and a second face as builder. Keep the board in mind. Ask: what did the teacher say Dalhousie 48-56 implemented, and via what? Chapter 14 title slide: Dalhousie 48-56 (1848-56): Peak of Expansion The whole chapter in one diagram. Dalhousie 48-56 implemented the Policy of Paramountcy to expand the British empire "via" three routes: Wars, Doctrine of Lapse, and territory (T) in place of subsidy. The fan of lines is the other face of the same man: Wood's Despatch 1854, the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856 (the bracket says it was passed during Canning 56-62, so he only supported it), Railways, Post and Telegraph, Canals. The teacher marks these as "Future syllabus" (topics he returns to later: see Chapter 19 for education and social reform). Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58) Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58), by Francis Hastings 13-23. Paramount = Supreme. The core idea in his words: "Among all States in India, the Company State is paramount; British interests are supreme, and to guard those interests the EIC will do anything, even annexation." He draws India as a circle cut in two: the Company State (63% of territory, 78% of population) and the 565 Indian States. He adds a bracket: the Policy of Paramountcy "contributed to the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19" (Chapter 13). He also notes that "Paramountcy of the British Crown" (1858 to 15 August 1947) is a legal relationship between the Crown and the Indian Prince, "not British India" (British India is the part ruled by the British). Do not mix the two Paramountcies: the EIC's (1813-58) and the Crown's (1858-1947). Slide 4 is a board without an explanation. It shows a circle with a curved line cutting off a small segment marked "MMP" and the words "Notes of Foundation" underneath. It reads as: the large part of this chapter's material is the "foundation" (this notebook), and a small part is covered in the teacher's MMP. The slide itself says no more than that.

items.t: 1 · Peak of Expansion: how far and by what means
items.x: Because Paramountcy made British interests supreme, expansion had a policy behind it. Ask: what were the three instruments, and what share of land and people did the Company State hold by 1856? Peak of Expansion table By the end of Dalhousie 48-56's tenure the Company State controlled 63% of India, home to 78% of its population. After Dalhousie 48-56 there were no further annexations. He used the Policy of Paramountcy (PoP 1813-58) in three ways: 1. Doctrine of Lapse: annexation by refusing to recognise adopted heirs. 2. Wars: the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War 1848-49 (Punjab annexed) and the 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 (Pegu annexed). 3. Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar 1853 from Hyderabad. Besides these: the Maritime Ring Fence, the modernisation infrastructure and the five-policy framework. "Annexation of the Indian mainland" means annexation "into British-ruled India, that is British India." He writes "i.e. Br India" and underlines British India. On the Lapse row he supplies the logic of why the British cared about succession: succession disputes (R v R, read as ruler against ruler) → instability → hurt British business interests; and "British interests = Paramount." So the Doctrine of Lapse is not just a legal trick: instability in an Indian State threatens British trade, and British interests are supreme. The small BERAR / HYD circle is the picture for the third instrument: Berar sits at the top of the Hyderabad circle.

items.t: 2 · The Doctrine of Lapse: legal principle against pretext
items.x: Because succession disputes hurt trade, a rule about heirs became a tool of expansion. Ask: who formulated it, who implemented it, and what did it override? The Doctrine of Lapse was formulated by the Court of Directors of the EIC in 1847 but implemented systematically by Dalhousie 48-56. The rule was simple: if an Indian ruler died without a biological heir, his rights lapsed and the State was annexed into British India. Under Hindu law, adoption was a legitimate mechanism for succession: adopted sons inherited with full legitimacy. The Doctrine of Lapse refused to recognise this. The Court of Directors is the "top decision-making body of the EIC," that is the Board of Directors, "not a Government body." He writes "PRELIMS" beside it, so the Prelims trap is: who formulated the doctrine (the Court of Directors, 1847) against who implemented it (Dalhousie 48-56). His bracket: "Dalhousie 48-56 # Author of DoL" (he is credited as author in common speech because he applied it). "Rights lapsed" means e.g. R2 Rule, R2 Pension: the right to rule and the right to the pension both lapsed (read R2 as "right to"). And "DoL overrides Hindu Law." "Author of the Doctrine" is not the same as "formulator." The handout and slide say formulated by the Court of Directors in 1847, implemented systematically by Dalhousie 48-56. The teacher's bracket lets you call Dalhousie 48-56 its author in a loose sense. In a Prelims statement, choose by the verb: formulated = Court of Directors; implemented = Dalhousie 48-56.

Because the rule was applied State by State, seven fell in seven years. Ask: which was first, which two share 1849, and which Udaipur is meant? Under the Doctrine of Lapse, Dalhousie 48-56 annexed seven States in seven years. 1 1848 Satara Maharashtra 2 1849 Sambalpur Odisha 3 1849 Jaitpur Uttar Pradesh, Bundelkhand region 4 1850 Baghat Himachal Pradesh: a small hill State near Solan 5 1852 Udaipur Chhattisgarh (formerly part of the Central Provinces) 6 1853-54 Jhansi Uttar Pradesh 7 1854 Nagpur Maharashtra His mnemonic, written beside each State: "BHAGAT SAMBHAL, JA JHAdio mein, UDta SA NAG". The order of the mnemonic is Baghat, Sambalpur, Jaitpur, Jhansi, Udaipur, Satara, Nagpur, which is not the date order; use the table for dates. Under Nagpur he writes "L 1816 Subordinate Alliance" (he links Nagpur's earlier treaty of 1816 to its later fate; the 1816 treaty is in Chapter 13). The Udaipur annexed in 1852 is NOT the famous Rajput kingdom of Udaipur (Mewar) in Rajasthan. It is a smaller princely State in present-day Chhattisgarh (then the Central Provinces). The handout and slide 10 both flag this trap. Flowchart of the Lapse annexations (handout figure): Satara 1848 (no biological heir; Pratap Singh's adopted son rejected), Jaitpur 1849 (Bundelkhand, UP), Sambalpur 1849 "Common mistake": Awadh 1856 is not a Lapse annexation. He draws a line from his note to the yellow Awadh box at the end of the Lapse chain. Details of why are in Section 7. A date wrinkle. The handout table gives Jhansi as 1853-54; the flowchart and the Prelims 2004 answer give 1854. For a sequence question use 1854. (Satara 1848, Sambalpur 1849, Jhansi 1854 gives order 3, 2, 1.) The flowchart lists Jaitpur before Sambalpur; both are 1849, so the table's order (Sambalpur, then Jaitpur) is the one to learn.

Because the same logic was turned on land, tax-free grants were tested for proof of title. Ask: where, in what year, and how many estates? Dalhousie 48-56 also targeted privileged landholdings. In 1852 the Bombay Presidency set up the Inam Commission to investigate inams (tax-free grants) made by earlier Indian rulers to Brahmins, temples and others. The Commission demanded proof of title; grants with insufficient proof were confiscated. Around 20,000 estates were seized in the Bombay Presidency alone. The logic: the Inam Commission was the Doctrine of Lapse applied to land titles instead of thrones. If you cannot prove your claim to the Company's satisfaction, the Company takes it. The logic was identical. He underlines Bombay Presidency, tax-free grants (inams), proof of title and about 20,000 estates as the four facts to hold. Beside the Logic row label he writes "ignore" (underlined): the comparison with Lapse is a handout aid, not something he wants memorised for the exam. The handout repeats it later in the legitimacy discussion (Section 13).

items.t: 5 · The Doctrine of Lapse applied to pensions: Nana Sahib
items.x: Because Lapse also reached pensions, a Peshwa's adopted son was refused. Ask: why did this make Nana Sahib an 1857 leader? Dalhousie 48-56 extended the Doctrine of Lapse to pensions. Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 died in 1851. Dalhousie 48-56 refused to continue the State pension of Rs 8 lakh per annum to his adopted son Nana Sahib. The argument: adopted sons inherit private wealth, not political titles or State pensions. The refusal made Nana Sahib a key 1857 leader from Bithur, where Bajirao II 96-18 had been pensioned off in 1819 after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War.

items.t: 6 · Annexation in lieu of subsidy: Berar (1853)
items.x: Because Hyderabad could not pay its subsidy, land became payment. Ask: which province in which year, and which earlier case follows the same pattern? Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy is the second instrument (the slide's order) of Dalhousie 48-56. Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 and had been paying ever-rising subsidy ever since. By 1853 Hyderabad could not pay. Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Berar as permanent payment of the subsidy. Recall: in 1801 half of Awadh was annexed as subsidy (Section 7). The pattern is the same: unpaid subsidy becomes territory.

Because Awadh fell over six steps from 1765, it was not a Lapse case. Ask: why could Lapse not apply, and what pretext was used? Teacher's board: Clive, Wellesley 98-05, Dalhousie 48-56 on Awadh Annexation of Awadh (1856), 6 steps The six steps of Awadh's fall: 1. 1765: Treaty of Allahabad (by Robert Clive 57-67) established PoIR + PoRF + a mini Subsidiary Alliance in Awadh. 2. The EIC gradually increased its subsidy demands on Awadh. 3. 1798: John Shore 93-98 replaced Wazir Ali 97-98 as Nawab with his uncle Sadat Ali Khan II, in return for an annual subsidy of Rs 76 lakh and the cession of Allahabad fort. 4. 1801: Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted. Wellesley 98-05 imposed the full Subsidiary Alliance by sending Henry Wellesley. Half of Awadh (Gorakhpur, Rohilkhand and the Doab) was annexed as permanent payment of the subsidy, called the Ceded Districts; it was unjust, as the revenue was twice the subsidy. 5. The EIC kept demanding more subsidy despite the permanent payment. The Nawab had to raise taxes and by 1855 there was a threat of peasant revolts. 6. 1856: Dalhousie 48-56 annexed the rest of Awadh on grounds of maladministration. By 1855 the British Resident had established Indirect Rule and Nawab Wajid Ali Shah had no real power, hence no power but all responsibility. How the three men line up on one timeline: Clive 57-67 (ToA 1765): PoIR initiated, and by 1855 Indirect Rule of the British Resident. The bracket "90 yrs vs 7 yrs in Bengal" compares how long Indirect Rule lasted in Awadh (1765 to 1855, 90 years) against Bengal (about 7 years, 1765 to 1772). He calls the 1765 arrangement "mini SA" or "quasi SA." Wellesley 98-05 (1801 SA): the Doab is the land between two rivers, very fertile, high land revenue; Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand had been with Awadh since 1775. Dalhousie 48-56: rising land revenue, therefore rising subsidy, therefore by 1855 the threat of peasant revolt, therefore British business interests under threat [PoP 1813-58]; the Nawab is accused of maladministration, so Awadh is annexed. The teacher's side list on slide 15 for the mini SA reads "X DCFA, X Awadh Army = 0, Rest Yes" (read: Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs not fully taken over, Awadh's army not reduced to zero, the rest yes: subsidy, an EIC army, military alliance, a British Resident) [unclear: check your notebook for the exact reading]. He writes "= military alliance" over PoRF and "Be-SHaram" (shameless, said of step 5: the EIC demanded more after taking half the State). The 1856 Awadh annexation was NOT under the Doctrine of Lapse: Wajid Ali Shah had heirs. Prelims 2008: "Which State's ruler was removed on the pretext of misgovernance?" Answer: Awadh (a). Jhansi and Nagpur went by Lapse; Satara was the first Lapse State, 1848. Handout and slide order: step 3 names the Nawab placed in 1798 as Sadat Ali Khan II. Ch 10 notes the formal alliance with Awadh as 1801 (Chapter 10). The handout also describes the 1765 treaty as "PoIR + PoRF + mini SA"; that is the Clive 57-67 chain taught in Chapter 10 and Chapter 11. Teacher's board: Awadh A (1801) and B (1856), and the naming of United Provinces 1801 Ceded Districts formed from the annexed half of Awadh 1836 Given full province status as the North-Western Provinces (NWP 1836) (the teacher: capital Agra) 1856 Rest of Awadh annexed (the teacher: capital Lucknow) 1877 Both territories reorganised as the "North-Western Provinces and Oudh" 1902 Renamed "United Provinces of Agra and Oudh" 1937 Renamed "United Provinces" 1950 Became Uttar Pradesh after independence 2000 Uttarakhand carved out of it (the teacher: "UK + UP")

items.t: 8 · The Sikh State: from ideal buffer to annexation target
items.x: Because Ranjit Singh 01-39 held the buffer together and factions tore it apart after 1839, the EIC moved from treaty to annexation. Ask: what did Lahore take, and what did Amritsar 1846 do? 8.1 Buffer to target Under the Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) the EIC wanted stable, strong, friendly border States as a protective buffer around British India. If stability could not be achieved, the EIC either: established Indirect Rule: Nepal 1814-16, Afghanistan 1839, Punjab 1845; or directly annexed: Assam and parts of lower Burma 1824-26, Punjab 1849, Burma 1852-53. Sikh State: From Buffer to Target The Sikh State had been that ideal buffer under Maharaja Ranjit Singh 01-39. After his death in 1839, factionalism tore the State apart: 1. Royal family members fought for succession. 2. The Sindhanwaliyas, a Jat clan or misl. 3. Dogra Rajputs who served as Wazirs at different times. 4. The Khalsa Army itself. Succession disputes and political murders followed; the PoRF was now useless as the State weakened from within. "Imp" is written over "stable, strong, friendly": the three qualities the EIC wanted in a buffer State. His Great Game sketch: Russia → Afghanistan → Punjab (with the Sutlej) → British India. "This fear led to 1809: the Treaty of Amritsar" (the EIC's PoRF with the Sikhs). 1838 Tripartite Treaty: the EIC aimed PoIR in Afghanistan via installing a puppet, Shah Shuja, against Dost Md (a cryptic scribble beside it reads like "R30139 EIC Shah Shuja" [unclear: check your notebook]). His general law of power: power centralises in a strong personality, BUT if the personality weakens, power leaves either "vertically downward" [R v N, R v R, N v N: read as ruler against noble, ruler against ruler, noble against noble] or by "horizontal replacement" [annexed by the British, 1849]. Ranjit Singh 01-39's strength held the Sikh State; after 1839 power leaked down into factions, then sideways to the British. Beside the Dogra Rajputs he notes they were also "Rulers of Jammu (part of the Sikh empire)." This sets up Gulab Singh in the Treaty of Amritsar 1846 (Section 8.2). The Khalsa Army's democratic spirit: the handout adds that it wanted governance by Panchayats, a form of collective military and civil self-governance, and was harder for the EIC to manage than a feudal-loyal army. 8.2 The First Anglo-Sikh War and the Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) Result of the 1st Anglo-Sikh War: the Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846). 1. Military restraint: the Khalsa Army was reduced in size and an EIC army was stationed. The Khalsa was not fully disbanded out of respect for Sikh religious sentiment. 2. Territorial cession: the fertile Jalandhar Doab (the land between the Beas and Sutlej) was annexed by the EIC. 3. The Kashmir mechanism: the Lahore Darbar could not pay the full war indemnity of Rs 1.5 crore, so it ceded the hills between the Beas and Indus (Kashmir and Hazara) to the EIC. The EIC then transferred (sold) these territories to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees. Gulab Singh was recognised as Maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir, subordinate to the British. This was formalised by the Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846). 4. Administrative oversight: PoIR was initiated in Punjab: a British Resident (Henry Lawrence) was stationed as the effective Regent. "Signed after the 1st war." He links it to ToA 1765 at Awadh: both are "quasi / mini SA": a defeated State keeps its ruler but its army is cut, an EIC army is stationed, and a Resident is placed. Beside clause 1 he writes "[Khalsa by GGS 76-08 in 1699]": the Khalsa was founded by Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 (GGS) 76-08 in 1699 (so "Khalsa Army" ties to the religious sentiment the handout mentions). Under the Kashmir mechanism: "Took from Punjab and sold to Dogras." (Dogras: Gulab Singh, ruler of Jammu, see slide 20.) Strategic Note. Kashmir, of enormous strategic importance, was sold to reward Gulab Singh's neutrality. The "Kashmir Question" has its legal origin here, creating a Hindu monarchy over a Muslim-majority population. Two Treaties of Amritsar must be distinguished. (1) Treaty of Amritsar 1809: between Ranjit Singh 01-39 and the EIC; it established the Sutlej as the Sikh-EIC boundary (PoRF with the Sikhs). (2) Treaty of Amritsar 1846 (16 March): formalised the Kashmir sale to Gulab Singh; the legal foundation of the Princely State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) is a third document, signed seven days earlier. 8.3 The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) Reason. The Sikh Governors of Multan (Mulraj) and Haripur (Chattar Singh) revolted, giving empire-builder Dalhousie 48-56 the opportunity he needed. Result. 1. Annexation: Punjab was annexed from Maharaja Duleep Singh 43-49 (a child of 5 at accession). 2. The Koh-i-Noor: as part of the terms of surrender, the diamond was taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh 43-49 and surrendered to the British Crown. 3. Administrative shift: Punjab was initially governed by a "Board of Administration" (the Lawrence Brothers and Charles Mansel). Conclusion. The last major independent State outside the Company State was gone. The EIC's frontier now touched the natural boundaries of the Afghan foothills. "British interest paramount" is written at the end of the Reason row: the revolt of two governors was an opportunity, and the real reason is the same as for Lapse: PoP means British interests come first. For the Conclusion he adds "Khyber Pass: entry point" (underlined): the frontier now reached the pass through which invaders came into India. Chilianwala (1849) was a battle of the 2nd Anglo-Sikh War between the EIC and the Sikhs, not "Dalhousie 48-56 against the Marathas." This is the Prelims 1995 trap (slide 63). The slide answer names Chilianwala only through this PYQ; no other detail of the war's battles is given in the notes.

items.t: 9 · The Second Anglo-Burmese War (1852-53): Lower Burma and Pegu
items.x: Because the Ring Fence also faced east, Pegu was taken in 1852-53. Ask: which three Burma wars, and which governor general for each? The war was fought on the PoRF logic of securing the eastern frontier from an expansionist Burma. Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Lower Burma / Pegu. Combined with Arakan and Tenasserim (annexed 1824-26 under the 1st Anglo-Burmese War and the Treaty of Yandabo 1826), this brought the eastern shore of the Bay of Bengal under British control: the Bay was now effectively a British lake. Teacher's board: Burma annexation diagram Arakan, Tenasserim (the rest of "Lower Burma") 1st Anglo-Burmese War (Treaty of Yandabo 1826) 1824-26 not named Pegu 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 Dalhousie 48-56 Upper Burma 3rd Anglo-Burmese War the board gives no years (see the alert below) Dufferin 84-88 Dates for the 3rd Burmese War. The teacher's board names the war and writes only [Dufferin 84-88] (the Viceroy's code), not the war's years. The chapter index of the handout lists "Dufferin 84-88's Upper Burma (1886)" under the next chapter (Chapter 15). Use Dufferin 84-88 for the code and see Chapter 15 for the year. Burma was "annexed into British India" and "separated in 1937 [GOI Act 1935]." The three Burmas of the board: Lower Burma (Arakan, Tenasserim) 1st war, Pegu 2nd war, Upper Burma 3rd war. Sindh 1843 was NOT Dalhousie 48-56's. It was annexed by Charles Napier under Ellenborough 42-44. Dalhousie 48-56's annexations: Lower Burma 1852-53, Berar 1853, Punjab 1849 and the seven Lapse States. NE India and Burma map plus the teacher's Bay of Bengal sweep Bay of Bengal sweep, clockwise: Bengal 1757 → Northern Sarkars 1766 → (1798 SA with Hyderabad) → Carnatic 1801 → Orissa 1803 → 1826 Arakan and Tenasserim → 1853 Pegu. Inside the loop: "Bay of Bengal 100 yrs" (from 1757 to 1853 the whole coast fell in about a century). Note this lists the Bay's coastal acquisitions in the order of his curve, not strictly by date. Map "Expansion of the British Empire" with the periods: till 1765 (green), 1765-1805 (yellow), 1805-1858 (pink), after 1858 (purple), princely States (orange) One yellow line on this map points to the Assam and Cachar area and has no label. Add it from your notebook if the teacher said a name. The handout's version of the same map carries only a small blue dot at Cachar.

Because the Ring Fence did not stop at the coast, the sea was also controlled. Ask: which coast runs clockwise, which anticlockwise, and which treaties lie beyond India? A land empire is visible on a map. A maritime empire is harder to see but just as deliberate. While the EIC was annexing territories inland, it was simultaneously, piece by piece, bringing every coastline touching the Indian Ocean under British control. By the time Dalhousie 48-56 left in 1856, the picture was complete. PoRF logic did not stop at India's coastline: every sea approach had to be controlled, through whichever instrument was cheapest and most effective (not always annexation). 10.1 The Indian Ocean coastline (Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, 1668-1853) The three-column timeline of the maritime Ring Fence (handout figure) Bay of Bengal (clockwise sweep) 1757 Bengal, 1766 Northern Sarkars, 1801 Carnatic, 1803-05 Orissa, 1824-26 and 1852-53 Burma Arabian Sea (anticlockwise sweep) 1668 Bombay, 1789-99 Mysore / Malabar, 1802 Gaikwad-Baroda and Peshwa SA, 1805 Travancore, 1818 Svarajya annexed, 1843 Sindh Beyond India (strategic frontier) 1854 Treaty of Kalat, 1876 Treaty of Jacobabad, 1856-57 Anglo-Persian War, 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention, 1909 Anglo-Persian Oil Co. The teacher's yellow zigzag on slide 32 and its three circled numbers (3, 2, 3) cannot be read with confidence. It seems to retell the three panels in a different order from the printed red 1, 2, 3. 10.2 Sea approaches beyond India: Balochistan and the Persian Gulf (self read) Slides 28 to 31 (Balochistan, Treaty of Kalat, Treaty of Jacobabad, Gwadar, Persian Gulf) are marked "Self Read, not MIH syllabus" (MIH is Modern Indian History). They are in the handout and slides, so they are covered here fully, but he does not expect them to be taught or tested as core. Balochistan coast and Gwadar. The Makran coast (today's Balochistan coastline) belonged to the State of Makran, itself a vassal of the Khan of Kalat. The British brought this region under control through two treaties that fall on opposite sides of 1857 and the Government of India Act 1858: Treaty of Kalat (1854) The EIC, under Dalhousie 48-56 Major John Jacob The Khan of Kalat surrendered foreign policy and allowed EIC military outposts inside Kalat; in exchange the EIC paid the Khan an annual subsidy of Rs 50,000. A reverse-SA pattern: the imperial power pays the local ruler for special rights to an external power Treaty of Jacobabad (1876) The British State (the Crown) Robert Sandeman, under Viceroy Lytton 76-80 By 1876 the Government of India Act 1858 had abolished the EIC. This treaty ran under the Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1947), not the EIC's PoP. It went further: the British State could station troops permanently in Kalat, build railways and telegraphs through it and act as supreme arbitrator between the Khan and his tribal chiefs (Sardars) PoIR had fully arrived in Kalat in 1876: the Resident was not just in the court, he was now the court. The shift from 1854 to 1876 in Kalat mirrors what happened to all 565 Indian princely States overnight in 1858: from subordinates of a trading company to legal subjects of the British Crown. The same geography and subordination, with a different legal authority above them. (The handout leaves the detail to the chapters on 1857 and the constitutional Acts: Chapter 17, Chapter 21.) Gwadar: a unique 170-year Omani enclave inside Balochistan. In 1783 the Khan of Kalat gifted the port of Gwadar to a prince of Oman, so Gwadar became an overseas territory of the Sultanate of Oman for over 170 years. The British Empire controlled everything around Gwadar but never owned it. Pakistan purchased Gwadar from Oman in 1958, eleven years after Independence. Today Gwadar is at the heart of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The Persian Gulf and Iran (Persia). Persia stayed a formally independent sovereign State; the British never annexed it. But formal independence did not mean freedom from foreign control. Three mechanisms: 1. Temporary military force (1856-57). The Anglo-Persian War (1856-57) captured coastal cities including Bushehr and Kharg Island. Under the Treaty of Paris (1857) the British withdrew in exchange for Iran giving up its claims to Herat in Afghanistan (PoRF logic: protect the western land approach to India, not for Iran's sake). 2. Formal diplomatic partition (1907). Under the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence. The southern coastal region along the Persian Gulf was recognised as the British sphere: naval dominance without a single annexation. 3. Economic control (1909). The Anglo-Persian Oil Company (1909), later the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (today's BP), gave Britain economic control of the Iranian coastline; oil was extracted and shipped under British naval protection. The handout's closing remark: economic imperialism at its most efficient: control the resource, control the coast, without the cost of running a colony. The British learnt that formal annexation was expensive; a sphere of influence and an oil company could do the same more cheaply.

Because the empire needed troops and trade routes, he also built. Ask: what came in 1853, what in 1854, and which university year is not his? Not just an annexationist: the most transformative Governor General in physical and institutional infrastructure. A follower of Utilitarianism (James Mill: reform through laws by a strong State), he built the skeleton of modern India's communication and administrative framework. Slide 33 (Moderniser 1/3) has "MMP" circled beside the title. This section is where his "future syllabus" fan (title slide) lands: Railways, Post and Telegraph, Canals, Wood's Despatch. Dalhousie 48-56 as Moderniser (1/3) 1 Railways (1853) Built primarily for army movement, secondarily for administration, raw-material extraction and market creation. First line: Bombay to Thane, opened 1853. By 1856: Calcutta-Raniganj (coal-rich) and Madras-Arakkonam. The teacher's board: West (1853), East (by 1856), South (by 1856) 2 Telegraph (1853) Telegraph Department established; about 4,000 miles laid across major cities 3 Post Office Act (1854) A network with a uniform half-anna (2 paise) rate from Peshawar to Calcutta 4 Public Works Department (PWD) Removed from military control, made civilian. GT Road (Peshawar to Calcutta) restored to functionality. Canals and bridges built across India 5 Wood's Despatch (1854) Sometimes called the "Magna Carta of Indian Education": a blueprint for mass education: vernacular elementary schools, universities, structured education administration. Dalhousie 48-56 supported and implemented it 6 Vernacular push Favoured vernacular elementary schools for their utilitarian value, expanding them in Bengal and Bihar. Backed technical education: the goal was efficient labour, good consumers and cheaper administration 7 Female education J.E. Drinkwater Bethune (Law Member of Dalhousie 48-56's Council) opened a girls' school in Calcutta in 1849: the Bethune School, India's first successful secular school for girls. (Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule's Pune school, 1 January 1848, predates it as India's first girls' school overall; secular = completely free from religious instruction) 8 Widow remarriage Dalhousie 48-56 supported Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's work on girls' education and the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act 1856. Vidyasagar became Principal of Sanskrit College in 1851 and Inspector of Schools in 1856, both under Dalhousie 48-56's tenure 9 Universities Groundwork through Wood's Despatch, but Dalhousie 48-56 left India in 1856. The three universities (Bombay, Madras, Calcutta) were officially established in 1857 under Canning 56-62. Also the Engineering College at Roorkee; a Director of Education at the Provincial level with an Inspector at the District level The teacher writes "Woods Despatch" above the vernacular-schools row: the vernacular push comes from Wood's Despatch. On the title slide he lists "implement Wood's Despatch 1854" and the Hindu Widow Remarriages Act 1856 with a bracket: "Though passed during Canning 56-62." Dalhousie 48-56 supported the reform; it was passed after he left in 1856 (Canning 56-62 took over in 1856). Source note on dates. The slide 33 table and the handout write Telegraph (1853); the flowchart (slide 36, handout figure) writes Telegraph 1854. The teacher underlines (1853) beside the Telegraph row on slide 33, so use 1853. The flowchart also gives Bombay-Thane = 21 miles, and adds Ganges Canal and Port reform (Calcutta, Bombay and Madras upgraded for steamships), which are in the handout figure but not in its text. Universities and Wood's Despatch belong to Chapter 19. The handout says the three universities were established in 1857 under Canning 56-62 and that Dalhousie 48-56's part was groundwork. For the details of Wood's Despatch (grants-in-aid, universities, aims) see Chapter 19. The question bank lists Prelims PYQs on it for that chapter. Why the infrastructure was built, in the handout's own words: easier troop movement, cheaper administration, raw-material extraction and market creation. The infrastructure outlasted its purpose: India inherited it and built a nation on it. The Mains 2013 skeleton Mains 2013 (10 marks, 200 words): "In many ways, Lord Dalhousie 48-56 was the founder of modern India." Elaborate. The directive "Elaborate" asks for examples and reasoning, not a yes-or-no debate. The phrase "in many ways" accepts a qualified yes: list the ways and say why they were foundational. Intro (about 25 words): Dalhousie 48-56 was in many ways the founder of modern India: the physical and institutional infrastructure he built for colonial purposes outlasted them, and India inherited it. Body (pick 4 to 5): (1) Railways 1853 (Bombay-Thane; by 1856 Calcutta-Raniganj and Madras-Arakkonam). (2) Telegraph 1853, about 4,000 miles. (3) Post Office Act 1854, half-anna uniform rate, Peshawar to Calcutta. (4) PWD made civilian, GT Road, canals and bridges. (5) Wood's Despatch 1854, "Magna Carta of Indian Education": vernacular schools, universities, an education administration. (6) Three universities (established 1857 under Canning 56-62; groundwork his). Add the colonial purpose (troops, cheaper administration, raw materials, markets). Closing (about 25 words): What he built for empire became the skeleton of an independent nation: the infrastructure outlasted its colonial purpose. The strongest single anchor is Wood's Despatch.

items.t: 12 · The five-policy arc (1600-1858) and the Policies towards Indian Kings
items.x: Because each policy built on the last, the arc explains the timing of 1857. Ask: which five, which dates, and what is Paramountcy minus? This section is the teacher's "Next Topic: Policies of British towards Indian Kings." His board splits it in two: "EIC till 1858" and "Br State 1858+". It is the handout's Sec 12 (Five-Policy Arc) and so belongs to this chapter, not to Chapter 15 (which starts on slide 64 with "British Imperial Ideology"). Slide 44, the first of the arc's table slides, has "MMP" boxed with "1 Q" under it. Teacher's board: "Next Topic": a yellow box "Policies of British Towards Indian Kings" with a branching line to "EIC Till 1858" ("Till 1858" underlined) and "Br State 185 Flowchart of the policy phases (handout figure) with the teacher's ink The rising-aggression arrow: the level of aggression by the EIC rises from the top box to the bottom: more army, then more confidence. The army grew from three sources: Plassey plunder, subsidy (SA) and land-revenue income (and, after annexation, the revenue of annexed land: his last arrows read "post annexation → army"). PoIR in his sketch: ① a puppet Nawab, ② a British Resident, ③ the Resident controls the puppet. Relative isolation in one line: the EIC did not annex because it was a company, "here for business, not for ruling," e.g. it did not annex Awadh after Buxar 1764 (Chapter 10's ToA 1765). This is the reason the first policy is called "relative". The slide flowchart and the handout give different dates for the phases. Teacher and handout win. Flowchart: Relative Isolation pre-1757; PoIR + PoRF 1757-1813; PoSA 1798-1818; Paramountcy 1813-1857; Subordinate Union post-1857. Handout: Relative Isolation until 1813 (the "arc" starts at 1600); PoIR and PoRF run alongside, with military alliances from 1765; PoSA 1798-1858; Paramountcy 1813-58; Subordinate Union 1858-1947. The teacher's own board for Paramountcy says (1813-58) and for isolation includes ToA 1765 inside it (slide 39). For answers use the handout's dates, and know the flowchart's version exists. 12.1 Relative Isolation (until 1813) The EIC was militarily not confident in its early decades; its primary interest was international trade. It stayed out of Indian politics as far as possible but not absolutely. It defended and expanded its trading interests through diplomacy and selective warfare, signed military alliances (Treaty of Allahabad 1765, Treaty of Salbai 1782) and interfered in succession disputes (Treaty of Surat 1775) to extract territories for trade expansion. (The Treaty of Purandhar 1776 shows the isolation pull: Hastings 73-85 wanted to settle commercially and avoid full war.) Teacher's board: Policy of Relative Isolation Relative isolation, point by point. (1) Primary motive = trade, not Indian politics. The EIC's army was initially small: his proof is the "Child's war 1686-90" in which "[a Mughal ruler, written A2S807 and not readable with confidence] thrashed the EIC" [unclear: check your notebook; the scribble resembles Aurangzeb 58-07's code]. Therefore the EIC stayed isolated from Indian politics. (2) "Relative" = not 100% = not absolute: if an opportunity presented itself, the EIC "temporarily" interfered (the word is boxed), extracted trade or rupee benefits, then reverted back to isolation. Two examples he gives: the 1st Anglo-Maratha War 1775-82 (the reason: RR 73-74 promised Salsette and Vasai/Bassein if made Peshwa, therefore the Treaty of Surat 1775 and then war: see Chapter 13) and Shuja 54-75, Shah Alam II 60-06 and Qasim 60-63 attacking the EIC (Buxar): victory was an opportunity, giving ToA 1765 (underlined: see Chapter 10). Teacher's board: "No interference" with a long curved arrow to "PoParamountcy" From no interference to Paramountcy: after 1757 the power of the EIC (the Company State) kept rising; therefore interference and aggression kept rising; by 1813 this became the Policy of Paramountcy. The curved arrow from "No interference" to "PoParamountcy" is the whole story of the arc in one line. Slide 42, a board on geopolitics. The teacher uses a general rule to explain why policies change: "In geopolitics, States behave in line with their power" (political, military, economic, intellectual/tech, social and soft power). When power is very low, States invoke ethics; when it is very high, they choose national interest first and then develop a language of ethics in line with it. He applies it to India's own rise: yesterday NAM, today NAM partially, tomorrow "we will/should interfere in others' affairs." He gives no more detail; it is an analogy for the EIC's rising aggression. 12.2 Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) and Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) PoIR (Indirect Rule) A British Resident in the court controlling administration without formal annexation Bengal by 1772, Delhi 1803, Travancore by 1809, Satara by 1818, Punjab 1846, Awadh by 1855 PoRF (Ring Fence) A military alliance with a frontier State as a buffer against external threats Awadh (ToA 1765), Hyderabad (Treaty of Hyderabad 1766), Mysore (Treaty of Madras 1769), Marathas (Treaty of Salbai 1782), Sikh (Treaty of Amritsar 1809) Beside the title he boxes "MMP" and writes "1 Q" (one question is expected from this part; the notes do not say more). 12.3 Policy of Subsidiary Alliance (PoSA, 1798-1858) PoSA (1798-1858): the EIC subordinated Indian rulers as junior alliance partners by taking over their foreign policy and military, both funded by an annual subsidy from the Indian State, while formally promising non-interference in internal affairs. The promise was routinely broken through illegal PoIR. Bajirao II 96-18 signed the SA via the Treaty of Bassein 1802 to regain his throne; the treaty promised non-interference, but British Resident Mountstuart Elphinstone soon bypassed the Peshwa and interfered directly: creeping PoIR through the back door. When Bajirao II 96-18 launched the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817), it was not aggression: it was a ruler trying to shake off interference the treaty had explicitly promised would never happen. No powers, but all the blame: the same pattern as Awadh 1856 (Section 7). 12.4 Policy of Paramountcy / Subordinate Isolation (1813-58) Initiated by Francis Hastings 13-23. From 1813 the EIC formally declared itself paramount: the supreme power among all States in India. To protect British interests it would interfere in internal affairs and annex if needed. (Earlier this happened in practice; from 1813 the EIC shed the pretence. Indian States were to have no rights if British interests demanded otherwise.) Diplomatic isolation (cutting off a State's right to deal with other States independently) had existed since early SA treaties. After 1813 every Indian State, large or small, was locked in a sealed bubble: no communication, negotiation or alliance with any other State without the EIC as absolute gatekeeper. Conceptually: Policy of Paramountcy = Policy of SA minus the rights of the Indian State. 12.5 Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1947) Teacher's board: Policy of Subordinate Union Teacher's board: Subordinate Union and symbolic sovereignty After 1857 the EIC was abolished and the British State took direct control. Indian rulers were now not just subordinate but legally part of the British Empire, hence "union." Paramountcy became the formal legal relationship between the British Monarch and the Indian Prince. (Prince, not King: Indian rulers were now legally junior members of the British imperial family.) Sovereignty and the external sovereign functions (Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) were with the British Crown; domestic sovereign functions remained with the Indian Prince. Conceptually: Policy of Subordinate Union = Policy of Paramountcy + sovereignty formally with the British Crown. Two words, two circled numbers: ① SUBORDINATE: Indian kings will be junior to the British State. ② UNION: the British Crown = the monarch of Indian kings (and he draws "not Mughal": the monarch is the British Crown, not the Mughal emperor). That is why from 1858 Indian "Kings" were called Indian "Princes": a Prince is the son of a King, and the King is the British monarch. Therefore the whole of India is part of the British empire, and it splits into British India (ruled by the British) and 565 princely States (ruled by an Indian Prince). Symbolic sovereignty: under Subordinate Union the British hold external sovereignty (D, C, FA: Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) and the Indian Prince holds domestic sovereign functions; under SA the same split existed but the Indian king held symbolic sovereignty and the EIC held the external functions (D, C, FA). Do not use "Prince" and "King" loosely in answers about 1858 onwards. The handout and the teacher both say: after 1858 the correct word is Indian Prince; "King" is the pre-1858 word. Paramountcy of the EIC (1813-58) and Paramountcy of the Crown (1858-1947) are two different legal relationships. 12.6 The arc in five steps The arc: 1600 to 1858 in five steps 1600: a trading company that wanted to be left alone (Relative Isolation) 1765: a military alliance partner (PoIR and PoRF; ToA 1765) 1798: a dominant power controlling neighbours' armies and foreign policies (PoSA) 1813: a State openly declaring all others subservient to its interests (Paramountcy, Francis Hastings 13-23) 1858: a Crown that absorbed 565 Indian princes as legal subordinates (Subordinate Union) Each stage built legally and institutionally on the previous. This logical unfolding is exactly why 1857 happened when it did. (Handout, Sec 12.)

items.t: 13 · Critique: consolidation at the cost of legitimacy
items.x: Because annexation made enemies, legitimacy was lost. Ask: which three leaders, which grievance each, and what did the Proclamation of 1858 reverse? 13.1 Consolidation at the cost of legitimacy Dalhousie 48-56 consolidated the Company State but destroyed its legitimacy. Almost every major leader of the 1857 revolt was annexation-aggrieved: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi Lapse 1854 (Section 3) Nana Sahib Bajirao II 96-18's pension refused, 1851 (Section 5) Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57 The last Mughal, whose titular dignity Dalhousie 48-56 sought to end The court of Awadh (Section 7), the disbanded Sikh soldiery (Section 8), the dispossessed talukdars and the inam-holders stripped by the Inam Commission 1852 (Section 4) all joined or supported the revolt. (Recall: the Inam Commission was Lapse applied to land titles: the same legitimacy-override logic.) See Chapter 21. 13.2 Post-Dalhousie: Canning 56-62 inherits and the Queen ends Lapse Dalhousie 48-56 handed power to Canning 56-62 in 1856, who inherited the empire Dalhousie 48-56 built and the revolt his annexations had sown the seeds of. After the suppression of the 1857 revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 abolished the Company State and transferred power to the British Crown. Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 formally ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged that the treaties and rights of Indian rulers would be respected: an explicit reversal of Dalhousie 48-56's core policy. Paramountcy became Subordinate Union (Section 12.5). No further annexations followed, a line Dalhousie 48-56's successors (including Viceroy Lytton 76-80) did not cross, even where Paramountcy-era instruments were tightened (the Treaty of Jacobabad 1876 with Kalat). The empire was complete; it only needed managing.

A trading company that wanted to be left alone. In 1600 the EIC was a trading company, here for business and not for ruling. Its army was small (the Child's War 1686-90 showed it), so it stayed out of Indian politics, but not absolutely: when an opportunity came, as after Buxar 1764, it interfered, took a benefit and went back. After 1757 its power kept rising, and so did its interference. Paramountcy: British interests first. Francis Hastings 13-23 began the Policy of Paramountcy in 1813: among all States in India the Company State is supreme, British interests come first, and the EIC will annex if it must. Every State was locked in a sealed bubble with the EIC as gatekeeper. Paramountcy was the Subsidiary Alliance minus the rights of the Indian State. Three roads to expansion. Dalhousie 48-56 used Paramountcy in three ways: the Doctrine of Lapse, wars (Punjab 1849, Pegu 1852-53) and annexation in lieu of subsidy (Berar 1853). By 1856 the Company State held 63% of India and 78% of its people, and no more mainland was annexed after him. The teacher's logic: a succession dispute means instability, which hurts British business, and British interests are paramount. The Doctrine of Lapse. The Court of Directors formulated it in 1847; Dalhousie 48-56 implemented it. If a ruler died without a biological heir his rights lapsed, overriding adoption under Hindu law. Seven States fell in seven years: Satara 1848, Sambalpur and Jaitpur 1849, Baghat 1850, Udaipur 1852 (in Chhattisgarh), Jhansi and Nagpur 1854. The Inam Commission of 1852 applied the same logic to land, seizing about 20,000 estates in the Bombay Presidency, and the pension of Bajirao II 96-18 was refused to Nana Sahib. Berar and Awadh: subsidy turns into land. Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance in 1798; by 1853 it could not pay, so Dalhousie 48-56 annexed Berar. Awadh followed the same chain: Clive 57-67's treaty of 1765, Shore's swap of Wazir Ali 97-98 for Sadat Ali Khan II in 1798 for Rs 76 lakh, half of Awadh taken in 1801 under Wellesley 98-05, and in 1856 the rest, on maladministration. Wajid Ali Shah had heirs, so this was not Lapse. The Sikh State: from buffer to target. Under Ranjit Singh 01-39 the Sikh State was the ideal stable, strong, friendly buffer. After 1839 four factions tore it apart: the royal family, the Sindhanwaliyas, the Dogra Rajputs and the Khalsa Army. The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) cut the army, took the Jalandhar Doab, and sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanakshahee rupees against a 1.5 crore indemnity, formalised by the Treaty of Amritsar (16 March 1846). Punjab annexed, the Koh-i-Noor taken. In 1848 the Sikh Governors Mulraj (Multan) and Chattar Singh (Haripur) revolted, the opportunity the empire-builder Dalhousie 48-56 needed. Punjab was annexed in 1849 from Duleep Singh 43-49, a child of 5 at accession; the Koh-i-Noor went to the British Crown and a Board of Administration (the Lawrence Brothers and Charles Mansel) ruled. The frontier now touched the Afghan foothills. Pegu and the sea ring. The 2nd Anglo-Burmese War 1852-53 annexed Pegu; with Arakan and Tenasserim (1824-26) the Bay of Bengal became a British lake. The Bay's coast fell clockwise from Bengal 1757 to Pegu 1853, and the Arabian Sea anticlockwise from Bombay 1668 to Sindh 1843 (not Dalhousie 48-56's, but Ellenborough 42-44's). Beyond India came Kalat 1854, Jacobabad 1876, Persia 1856-57, 1907 and 1909. The moderniser. A follower of Utilitarianism, Dalhousie 48-56 built the skeleton of modern India: railways from 1853 (Bombay-Thane first), the telegraph (about 4,000 miles), the Post Office Act 1854 with a half-anna rate, a civilian PWD and the restored GT Road, and Wood's Despatch 1854. The motives: troops, cheaper administration, raw materials and markets. The three universities came in 1857 under Canning 56-62. The five policies and the hidden bill. The arc ran from Relative Isolation through PoIR and PoRF, the Subsidiary Alliance 1798 and Paramountcy 1813 to Subordinate Union 1858; each step built on the last, which is why 1857 came when it did. Dalhousie 48-56 consolidated the Company State but destroyed its legitimacy: Rani Lakshmibai (Lapse 1854), Nana Sahib (pension 1851), Bahadur Shah Zafar 37-57, the Awadh court, disbanded Sikh soldiers, talukdars and inam-holders were all aggrieved. 1858: the reversal. Dalhousie 48-56 handed over to Canning 56-62 in 1856, who inherited the revolt. The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the Company State, and Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 ended the Doctrine of Lapse and pledged respect for the treaties and rights of Indian rulers. Paramountcy gave way to Subordinate Union, Indian Kings became Indian Princes, and there were no further annexations.
