Because the State's duty to its people is economic security in an agrarian economy, every land system is judged on five questions. Ask: who owns, how is it assessed, who settles, who collects, and what do tenants get? Chapter 16 title slide Why this chapter matters for UPSC: the State's duty to its people is economic security, and in a pre-industrial country that means the agrarian economy: agriculture is the big share of GDP, and ryots are the big share of the work profile. Then he gives the five-question frame he repeats for the Mughal system, Ijaradari, PS 1793, Ryotwari and Mahalwari: who is the landowner, how is the revenue assessed, with whom is the settlement made, who collects, and what rights do tenants have. Learn every system as a row of those five answers.

items.t: 1 · The Mughal blueprint for land revenue
items.x: Because the British inherited the Mughal chain, you must know it first: it is the yardstick the later systems fall short of. Ask: where did the Khudkasht's protection come from, and who really owned the land? Teacher's board: State, intermediaries and ryots The Khudkasht was the actual cultivator. He held customary occupancy rights over his land (he could not simply be thrown off). He paid land revenue by the Patta system: a document (patta) recorded the amount he owed, a legal safeguard against arbitrary over-extraction. He also paid abwabs (informal tributes) to his Primary Zamindar. The Mughal revenue chain: who collected, who paid up Khudkasht (cultivator): customary occupancy rights; pays LR per his patta; pays abwabs to the Primary Zamindar Primary Zamindar: keeps his commission, passes the rest up Intermediary Zamindar: collects, keeps his cut, passes the rest up Jagirdar if the land was a jagir; the State if it was khalisa land The figure's bottom box says "Amlas" (state-appointed, audit chain). The handout's text names the supervising State officers as Amils and Amalguzars. The teacher and the Mahalwari section stress that Amlas are different: private employees of Zamindars, not State officers (Section 4.1). Treat "Amlas" in the figure as a label slip and use Amils and Amalguzars for the State's supervisors. Amils and Amalguzars (government officers) supervised the chain so that Zamindars did not under-report collections. Critical point: the Zamindar was not the owner of land. He was a revenue collector on commission (the teacher's board: Vatan right to collect LR and keep a 10% commission). He also had police duties alongside revenue work. Legal private ownership of property was not a Mughal idea; it was British, imported from English law. Ijaradari: when the State needed money in a hurry it auctioned the right to collect land revenue to the highest bidder. The British would replicate this (Section 2.2). Teacher's board, pre-British era Legal against customary. In the Mughal era only the King was the legal owner and no individual legal property rights existed. The Khudkasht's right was customary (from custom, not from a law made by the State), recorded in his patta. Land was not a commodity: it changed hands only by conquest or gift, so there was no land market. The market in land develops with the British, from 1793. (The ink "Ded" beside "This" reads like "dev(elops)"; check your notebook.) Mughal LR system on the five-question frame Landowner Khudkasht (practically his milkiyat; legally only the King owned) Ryot or Khudkasht (practical) Assessment Detailed survey; % of gross produce (e.g. one-third); revisable Summary, by auction; an amount Settlement with The ryot (he gives a Qubuliyat to the State; the State gives him a patta) The Ijaradar, via auction Collection by A non-State actor: the Zamindar The Ijaradar Tenants Rightless, landless Pahikashts (not written)

Because the EIC held the Diwani from 1765, it had to collect land revenue, and Bengal became the laboratory. Ask: what did each of the three experiments do to the ryot, and why did the next one follow? 2.1 Experiment 1: Dual Government (1765-72) In 1765 the EIC received the Diwani (right to collect land revenue) of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar through the Treaty of Allahabad (ToA 1765) (the treaty itself is in Chapter 10). It did not administer directly. It appointed Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as its Diwan. The Mughal collection system continued: the EIC followed Orientalism (Indian traditions are best administered on their own terms). Ideology did not stop greed. In five years: frantic experiments to squeeze more revenue; the Patta system was ignored; rents were extracted far beyond what pattas recorded. Then back-to-back droughts. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed between 50 lakh and 1 crore. The EIC doubled the revenue demand in 1770 and used brutality to collect. For the first time some British men acted as whistleblowers, writing to London newspapers. Reza Khan was made a scapegoat: imprisoned without trial on corruption charges, 1772-74. In the Pre-British era the words "rent" and "revenue" were used interchangeably (his note beside the slide). Underlines: Deputy Subadar, Orientalism, Patta ignored, back-to-back droughts, doubled in 1770, brutality, imprisoned without trial, 1772-74. The famine fits his nature factor and human factor idea from Chapter 10: droughts were nature; the doubled demand, ignored pattas and brutality were human. The handout here gives the famine toll as 50 lakh to 1 crore. Chapter 10's handout says about 1 crore, one-third of Bengal. Quote the range in this chapter's answers; "about one crore" is the upper end. Since 1757 the EIC had bought Indian goods with India's own land revenue rather than gold from England, so a famine hit its income directly (the Drain logic of Chapter 10). Famine destroyed the agrarian economy and land revenue collapsed. By 1772 the EIC was on the verge of bankruptcy: rampant corruption by its officials (the "Nabobs"), the 1770 famine, and heavy expenses of the army and the Dual System. The EIC asked the British Government for an emergency bailout. Parliament granted 1.4 million pounds at 4% interest, on the strict condition of parliamentary oversight, which led directly to the Regulating Act of 1773 (Chapter 17). 2.2 Experiment 2: the Farming System of Warren Hastings 73-85 (1772) Farming System = the English name for Ijaradari; Revenue Farmer = Ijaradar. Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor of the Bengal Presidency. The ryot's sad face carries three blows in a row: 1757+ high LR, 1770 Great Bengal Famine, 1772 Ijaradari. On the right he lists events of Hastings's years (as written: "To Purandhar 1776 @ Ma", "To Salbai 1782", "HA 61-82: military alliance 1769", "2nd A-My 1780-84"); "To" reads as his shorthand for Treaty, "Ma" for Marathas, "HA" for Haidar Ali 61-82 ([unclear: check your notebook]). They belong to Chapter 12 and Chapter 13. Till 1813 the ideology was Orientalism: "Rule India the India way." That is why the EIC kept Mughal collection after 1765 and revived Ijaradari in 1772 (and why Hastings 73-85 is called an Orientalist). The turn away from it follows the Charter Act of 1813 (Chapter 17). Warren Hastings 73-85, himself an Orientalist, revived the Mughal Ijaradari system. The right to collect LR in each district was auctioned to the highest bidder: the Revenue Farmer (so named because, like a farmer, he aimed to extract profit through a contract; not a farmer who tills soil). Bengal Experiment 2: Hastings's Farming System (1772) The Revenue Farmer worked under a European District Collector (DC) (European = English, Scottish or Irish, not English alone). Outcome: farmers squeezed the maximum from ryots to recover their bids and make profit. The demand was often so high that peasants paid nothing: self-defeating. Revenue did not improve; the rural population was ruined. 2.3 Primer: tax, property, settlement (taught first in the lecture) The lecture teaches these concepts before the Mughal system (Lecture 17, slides 5 to 12, 21, 22); the handout puts them here as Section 2.3. Read them before the pillars of PS 1793. Teacher's board: rights Rights in land have five layers: a) The ryot's right to cultivate and occupy his plot b) The right to fair rents (tenant ryot) or fair land revenue (owner) c) The landowner's right to sell, lease, rent and mortgage land and receive those proceeds d) The right to collect taxes (State, or Vatan right holders such as Zamindars) e) The right to receive tax proceeds and revise tax rates (State; Jagirdars receive but by the State's grant) Two kinds of rights on his board (Lecture 17, slide 3): rights given by law (made by the State, an organisation, through rules) and customary or traditional rights (from the conventions of a society), e.g. the Vatan rights of Zamindars. (The star note "MIH" and the small "7 ... PPT" beside the law branch are [unclear: check your notebook].) Teacher's board: taxes and rents Teacher's board: the word "Zamindar" changes meaning Meaning of words changes, the word stays the same. Zamindar before 1793 = collector of LR, not owner; after 1793 = legal landowner (he stars "conditional ownership": the Sunset Clause can take the land); after 1947 "Zamindari abolition" meant abolishing big landownership. Assessment = deciding how much tax is owed, by detailed field survey (soil quality, irrigation, crop type, plot size, rainfall; the board adds frequency of drought or flood and past LR trends) or summarily (a rough estimate). The demand is a fixed absolute amount or a percentage of produce; it is permanent or revisable. Settlement = with whom the State negotiates the tax demand, and who is responsible for depositing it. Teacher's board: settlement with Mr XYZ Settlement = agreement on LR plus the duty to deposit it. His analogy: in GST the shopkeeper deposits a tax that the buyer bears, so the depositor need not be the one who bears the tax. In the land systems the owner always bears the tax, but the settlement may or may not be with the owner: PS 1793: with the landowner (Zamindar); Ryotwari: with the landowner (ryot); Mahalwari 1822: not the landowner (the Mahal, via its Lambardar). Rent is always paid by a tenant to a property owner. Taxes are always borne by the property owner. The State is always the ultimate recipient but may collect through its own officers or non-State intermediaries. In the Farming System of 1772, assessment was by auction and settlement was with the Revenue Farmer. 2.4 Experiment 3: the Permanent Settlement Act, 1793 Applied in: Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras, Benaras. Cornwallis 86-93 (GG of Bengal 1786-93) was sent with one primary assignment: fix the land revenue problem. After several experiments he passed the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 through the GG(Bengal)'s Council and extended it to Madras on his instructions. By 1801 Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in London to replace it with Ryotwari in Madras, though it survived in North Madras. Permanent Settlement Act, 1793 AUTHORITARIANISM under Cornwallis 86-93: "my way or highway." He came from a landlord family and was inspired by how agriculture was done in England (agrarian capitalism); his own words: CW 86-93 = Believer (a believer in English landlordism). The belief explains the model: see Pillar 1 below. Teacher's board: PS 1793 on the five questions Landowner The Zamindar Assessment No field survey; summary; an absolute amount (not %); not revisable Settlement with The Zamindar Collection by The District Collector (DC) Tenants No rights: the Zamindar can charge whatever rent and remove them from the plot Pillar 1: landownership went to the Zamindar. Zamindars got full proprietary rights for the first time, making them legal owners. Land became a commodity: sold, purchased, leased, rented, mortgaged. Hereditary, transferable within the family. Why? (a) Ideology: belief in English-style landlordism; convert Zamindars into agrarian capitalists like England's landed gentry; security of property would induce investment. (b) Agrarian capitalism would improve food security, boost agricultural trade and grow the EIC's LR income. (c) Loyalty of Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, would buy political stability. Revenue Farmers, though wealthy, were not made landowners: they were not part of the traditional agrarian economy and lacked agricultural expertise. Teacher's board: landowner criteria = a big landowner Teacher's board: why Zamindar chosen Why a big landowner? A rich man invests (irrigation, better equipment and machines as in England's Industrial Revolution of 1750-1850, hired labour), produces for profit, so production rises: food security and government LR income rise. Whom to make big landowner? An already rich person: the Zamindar (ticked; by 1727, 15 Intermediary Zamindars collected 50% of Bengal Suba's LR, the group Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) had built), a moneylender, or a merchant of urban areas. Why the Zamindar over the rest? He is part of the rural economy and the traditional leader of rural society, and thinks about agriculture 24x7 because his commission depends on production; merchants and moneylenders (Ijaradars) think about margin and interest and are outsiders to the rural economy. "PS 1793 = DnR" (Divide and Rule). His general picture: in any setting (company, country, society, politics, family, geopolitics) there are leaders and followers; DnR can pit leader against leader, follower against follower, or favour one tier over the other (L happy, F sad or L sad, F happy, the last with "Bangladesh, Nepal" as examples). The slide does not write which pattern PS 1793 is. Read from Section 2.5, it is leaders (Zamindars) rewarded, masses (ryots) stripped of rights; that is a reading, not his ink. Pillar 2: settlement with the Zamindar. Fewer, bigger counterparties (the teacher writes "LR payers" above "counterparties") made collection simpler. The State negotiated with Zamindars; the Zamindar was responsible for depositing LR. Pillar 3: assessment was permanent. LR was fixed at 10/11 of the Zamindar's pre-existing revenue (what he had collected from ryots before deducting his commission), with 1789-90 as the base year. Fixed forever, as an absolute annual amount, not a percentage. The arithmetic (Lecture 17, slide 30). Before 1793: ryot's produce Rs 100; LR = two-thirds = 66% = Rs 66, which the Zamindar collects (Z's revenue); ryot keeps Rs 34; Zamindar keeps 10% of 66 = Rs 6.6; the State gets Rs 59.4. After 1793: 10/11 x 66 = Rs 60, and Rs 60 is fixed forever (boxed FOREVER = Permanent-ly, "FIG not %"). Anything above Rs 60 the Zamindar can keep: in his example the Zamindar takes Rs 13 and the ryot keeps 40 - 13 = Rs 27 (the ink does not explain where the 40 comes from; [unclear: check your notebook]). Teacher's board: why LR fixed so high Teacher's worked example Why so high and why in rupees: inflation shrinks what the State receives each year (practically nothing in 100 years), so the initial demand was fixed very high to compensate the State for the long-term loss. And because it is a fixed amount, not a percentage: if the ryots produce Rs 120 in 1794 the State still gets Rs 60, so the Zamindar keeps the gain and is incentivised to invest; if they produce Rs 0 in 1795 the State still gets Rs 60 (the Zamindar carries the risk). Why permanent and absolute? (a) To incentivise the Zamindar: revenue would not rise however profits grew, so he had every reason to invest and produce more. (b) Certainty for the State: even in a drought year the State knew what it would receive. (c) Less administration: no repeat assessment surveys (the teacher adds: corruption would fall, since no officer could reduce the demand). (d) Trade-off: since the State gave up future increases, it set the initial demand very high. Estimates vary: some historians say double the 1765 level; others, 20% above 1757 levels. Pillar 4: the Sunset Clause. If a Zamindar did not pay LR by the evening of a pre-set deadline, his land was auctioned to anyone who agreed to pay the required land revenue. The buyer only had to agree to pay (not pay in full at once), given the large amounts. Collection was by State officers: the District Collector. The buyer bids for the LR, not the land's value. In his example the buyer agrees to pay Rs 60 a year; the board asks "who can pay the value of the land of 300 villages?" and answers "No one." That is why the Sunset Clause is workable. Prelims 2024: answer (b) 2 only. Statement 1 (F): Ryotwari is not Cornwallis 86-93's, and a bad harvest earned remission (a reduction of LR), not exemption (zero LR): the teacher ticks "Remit" and crosses "Exempt = zero LR." Statement 2 (T): a Zamindar who failed to pay lost his land at auction: the Sunset Clause. 2.5 Impact of PS 1793 The results diverged sharply from Cornwallis 86-93's intentions. 1. Short term: frequent land auctions; the demand was so high that many Zamindars defaulted. Buyers: Jotedars (rich farmers, less wealthy than Zamindars) and the Zamindar's own family members, who bid to keep land in the family. Over time it stabilised and Zamindars became loyal (in 1857 Bengal's Zamindars largely stayed on the British side). 2. Long term: the British got certainty and regularity of LR income. That objective was achieved. 3. But the core economic vision failed: Zamindars did not invest. The demand left little surplus, and they would not risk old family wealth in an uncertain colonial environment (the teacher writes "therefore LR" above "the demand"). 4. Absentee landlordism: Zamindars leased lands to intermediaries for a lease amount and moved to cities. The hands-on agrarian-capitalist vision was abandoned. 5. The ryot's situation became catastrophic. PS gave legal rights to Zamindars but did not recognise the ryot's customary rights. The ryot became a "tenant at will," evicted without legal protection; Patta ignored; high rents; abwabs, now illegal for lack of legal basis, still collected. Underlines: Auctions, frequent, Buyers, Jotedars, the Zamindar's own family, later stabilised, Zamindars became loyal; certainty and regularity; Zamindars did not invest; absentee landlordism, moved to cities, the agrarian-capitalist vision was abandoned; "tenant at will," Patta ignored, high rents, abwabs still collected. The loyalty is exactly the "Sustained" half of his DnR Mains question (Section 0). 6. Zamindars regained coercive powers in 1799. Cornwallis 86-93 had removed their police powers (a Zamindar is a businessman, not law enforcement). Wellesley 98-05 reversed this through Regulation VII of 1799. The Zamindar could now: (a) seize a tenant's property (crops, cattle) without a court order on rent default; (b) imprison tenants; (c) increase rents at will. (Class slide: the result was a wave of peasant revolts after 1793.) 7. Increased litigation after 1793 came from the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judicial changes that made the system inefficient in practice): (a) the District Collector was stripped of all judicial and magisterial powers, so revenue disputes once settled swiftly and informally on the spot had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats; (b) court fees were abolished to make justice "accessible," which flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits (fees reimposed in 1795); (c) formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) with a rigid hierarchy of appeals let cases be deliberately prolonged. "Not of this chapter, but here so the student knows" (his words on slide 36). The judicial reforms themselves belong to Chapter 18; here you only need the three points because of Prelims 2011. Prelims 2011: answer (d). The three options on offer are not the cause; the cause is the Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (point 7). (a) strong Zamindars did not mean more suits: ryots had no means to sue. (b) the EIC was already the overlord of the Zamindars' region since 1765 (the Diwani). (c) the courts became less efficient. Prelims 2001: answer (b) "no official check upon the Zamindar." The slide adds: Bengal Regulation VIII of 1793 required Zamindars to issue pattas (specifying rent and tenancy terms, so a patta is a rent agreement); the ryot could demand a patta. The gap was enforcement: the government cared about punctual payment of its fixed revenue. (a) trust does not explain it; (c) issuing pattas was the Zamindar's duty; (d) pattas protected cultivators. Mains FYQ on the board: "British empire in India was BUILT (1) and SUSTAINED (2) by policies and tactics of DnR FYQ-M: built and sustained by DnR. Built = created division (the Triple Alliance and the Treaty of Amritsar 1809; the Subsidiary Alliance, which takes over external affairs) and used division (factionalism as opportunity, e.g. the Treaty of Bassein 1802, an SA with Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18). Sustained = PS 1793 (his arrow). Treaties belong to Chapter 11, Chapter 13 and Chapter 6; here you only need to hang PS 1793 on the "Sustained" hook. 2.6 The Rent Act of 1859 and the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 After decades of peasant revolts the British were compelled to act. The Rent Act of 1859 (Bengal Presidency): a) A tenant who cultivated the same plot continuously for more than 12 years gained occupancy rights: no eviction without a court order; rent not raised without the Zamindar showing just cause b) With fewer than 12 years on a plot, rents could not be increased frequently c) The Patta system was revived: Zamindars had to collect rents at recorded rates d) Zamindars lost the power to imprison tenants "No more tenant at will of the Zamindar" (top right of slide 38). In practice it was poorly implemented: the loophole was to evict the tenant just before he completed 12 years, permanently denying him occupancy rights; Zamindars kept private armed men ("Z contd to keep LATHIYALS," the Zamindar's club-men, paid through bribery) and officials turned a blind eye. The failure drove the Indigo Revolt (1859-63) and the Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), where ryots fought specifically for occupancy rights (the revolts themselves: Chapter 20, Chapter 22). The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885) The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 (Act III of 1885) followed Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission of 1880 (passed under Dufferin 84-88's tenure, enacted by the Bengal Legislative Council): Rights of all stakeholders, Zamindars and ryots, clearly defined in law. Powers of Zamindars significantly reduced. Occupancy rights strengthened: even tenants who cultivated different plots in the same village for a total of more than 12 years now got occupancy rights over the last plot cultivated, closing the loophole. The government implemented it sincerely this time. He boxes "Tenancy" and ticks both "Tenancy" and "Act" with a note "only for ..." and sketches three circles joined by arrows (State, Zamindar and a third, unclear) ([unclear: check your notebook]). Underlines: Rent Commission in 1880, dufferin's tenure, Bengal Legislative Council, "even tenants who cultivated different plots ... more than 12 years", "got occupancy rights", "sincerely".

Because the Permanent Settlement could not be copied where Madras lacked big Zamindars, Munro built another model around the ryot. Ask: what made the field survey the crux, and why did assessment drift from gross to net? Ryotwari: where applied Applied in: Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras and Bombay. Ryotwari followed annexations. Sind 1843 (Charles Napier), Coorg 1834 (famous for coffee plantations), Assam 1824-26 (First Anglo-Burmese War; Yandabo 1826, written "Toyandobo 1826"), Bombay 1817-19 (Third Anglo-Maratha War). Madras came in pieces: 1766 Northern Sarkars; the Third and Fourth Anglo-Mysore Wars (Malabar and Baramahal from the 3rd, Kanara from the 4th, Dindigul too, as drawn); 1801 the Carnatic (see Chapter 12). Circled 1 and 2 above the table: [unclear: check your notebook]. The class map (Lecture 18, slide 24) lists Berar under Ryotwari as well; the handout's list does not. Both agree on the five places above. 3.1 Ryotwari in Madras (1801 onward, firmly from 1820) The first attempt in Madras was the same as Bengal: extend PS. Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 tried to create big Zamindars by recognising the Poligars (landed magnates with private armies, autonomous since the Vijayanagar Empire of 1336-1646) as landowners. The experiment failed. Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in London in 1801 to replace it with Ryotwari in Madras. He had first experimented in parts of Madras in 1792 under Alexander Read (the slide: in Baramahal, annexed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790-92). 1801-07 Ryotwari applied in Madras. Ryotwari in Madras: from the PS 1793 attempt to Munro It was diluted after he left for Britain in 1807; he re-established it firmly as Governor of Madras (1820-27). He died in India. Prelims 2017: answer (c) 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is wrong: Lord Cornwallis 86-93 was the PS 1793 architect and even tried PS in Madras through the Poligars. Read (1792) and Munro (1801-07, and 1820) are the Ryotwari pair. The teacher's years on the slide are the answer key. Handout hook: Read and Munro = Ryotwari (Scottish, yeoman); Cornwallis 86-93 = Permanent (English landlordism). Why Munro pushed Ryotwari over PS: five reasons. a) Scottish ideology Munro was from Scotland, where the hero of agrarian society was the Yeoman farmer (a landowner who also cultivates his own land, a more prosperous Khudkasht). As an Orientalist he argued ancient India had no intermediaries between the State and the cultivator b) No big Zamindars In Bengal, Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) created super-rich Intermediary Zamindars: by 1727, 15 of them collected 50% of Bengal's LR, which made PS viable. Madras had no such class c) State finances Madras was under stress from low productivity and past wars: three Carnatic Wars (1746-63) and four Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767-99). PS fixes LR forever in amount, not %, so there is no room to grow State income d) Eliminate intermediaries Poligars' profits came at the State's expense (the slide adds Deshmukhs). Remove them: the share can go partly to the State, partly to lighter burden on ryots e) Political stability Removing Poligars as a class of powerful non-State actors reduces resistance; loyalty of the masses comes from giving them land (the teacher: "To bar political authority") He ticks (a) Scottish ideology and writes beside (e) "To bar POLITICAL AUTHORITY" (the Poligars' private armies and autonomy are what he means). On slide 2 he restates the logic of PS: big landlords must be very rich, so they can pay the LR (10/11) and invest huge sums in land; Bengal had them (15 Zs, 50%), Madras did not. 3.2 Under Ryotwari Under Ryotwari Landowner The ryot, who held legal title Settlement Directly with the ryot: the State dealt with each cultivator individually Assessment Detailed field surveys (soil productivity, irrigation, acreage, crops, past trends), in %, revisable, with revision and remission in bad harvests Collection By State officers: the DC and his juniors (Indians) Tenants (not stated on the slides) Teacher's board: the field survey is the most crucial thing in Ryotwari, and very tough The field survey is the crux of Ryotwari (very tough). Improper survey → unjust LR demand → landlessness. Three roads to loss of land from high LR: people abandon the land; default on LR → government auction; higher interest on a moneylender's loan → default → loss of the mortgaged land. And: "name of officers who designed and implemented the survey = imp" (underlined imp), with "Bombay: Wingate Settlement = Ryotwari." Learn the surveyors' names. Assessment evolved in two phases. Where and when Madras, by Alexander Read and Thomas Munro (1792-1820) Bombay (Pringle 1830, Wingate 1835) and Madras (1855, 1864) Demand 33% to 50% of estimated gross produce Based on net produce (gross crop value minus cost of cultivation: seeds, manure, bullocks, labour, implements): the Ricardian theory of Economic Rent Flaw or fix Surveys often improper; method arbitrary and ignored the cost of cultivation Reformed after the ruin of the agrarian economy Result Severe over-assessment: poverty, land abandonment ("Kheti hi chhod diye"); crop failure → borrow from moneylenders at high interest → default → lose mortgaged land or lose it in government auctions Bombay: Wingate fixes it; Madras: capped at 50% Phase 2 in Bombay. Elphinstone brought Ryotwari to Bombay (the slide dates it 1819 and says he did no fresh survey and used existing Maratha revenue records and assessments). R.K. Pringle (1830) first applied the Economic Rent theory but faulty calculations gave an excessive 55% demand. The Wingate Settlement of 1835 (Bombay Survey System, by Wingate and Goldsmid, implemented across the Bombay Deccan by 1847) fixed the flaw: it assessed LR fairly and fixed a reasonable annual amount for 30 years. Beside "reasonable annual amount for 30 years" he writes "Check it was %" (is the Wingate demand a percentage? [unclear: check your notebook]; the handout says annual amount). His sketch splits the Deccan into the Bombay Deccan and the Hyderabad Deccan: Wingate applied to the Bombay part. Ryotwari assessment phase 2 reforms: Bombay Pringle's date. The handout says R.K. Pringle (1830); the teacher's ink on the comparison slide (Lecture 18, slide 23) reads "PRINGLE 1830" (next to a partly unclear "Bomb 44", [unclear: check your notebook]); the milestone slide (slide 22) places "Pringle's revenue survey" at 1824-1828. Use 1830 for the Economic Rent application, and treat 1824-28 as the survey years on that card. Phase 2 in Madras. Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) exposed severe oppression in revenue collection. The Madras Rules (1855/1864) capped LR at 50% of net produce or rental value for 30 years (the slide: the Court of Directors ordered 30-year settlements with lower LR in 1855; in 1864 SoS Charles Wood directed the half-of-net-produce cap). The handout adds that addressing these grievances kept Madras relatively quiet during the 1857 revolt. Corruption: the lower bureaucracy relied on Mirasidars (rich landowner-cultivators acting as village-level revenue officers). Ryotwari assessment phase 2 reforms: Madras Because the DC and his officers held concentrated judicial, police and revenue powers, Mirasidars oppressed ryots, forced defaults and bought the best lands in auctions. The goal of removing big intermediaries failed: Mirasidars became big landowners themselves. "Over concentration of powers": the DC and his juniors (the Mirasidars) held admin (LR collection), judicial and police powers together, so a village official could squeeze the ryot, force default and then buy the land. Prelims 2012 (handout and class agree): answer (c) 1, 2 and 3. (1) Rent paid directly by peasants to the government: settlement is with the ryot. (2) Pattas given to ryots: the patta system was preserved. (3) Surveyed and assessed before taxed: detailed field surveys. 3.3 Impact in Bombay Collection: after annexing the Maratha Svarajya (3rd Anglo-Maratha War 1817-19) the EIC first used Patils (village headmen) and Deshmukhs to collect revenue, a nod to Orientalism; later it used officers. a) Patils lost their historic status. Earlier a Patil held executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and earned a commission (the teacher: "earlier commission"); now he was an ordinary salaried officer. b) Massive indebtedness to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders swept the central Deccan in the 1850s. c) Not solely Ryotwari: crop failures and the collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65). Collection at Ryotwari (Bombay) Indian cotton boomed in 1861-65 because the Union naval blockade cut off Confederate cotton; when the war ended, US cotton flooded markets again and the premium vanished. Combined result: the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875. Underlines: Patils demoted, executive, judicial, revenue and police powers and a commission, indebtedness, Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders, "crop failures played a role", "collapse of cotton prices after the US Civil War (1861-65)", Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875.

Because neither clean model fitted Awadh and the north-west, a compromise grew from the Taluqdars' fall. Ask: who is the owner, who settles, and why did it feed 1857? Mahalwari: where applied Applied in: Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab. UP = Awadh, undivided, taken in two parts: 1801 and 1856. The 1801 ceded districts were the first part; they got Mahalwari in 1822 and were organised as the North-Western Provinces (NWP) in 1836; Awadh was annexed in 1856; Punjab was annexed in 1849. The name changed in four steps: 1877 "NWP and Oudh;" 1902 "UP of Agra and Oudh;" 1937 "UP;" 1950 "Uttar Pradesh." (The handout's note says the "UP of 1937 = United Provinces of Agra and Oudh created in 1902": the board untangles it: 1902 is when it was named so; 1937 the short form UP; 1950 the modern name.) 4.1 Origin in Awadh Before the British, Taluqdars (Intermediary Zamindars) and Primary Zamindars dominated Awadh's agrarian economy. Half of Awadh came under British administration in 1801 (the nucleus of the North-Western Provinces). 1801-22: severe over-extraction. Taluqdars who resisted lost their milkiyats (landed estates): an entire class of landed magnates was crushed. In Mahalwari areas the Mughal-era revenue officers (Amils and Amalguzars at the district level, Tehsildars at the sub-district level) grew powerful and bought the best lands in auctions (note: Amlas are different, private employees of Zamindars, not State officers). Moneylenders, bankers and merchants also acquired milkiyat lands. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations were implemented through Regulation VII of 1822, creating the Mahalwari Settlement. Mahal = a community of people at the village, estate or district level. Taluqdar = a traditional leader of rural society; milkiyat = personal lands (so milkiyat holders = big landowners). He writes "7th Law of 1822" against Regulation VII of 1822 (as he did "7th Law of 1799" in Section 2.5): two Regulation VIIs, 1799 for Zamindar powers, 1822 for Mahalwari. Teacher's board: Mahal = community of people at village level, or district level, or estate level [some other size] 4.2 The hybrid structure Teacher's board: a circle split in two Mahalwari: the final hybrid structure Landowner Most areas: the ryot. Some areas: the Taluqdar Settlement Most areas: with the Mahal, through the Lambardar (its representative; he is the interface between State and community, preserving village autonomy; the Mahal decides internally how to spread the total demand). Some areas: with the Taluqdar Assessment Mahal-level after 1833 (before: per field or ryot); 66% of rental value for 30 years, revisable Collection State officers (the teacher: DC) Tenants Where the Taluqdar was owner, the law recognised ryots' occupancy rights and required recording of rents: the Patta had legal backing Mahalwari = a HYBRID of Ryotwari and Zamindari (on landownership). The slide's rule of thumb: type A = Ryotwari minus settlement with the ryot (it is with the Mahal); type B = PS 1793 minus permanent assessment. 4.3 The Revised Mahalwari System (R.M. Bird, 1833) Initially LR was assessed at the individual field or ryot level, but improper surveys led to excessive demands. In 1833, R.M. Bird introduced the Revised Mahalwari System in the NWP: (a) assessment at the Mahal level, not plot level, respecting the community's collective character; (b) individual contributions decided by the community; (c) if the Mahal's collective LR fell short, the State could auction individual ryots' lands; (d) LR fixed at 66% of the Rental Value (Net Assets, the teacher: net produce) for 30 years, subject to State revision. Dalhousie 48-56 extended Mahalwari to Punjab and Central India. 4.4 Why Mahalwari failed Improper field surveys → unjust land revenue → ryots lose land in State auctions or fall into debt and lose mortgaged land. When Awadh was finally annexed in 1856 a summary settlement was made (revenue without field surveys, because surveys take time): unjust demands and landlessness. Crushing of Taluqdars (1801-22), unjust demands, the summary settlement of 1856 and landlessness of ryots fed directly into the 1857 revolt in the NWP and Awadh (see Chapter 21). Two sad groups, both heading to 1857. Taluqdars (the leaders) were crushed; the ryot may have gained in the short term (smiley) but suffered in the long term (sad: landlessness in the long term). Both arrows end at the boxed "1857 REVOLT." Why Mahalwari failed

Because all three systems demanded cash, the ryot turned to cash crops and the moneylender. Ask: how does the chain run from cash demand to famine? Teacher's board Commercialisation of agriculture: the cash-revenue chain Handout figure of the same chain: British land revenue demanded in cash (not kind); ryots pressured to generate cash and shift from food to cash crops; moneylenders and t Under the Mughals much of the demand could be met in kind (grain for grain). The British demanded revenue in cash. To get cash, ryots were compelled, or induced by moneylenders and traders, to shift from food crops (feed the family, low market price) to cash crops: indigo, cotton, opium, jute, sugarcane. The higher the demand, the greater the pressure to grow cash crops: a structural transformation. Land that grew rice, wheat and millets now served British factories or global commodity markets. Food security declined: less food grain in reserve when drought or flood struck. This is one of the most important long-term legacies of British land policy and fed directly into the famines of the late 19th century. Two Indias. Before the Industrial Revolution (1750-1850) India was a source of finished goods (e.g. finished cotton); after it, India became an export market for British machine-made goods and a source of raw materials (raw cotton to British factories). Britain wanted Indians to grow more cash crops (B) and fewer food crops (A) = commercialisation of agriculture, so a higher chance of famine. His starred Mains prompt: "Why so many famines in British India?" And on slide 20 he adds that the moneylender's role rises along with cash demand ("More role of Rs Lenders", and a circled AND joining cash demand and the shift). The handout figure also names tea and coffee (plantation crops), oilseeds and a debt trap, and ends with peasant revolts (1857, Pabna, Deccan 1875). The handout's text lists indigo, cotton, opium, jute and sugarcane; use the text's list for Prelims, and the figure's extras only as colour in a Mains answer. Prelims 2021: answer (c) commercialisation of Indian agriculture. Teacher: (a) F (before the IR India exported finished goods; in the 19th century, the mature IR stage, India became a source of raw materials and an export market, so handicraft exports fell: deindustrialisation); (b) F (no conclusive evidence of growing Indian-owned factories); (c) T ("RM": raw materials need cash crops); (d) F (no conclusive evidence of rapid urbanisation).

Because the three systems answered the same five questions differently, line them up side by side. Ask: what did Cornwallis 86-93, Munro and Mackenzie with Bird each believe, and what did the ryot suffer in all three? Why three systems? Ideology, geography and fiscal pressure pulled in different directions. Cornwallis 86-93, an Englishman who believed in landlordism, made the Permanent Settlement. Munro, a Scotsman who believed in the yeoman farmer, made Ryotwari. Mahalwari was a practical compromise where neither clean model fit. 6.1 Permanent Settlement against Ryotwari against Mahalwari Comparison: Permanent Settlement (1793) / Ryotwari (1801, 1820+) / Mahalwari (1822, rev Landowner Zamindar Ryot Mostly ryot; sometimes Taluqdar (hybrid) Settlement with Zamindar Ryot directly Mahal (via the Lambardar) or Taluqdar Assessment Permanent: fixed forever (10/11 of pre-existing revenue) Detailed field surveys; 50% of net rental value (Madras Rules 1855/1864) for 30 years Mahal-level; 66% of Rental Value (Net Assets) for 30 years Collection by District Collector State officers (teacher: / DC) State officers (teacher: / DC) Where applied Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, Benaras, North Madras (BOB + Benaras + N. Madras) Sind, Coorg, Assam, Madras, Bombay (SCAM-B) Central Provinces, United Provinces, Punjab (CUP) Architect or driver Cornwallis 86-93 (English landlordism) Alexander Read + Thomas Munro (Scottish yeoman); slide adds Elphinstone (Bombay) Holt Mackenzie + R.M. Bird (hybrid, practical) Key failure Absentee landlordism; ryot a "tenant at will"; Patta collapses Over-assessment; Mirasidar abuse; Bombay Deccan Riots 1875 Improper surveys; summary settlement 1856; 1857 NWP and Awadh epicentre Class map: Land Revenue Systems under the British (1793-1858) Reading the map. It shades by today's state and shows the dominant system only. Princely states (grey) had their own revenue arrangements and are not among the three. The north coastal Andhra and Benaras pockets belong to PS (the handout's "North Madras" and "Benaras"). Berar appears under Ryotwari on the map but not in the handout's list. 6.2 Common causes of ryot suffering What united all three was a common outcome: ryots suffered. Whoever the landowner was (Zamindar, ryot, Taluqdar), the mix of high land revenue demands, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the imperfect but customary protections of the Mughal system. Prelims 2000, the handout and the class slide disagree on the first two rows (see the alert in the Exam lens). Handout: A = Zamindari, B = Jagirdari, code A-4 B-1 C-2 D-3 = (b); class slide and teacher's circles: A = Jagirdari, B = Zamindari, code A-1 B-4 C-2 D-3 = (b). The letter (b) is common. C = Ryotwari and D = Mahalwari are common. If you remember only one rule: peasant with the right to sell = Ryotwari; village level = Mahalwari.

The Mughal patta. The Khudkasht (cultivator) holds customary occupancy rights and pays by a patta, a written record of what he owes, plus abwabs to his Primary Zamindar. The chain runs Khudkasht, Primary Zamindar, Intermediary Zamindar, then the Jagirdar or State, with Amils and Amalguzars checking. The Zamindar is a commission collector (Vatan right, 10%) and not the owner: only the King is legal owner. When the State needs money in a hurry it auctions the collection (Ijaradari). Diwani, but the old chain (1765-70). The Treaty of Allahabad gives the EIC the Diwani of Bengal, Orissa and Bihar. It keeps the Mughal collection (Orientalism) under Deputy Subadar Muhammad Reza Khan as Diwan. But the patta is ignored and rents run far beyond the record, then back-to-back droughts strike: the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 kills 50 lakh to 1 crore, the demand is doubled and brutality is used. Reza Khan is jailed without trial 1772-74 as scapegoat. Bankrupt (1772). Since 1757 the EIC bought Indian goods with India's own land revenue, so the famine hit its income directly. Nabobs' corruption, the famine and the army and Dual System expenses bring it to the verge of bankruptcy. Parliament lends 1.4 million pounds at 4% on condition of parliamentary oversight, which leads to the Regulating Act 1773. The auction year (1772). Warren Hastings 73-85, an Orientalist, revives Ijaradari as the Farming System: each district's collection is auctioned to the Revenue Farmer, who works under a European District Collector. The farmers squeeze the ryots to recover their bids, the demand is so high that peasants pay nothing, and revenue does not improve. Cornwallis 86-93, the Believer (1793). Cornwallis 86-93 comes from a landlord family and believes in English landlordism ('my way or highway'). His Permanent Settlement Act 1793 covers Bengal, Orissa, Bihar, North Madras and Benaras. Four pillars: the Zamindar becomes legal owner; settlement is with him; LR is fixed at 10/11 of the 1789-90 revenue forever (Rs 66 becomes Rs 60); and the Sunset Clause auctions his land if he misses the evening deadline. What the Permanent Settlement did. Frequent auctions at first (Jotedars and the Zamindar's family buy), later loyal Zamindars (largely on the British side in 1857) and certain revenue. But Zamindars do not invest, become absentee, and the ryot is a tenant at will with the patta ignored. Wellesley 98-05 gives back seizure, imprisonment and rent rises (Regulation VII of 1799), and the Cornwallis 86-93 Code clogs the courts. Patching the ryot's rights (1859 and 1885). The Rent Act 1859 gives occupancy rights after 12 years on the same plot, revives the patta and bans imprisonment, but Zamindars evict at year 11 and keep lathiyals; the Indigo Revolt 1859-63 and the Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873 follow. After Ripon 80-84's Rent Commission of 1880, the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 under Dufferin 84-88 counts 12 years across plots in a village and is implemented sincerely. Munro's Ryotwari (1792-1820). Cornwallis 86-93 and Wellesley 98-05 tried to create big Zamindars in Madras through the Poligars; it failed. Thomas Munro convinced the Court of Directors in 1801: Read had begun in Baramahal in 1792, Munro applied it 1801-07, and as Governor of Madras 1820-27 re-established it. His reasons: Scottish yeoman ideology, no big Zamindars, stressed finances, eliminating Poligars, political stability. The ryot owns, is settled with directly, after a field survey (SCAM-B). Over-assessment and the Deccan riots. Phase 1 took 33% to 50% of gross produce and ignored costs: ruin, abandoned land, moneylender debt. Phase 2 used net produce (Ricardian Economic Rent): Pringle 1830 reached 55%, the Wingate Settlement 1835 fixed it for 30 years; in Madras the Torture Commission 1855 led to a 50% cap. Mirasidars wore three hats, Patils were demoted, and when the cotton boom of the US Civil War years (1861-65) collapsed, debts to Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders plus crop failures led to the Bombay Deccan Peasant Riots of 1875. Mahalwari (1822-1856). In Awadh half came under British rule in 1801 and the Taluqdars were crushed 1801-22. Holt Mackenzie's recommendations became Regulation VII of 1822: settlement with the Mahal through its Lambardar, a hybrid where the Taluqdar owns in some areas. R.M. Bird's Revised Mahalwari of 1833 assesses at Mahal level, 66% of rental value for 30 years; Dalhousie 48-56 carries it to Punjab and Central India (CUP). Improper surveys and the summary settlement of Awadh in 1856 feed the 1857 revolt. Cash instead of grain. The Mughals took much in kind; the British demanded cash. Ryots, compelled or induced by moneylenders and traders, shifted from food crops to indigo, cotton, opium, jute and sugarcane. Land that grew rice, wheat and millets served British factories (after the Industrial Revolution India became an export market and a source of raw materials). Less grain in reserve fed the famines of the late 19th century. Why three systems, and why the ryot lost. Cornwallis 86-93 the landlordist made PS, Munro the yeoman man made Ryotwari, and Mahalwari was a practical compromise: ideology, geography and fiscal pressure. In all three, high demand, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability and predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than under the Mughal patta.
