Story so far: the EIC holds the territory; now it must run it. The teacher's four verdicts set the weight of this chapter. Ask: why does he call the whole thing PubAd in British India? Chapter 18 title slide: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police Four verdicts on this chapter: no questions in Mains, few and rare questions in Prelims, it still troubles aspirants in every book, and this handout is the best version. He calls the whole subject the history of Public Administration (PubAd) in British India. That is how to read it: not as a list of Acts but as how a Company State built its working machinery. Administration: Machinery of the State

items.t: 1 · Administration as the machinery of the State
items.x: Because the State needs machinery to work, the EIC had to build or borrow it. Ask: which three pillars carry the chapter, and what are 'T' and 'Ppl'? Administration is the machinery of the State: how the State implements its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC changed from a trading company into a Company State (the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function; the slide dates the Company State 1765-1858), it had to build this machinery from scratch. More accurately, it had to decide how much of the existing Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. The chapter covers three pillars: Judiciary, Civil Services and Police. ORG with three arrows up: the organisation (the State) is made of its three machines. "WORK = RULE", and rule splits into T (territory) and Ppl (people). The State's work is to rule a territory and its people, and administration is how it does that work every day. This links to his L, E, J shorthand (legislative, executive, judicial power) from Chapter 8 and Chapter 10: the Company State had taken the territory; this chapter is about how it handled the people. Note for Mains (the handout's own warning). UPSC Mains PYQs mapped to administration overwhelmingly ask about the economic impact of British rule: Drain of Wealth, de-industrialisation and the Sepoy Army as an imperial tool. They cannot be answered from this chapter alone: Drain of Wealth and the economic critique are in the Moderates / Drain Theory chapter; de-industrialisation and the destruction of handicrafts are in the British Imperial Ideology and Land Revenue Systems chapters; Sepoy Army composition and grievances are in the 1857 Revolt chapter. This chapter provides the administrative skeleton; those chapters supply the economic and military flesh.

Because law was sensitive, the EIC began with Mughal courts and changed them only step by step. Ask: which six questions did every reform have to answer? 2.1 Why judicial reform was so complicated The EIC was not walking into a blank slate. It entered a society with established legal traditions, different religious communities and a functioning (though imperfect) court system. It had to answer six questions: 1 Which law should apply: Hindu, Islamic or British? Personal laws kept; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Supreme Court on British law 2 Should laws be written down or left to the judges' discretion? Codification: Gentoo Code, Hedaya, Code of 1781, Cornwallis 86-93 Code 3 What hierarchy of courts? 1772, 1773, 1793, Bentinck 28-35 4 Should lawyers be allowed to represent parties? Yes, from 1793 5 Should judges be Indians or British? All senior posts European under Cornwallis 86-93; lower posts opened from 1833 6 In which language should courts function? Persian replaced in 1835 Each question carried political, social and financial implications, and the answers changed as British confidence, ambition and administrative needs evolved. 2.2 The Mughal judicial system in Bengal (before 1772) The Mughal system in Bengal had two separate hierarchies, one for civil and one for criminal matters. Civil matters (Diwani = finance, land revenue and civil justice): Courts ran from the local level up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA) at the suba (provincial) level. In inter-personal matters (marriage, inheritance) the personal laws of Hindus and Muslims applied. Teacher's board: Traditional Mughal (J) system in Provinces Pandits judged Hindu cases and Maulvis judged Muslim cases. At the top the Diwan served as Chief Justice of the SDA. For land revenue and non-personal civil disputes, the original jurisdiction lay with the Zamindar at the local level, in his revenue court, the Kachari. Appeals went up: Zamindar, then Amil (the provincial revenue officer at district level), then the SDA at the provincial capital (Murshidabad), presided over by the Diwan or Naib Diwan. Around this time Muhammad Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held the posts of Chief Justice of both the SDA and the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. "Amil" versus "Amalguzar." The handout uses Amil only because it is a snapshot of the corrupted, mutated system of 18th-century Bengal; the canonical Mughal-administrative term is Amalguzar. The teacher's general board (slide 5) writes Amalguzar = revenue officer at district level; his Bengal board (slide 6) writes Amil (Rev officer). Same post. Criminal matters: Nizamat Adalats (commonly called Faujdari Adalats) sat at the district level, with the Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA) at the top. The Mughal State was an Islamic state, so Islamic law governed criminal proceedings, applied uniformly regardless of religion. At the village level the Zamindar held petty criminal jurisdiction alongside his police duties. Major crimes bypassed the Zamindar and went straight to the district Faujdari Adalat. Strict division of labour: the Kazis were the actual judges who pronounced verdicts (the board calls it a "2 People Bench," Kazi with Mufti), the Muftis gave expert interpretation of Islamic law, and the district Faujdar (executive police chief) secured the accused and physically executed the sentence. The Naib Nazim headed the SNA. Civil courts were religion-specific (your judge depended on your faith); criminal courts were State-uniform (the law of the ruling State applied to everyone). On the board: civil has two tracks under the SDA: the personal-law track (Diwani Adalat, Pandits and Maulvis) and the LR / non-personal track (Amalguzar, then the Zamindar's Kachari). Criminal has one track, with "Law = Islamic Law." Teacher's board: 18th c BENGAL at the SUBA level Who is Chief Justice of the SNA? Two boards, two answers, one reason. The teacher's general Mughal board (slide 5) writes SNA [CJ = Nazim / Subadar]; his 18th-century Bengal boards (slides 6, 7, 12) and the handout write CJ = Naib Nazim. The difference is the date: by the 18th century the real Subadar had become a distant authority and the Naib Nazim (Muhammad Reza Khan) ran the courts. For Bengal before 1772, use Naib Nazim for the SNA, and for the SDA the handout says Diwan (the board adds that Reza Khan, the Naib Nazim, held both chief justiceships, having been made the EIC's Diwan in 1765). Teacher's board: "Standard Books focus = Personal matters in Civil AND Criminal matters", with a circled "Remember" Most standard books stop at "personal law in civil matters AND criminal law in criminal matters," and the teacher tells you to remember exactly that pair. Civil = Hindu law for Hindus, Muslim law for Muslims. Criminal = Islamic law for everyone. Teacher's board: "FAUJDAR = Like SP at DISTRICT", with a brace giving two functions: "LEO" and "execute Judgement of NA/FA". The Faujdar is like today's SP (Superintendent of Police) at the district, and he did two jobs, which the board lists as LEO (as written on the board; the handout describes the Faujdar as the executive police chief who secured the accused) and executing the judgement of the Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat. He does not judge; the Kazi judges. Teacher's board: PRE 1772 Suba (province) Sadar Diwani Adalat (SDA), CJ the Diwan (Reza Khan held both chief justiceships) Sadar Nizamat Adalat (SNA), headed by the Naib Nazim District Diwani Adalat: Pandits (Hindu cases) and Maulvis (Muslim cases); revenue side: Amil (Amalguzar) Nizamat or Faujdari Adalat: Kazi judges, Mufti interprets, Faujdar executes Local Zamindar's Kachari: land revenue and non-personal disputes Zamindar: petty crimes only; major crimes go straight to the district court Law applied Personal law (Hindu law, Muslim law) Islamic law for all 2.3 The Dual Government period (1765-1772) After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC gained the Diwani rights over Bengal: revenue administration, Treasury and control of property / civil courts. (Modern welfare duties such as health and education were not included: they were traditionally handled by private or religious patronage, not by the Mughal government.) The Nawab retained the Nizamat (law and order). This created the Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism ("rule India the Indian way"), the EIC did not rush to impose its own system. Muhammad Reza Khan continued to head both the Diwani (on the EIC's behalf) and the Nizamat (on the Nawab's behalf). Indian officials remained the effective decision-makers on the ground. The EIC was mainly concerned with collecting land revenue. Outcome: revenue collection was poor; law and order deteriorated, made catastrophic by the Great Bengal Famine of 1770, which killed roughly one-third of Bengal's population. There is no ink on slide 11, but its typed outcome row carries a starred note: "Poverty leads to Crimes". Hunger pushed people into crime, so law and order failed because of the famine, and the famine was worsened by a hands-off administration. (For the Dual Government itself, Diwani versus Nizamat and Reza Khan as the EIC's Diwan, see Chapter 10.) 2.4 Direct Government (1772) and the judicial plan of Hastings 73-85 In 1772 Hastings 73-85 (Governor from 1772, GG of Bengal 1773-1785) ended the Dual Government and took direct administration of both the Diwani and the Nizamat. Rationale: EIC administration, based on rule of law and equality before law, would be fairer and more efficient and would firmly establish British authority. (The ideology shifts slightly from pure Orientalism to a hybrid: rule more directly, but still use Indian legal frameworks.) Diwani (civil) courts at the district The British DC is the judge, assisted by Pandits and Maulvis Personal laws continued in marriage and inheritance Nizamat (criminal) courts at the district Kazis and Muftis continue as judges, now supervised by the European DC The British thought law and order too sensitive to replace fully Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat Headed by the Governor (from 1773, the GG of Bengal) and his Council members The top of both ladders passes to the Company Teacher's board: 1772 CHANGES Muhammad Reza Khan (Naib Nazim) was imprisoned without trial from 1772 to 1774, accused of corruption and poor law-and-order maintenance. Conditions did not improve, so he was released in 1774 and reinstated as head of the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Why Kazis and Muftis stayed in the criminal courts: "Law and order (L and O) = sensitive, therefore the British continue with K and M as J." Taking over civil justice was safe; taking over criminal justice from the Muslim judges was too risky, so the DC only supervises there. Civil: the DC sits as judge. Criminal: the DC watches. 2.4.1 The changes of 1773 Two further adjustments: 1. A proper attempt at separation of revenue and judicial powers: an officer serving as DC was not to serve as judge too. In practice the overlap remained, but the principle was established. 2. To bring justice physically closer to the people, the district-level Diwani Adalats were replaced by 18 Mofussil courts, each headed by a European judge. Teacher's board: 1773 Act (Mofussil = rural areas and countryside districts below the district headquarters.) "PROPER SoP @ DC by CW 86-93." The handout calls 1773 a "proper attempt" at separation; the teacher corrects the weight of the word: the real, proper Separation of Powers at the level of the DC was done by Cornwallis 86-93 in 1793. In 1773 it was only the principle. Expect the exam to attach the DC's loss of judicial power to 1793 and Cornwallis 86-93 (this is Prelims 2010). 1773 versus 1793, do not mix. 1773 (Hastings 73-85): separation attempted, overlap remained, 18 Mofussil courts. 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): the DC is stripped of all judicial powers, the 18 Mofussil courts are abolished and the district Diwani Adalats come back (the teacher's slide 19 note: "Mofussil courts ended, DA back"). 2.4.2 The Supreme Court (1774) The Regulating Act 1773 led to a Supreme Court in Calcutta in 1774, specifically to hear cases involving British subjects in Bengal, under British law. (British people, British judges, British law: a completely separate judicial track.) Supreme Courts followed in Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823). The Supreme Court was entirely separate from the Indian court hierarchy. Teacher's board: 1774, in yellow circle The 1774 picture on one board: SDA headed by the GG; SNA headed by Naib Nazim Md Reza Khan (reinstated 1774); Mofussil courts with a European judge assisted by Pandits and Maulvis; Nizamat courts with Kazi and Mufti under the European DC's supervision. The Supreme Court sits outside this ladder, only for Britishers. 2.4.3 Codification of laws 1775: a committee of 11 Pandits compiled Hindu law into a single coherent code so courts could interpret it uniformly. The English translation was published as the Gentoo Code (1776). ("Gentoo" comes from the Portuguese "Gentios," a derogatory term for Hindus, used because Hindus worshipped multiple Gods unlike monotheistic Christians.) 1778: a similar effort for Islamic law. Because of Mughal rule, Islamic law was already well organised, so the EIC simply translated the most authoritative existing Arabic legal manual, the Al-Hidayah, first into Persian by Indian scholars and then into English as The Hedaya (1791). The Code of 1781 made written orders compulsory and prescribed rules for court functioning. "WRITTEN LAW": this answers question 2 of slide 4 (written or discretion?). "ENGLISH WRITTEN": the Gentoo Code and the Hedaya are both the English written versions of Indian law, so British judges could use them. The Code of 1781 is boxed "in Bengal": it applied only in Bengal (see slide 22 below). 2.5 The Cornwallis 86-93 Code of 1793 (judiciary) Cornwallis 86-93 (GG 1786-1793) introduced the most systematic judicial reform of the early period. He is rightly called the father of civil services, but his influence on the judiciary was equally significant. 2.5.1 Why did Cornwallis 86-93 reform the judiciary? He had just introduced the Permanent Settlement of 1793 (PS1793), creating a new class of large zamindars as private property owners. For this to work, zamindars needed secure property rights: courts they could trust, and revenue officials who could not harass them. An officer who collected your tax should not also be the judge hearing your appeal against his own actions. So Cornwallis 86-93 properly implemented Separation of Powers at the level of the DC: the District Collector was stripped of all judicial powers and confined to revenue collection and administration. Teacher's board: why Cornwallis separated powers "Imagine": PS1793 has a sunset clause (on his board, applying it lands the zamindar's estate up for auction). Suppose the DC applies the sunset clause on a zamindar (Z) and his land goes up for auction. The zamindar files a case in the Diwani Adalat. What if the judge is the same DC? Then there is a conflict of interest, and security of property falls for the zamindar (he draws a sad face). That is why the DC could no longer be a judge. Beside it, in yellow: Cornwallis 86-93 = AUTHORITARIAN, therefore he removed Indians from all senior positions (the other side of the same reform). Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 2.5). "By a regulation in 1793, the DC was deprived of his judicial powers and made the collecting agent only. Why?" Correct: (c) absolute power in one person was undesirable (separation of powers; the post-PS1793 zamindar class needed independent courts). (a) efficiency of revenue collection is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. (b) "judicial power must be European-only, revenue can be Indian" is wrong: Cornwallis 86-93 in fact removed Indians from all senior positions, including revenue. (d) "judicial work demanded deep India knowledge" is a partial truth, not the principal motivation. Teacher's board: 1793 CW 86-93 CODE 2.5.2 In civil matters The 18 Mofussil courts were replaced by Diwani Adalats at the district level and City Courts for urban areas. Bengal was divided into four divisions: Patna, Murshidabad, Calcutta and Dacca, and a Provincial Court of Appeal was set up in each. Appeals: district Diwani Adalats and City Courts, then the Provincial Court of Appeal, then the Sadar Diwani Adalat, shifted from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Personal laws of Hindus and Muslims continued in civil matters. PS1793 governed land revenue disputes. Per Charter Act 1793, all regulations for governing Bengal were codified, written orders made compulsory and laws printed in the vernaculars so people could know their rights. The Code of 1781 versus the Code of 1793: the difference is the ISSUING AUTHORITY. The 1781 code (by Hastings, applying only to Bengal) was issued by the GG (in Bengal), so a future GG could change it. The 1793 Code came through the Charter Act 1793, so it was issued by the British Parliament (the circled P) and carries more weight. Next to the Charter Act 1793 row he writes "By Br (P)": British Parliament. 2.5.3 In criminal matters Faujdari / Nizamat Adalats at the district level were abolished. Four Provincial Courts of Circuit were set up in the four divisions. A Court of Circuit is a court that physically moves around its division, hearing cases in different areas in rotation. This eliminated the need for a district-level criminal court. Appeals from the Courts of Circuit went to the Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Islamic law continued in criminal matters, but with British legal modifications. This hybrid was Anglo-Muhammadan law. For about 70 years, until the Indian Penal Code 1860, courts applied it. The circle on slide 21: a Court of Circuit spends week 1 in district 1, week 2 in district 2, week 3 in district 3, week 4 in district 4, then returns to week 1. It is a travelling bench, so no district needs its own criminal court. He underlines Anglo-Muhammadan law and IPC 1860 and adds the three codes: CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861 (see Section 2.7). 2.5.4 Anglo-Muhammadan law in practice: three examples (handout only, no class notes) Handout only (no class notes). The slide (23) stops at the name "Anglo-Muhammadan law"; the three examples below come from the handout alone. A: weapon rule replaced by intent rule Whether a killing was capital murder depended on the weapon used: a sharp iron instrument (sword) meant murder; strangling, drowning or a heavy stone was often a lesser crime (the instrument was not "designed" to draw blood) He abolished this loophole: the intent of the accused decides, not the instrument. This matches the modern principle of mens rea B: the end of "blood money" (Diyat) Murder was largely a private dispute between families: the victim's heirs could pardon the killer for financial compensation (blood money, Diyat) Relatives could no longer pardon a murderer. This set the principle that a major crime is an offence against the State, not just a private injury C: abolition of mutilation The standard punishment for serious theft or dacoity was amputation of a hand or foot The EIC completely outlawed mutilation and replaced it with hard labour and rigorous imprisonment, typically 7 to 14 years 2.5.5 Personnel and a new profession: lawyers Cornwallis 86-93 was authoritarian. He removed Indians from all senior positions. All courts were headed by European officials. Kazis and Muftis were retained only as assistants, not judges. The office of Naib Nazim was abolished. Cornwallis 1793: Personnel and a New Profession One progressive change: lawyers were now permitted to appear in courts. This created a new professional class, the Indian lawyer, and, along with PS1793 (which made land a tradeable commodity), also a class of property dealers. "[NA ABOLISHED]": the Nizamat Adalat at district level is gone. "Cornwallis 86-93, father of: CS (civil services), property dealers, lawyer." One man, three offspring. Under the fork there is a short word that reads like "SHO" (the station house officer, which would be his police Daroga of Section 4.3): [unclear: check your notebook]. 2.5.6 Why the new system increased litigation (class slide only, not in the handout) Lecture 20, slide 25 only (the handout does not carry this table). The slide gives three reasons litigation rose after PS1793, with no ink on it. 1. Separation of Powers (key reason) The DC lost all judicial and magisterial powers. Earlier the Collector could resolve revenue disputes swiftly and informally on the spot; after 1793 every such dispute had to be formally filed in the Diwani Adalats 2. Abolition of court fees Cornwallis 86-93 initially abolished court fees to make justice "accessible," which instantly flooded the courts with genuine and frivolous suits. Fees were reimposed just 2 years later, in 1795 3. A legal profession Formal recognition of lawyers (Vakils) and a rigid hierarchy of appeals: cases were deliberately prolonged and appealed 2.6 Judicial system in Ryotwari areas The Bengal model of separated judicial and revenue functions worked in a zamindari system. In Ryotwari areas, where the ryot is recognised as the direct landowner, conditions were very different: A very large number of small landowners meant a very large number of land-related disputes. District courts were physically distant for poor ryots in villages. Judicial System in Ryotwari Areas Madras, 1814: the Bengal system was replaced on Munro's advice. Separation of judicial and revenue powers was ended. The European DC and his subordinates were given judicial powers so disputes could be resolved at the ground level. (Less paperwork, less travel, faster justice, at least in theory.) This led to greater Indianisation at the lower judiciary, because the DC's subordinates included Indian officials. The downside: enormous concentration of power in one official. The DC now collected taxes, maintained order and judged disputes, including disputes arising from his own tax collection decisions. Bombay, 1819: the same Ryotwari system was applied by Elphinstone, a follower of Munro's philosophy. Why Bengal separated and Madras merged: "WHR (where) the number of landowners is LESS" (the line points at "zamindari"): in a zamindari area there are few big landowners, so few disputes and a distant court is workable. In a ryotwari area the landowners are many, so the courts must come to the village. On the downside row he adds "+ his juniors": the DC's juniors (the subordinates, including Indians) also gain judicial powers. The Madras Torture Commission Report of 1855 is his example of what the concentrated power led to: "oppression by Mirasidars revealed." The pyramid of 300, 200 and 100 beside the word INDIANS [unclear: the currency sign and the triangle are not labelled; check your notebook] seems to show pay or rank scales for Indians below a DC above 300. Same Commission, two homes. The handout mentions the Madras Torture Commission report of 1855 in the police section (4.3.2) as the exposure of the atrocities of revenue officials after the Daroga system failed in Madras. The teacher hangs it on the Ryotwari judicial system (a DC with all powers, plus juniors) and writes Mirasidars (the village landholders of Madras). Learn the fact once, 1855, Madras Torture Commission, oppression exposed, and use it in either answer. 2.7 Charter Act 1833 (judicial impact) The Charter Act of 1833 made the GG of India the single central legislative authority for all of British India, and the laws passed were to apply equally to Indians and Britishers alike. (A major shift: one law for everyone, regardless of race.) One Law Member was added to the GG's Council: Thomas Macaulay was appointed, and a Law Commission (1834) was set up under him to codify all laws systematically. Codification was substantially complete by 1837, but full implementation came after 1857: Civil Procedure Code (CPC) 1859 Indian Penal Code (IPC) 1860 Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) 1861 Subordinate judicial positions below the rank of District Judge were opened to Indians. Impact on the common Indian: justice became psychologically distant (new laws were western, complex and unfamiliar), physically distant for rural areas and financially distant (legal fees few could afford). The system was more systematic, but it served the educated and propertied far better than the poor. "Personal laws continued in personal matters": even with the IPC, CPC and CrPC, marriage and inheritance stayed under Hindu and Muslim personal law. "Indianisation of the lower J": the opening of posts below District Judge is the lower judiciary's Indianisation (note how it follows the 1814 Madras Indianisation in Section 2.6). "Western Edu 1835": the new western, English-language law goes with western education from 1835 (Chapter 19: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture): the English-educated class is the one that could use the new courts. 2.8 Reforms by Bentinck 28-35 (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35) Concept versus reality. In concept the polity has three equal organs: L (legislature), E (executive), J (judiciary). In reality the E is the top prestige: DC and senior civil servants want to be in E, and an inefficient officer is posted as a punishment to the Divisional Court. So the judiciary (J) was the dumping ground. This is the setup for why Bentinck 28-35 abolished those courts. Teacher's board: Bentinck 28-35, "Decs in (J)" (decisions in the judiciary) Teacher's board: Bentinck 28-35 Reforms Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts: both the Provincial Courts of Appeal (civil) and the Courts of Circuit (criminal) that Cornwallis 86-93 had created. Why: these courts had become parking grounds for inefficient officers (punishment postings for non-performers), which contributed to high pendency. High-ranking officers also meant high State expenditure, so the courts were ended as a fiscal-prudence measure. Transfer: judicial powers and pending cases went to District Judges. After Bentinck 28-35 the ladders are shorter: civil: District Diwani Adalat + City Courts go straight up to the SDA (the four Provincial Courts of Appeal are crossed out); criminal: Nizamat Adalat goes straight up to the SNA (the four Courts of Circuit are crossed out). He underlines "high State expenditure" on slide 30 and writes "86-93" (small, no name) beside "Cornwallis 86-93 had created": the courts he removed were Cornwallis 86-93's. Reforms by William Bentinck (GG 1828-33; GG of India 1833-35) 1835, language of the courts: Persian was replaced: vernaculars in the lower courts and English in the higher courts. Legal backing: Act XXIX of 1837. The removal caused anxiety among Muslim elites, because Persian education had been an important pathway to administrative careers. Courts for the Northwest Provinces: he created a Sadar Diwani Adalat and a Sadar Nizamat Adalat in the Northwest Provinces (the portion of Awadh annexed in 1801, given full province status in 1836), so people from this region did not have to travel to Bengal to file appeals. The NWP circle: 1801 (the Awadh portion annexed) leads down to NWP 1836, a province with full status; the other oval is the Bengal Presidency, and the dotted line between them is written "Distance." Appeals to Calcutta meant a long journey, so (his inserted word) the NWP got its own two Sadar courts. Context on Persian (slide 31, typeset, no ink). Persian was introduced under the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century. It got a major boost when Humayun 30-40, to win military support from Persia's Safavid dynasty to reclaim his throne from the Suri Dynasty (1540-55), accepted the condition of promoting Persian. Akbar 56-05, with finance minister Todar Mal, made Persian compulsory for all administrative records. 2.9 Indian High Courts Act 1861 and 2.10 the Federal Court (GOI Act 1935) The Indian High Courts Act 1861 led to High Courts in Madras, Bombay and Calcutta in 1862. The Calcutta High Court was created by merging three existing courts: the Sadar Diwani Adalat, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat and the Supreme Court at Calcutta. This finally ended the dual-track system of separate courts for Indians and the British. The GOI Act 1935, implemented from 1937, established a Federal Court, the direct ancestor of today's Supreme Court of India. It dealt with inter-governmental disputes (Centre versus Province, Province versus Province) and heard appeals from High Courts. Today's Supreme Court, set up under the Constitution of India 1950, continues this role with expanded jurisdiction. The judiciary: from Mughal courts to the Federal Court Before 1772: two ladders (civil: Diwan, Pandits and Maulvis, Zamindar's Kachari; criminal: Naib Nazim, Kazi, Mufti, Faujdar); personal law in civil, Islamic law in criminal Dual Government 1765-72: Reza Khan heads both Diwani and Nizamat; revenue poor; law and order falls; famine 1770 1772 (Hastings 73-85): DC as civil judge; Kazi and Mufti kept under DC supervision; Governor and Council head the two Sadar Adalats 1773-74: 18 Mofussil courts; Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), later Madras 1800 and Bombay 1823; Gentoo Code 1776, Hedaya 1791, Code of 1781 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): DC loses judicial power; four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit; Anglo-Muhammadan law; Indians out of senior posts; lawyers in 1814 and 1819: Madras and Bombay merge the DC's roles in Ryotwari areas 1833-37 (Bentinck 28-35 and Macaulay): divisional courts abolished; Persian replaced 1835; NWP Adalats; Law Commission 1834 1859-62: CPC, IPC, CrPC; High Courts 1862 end the dual track 1937: Federal Court, ancestor of the Supreme Court of India (1950)

Because courts and revenue need officers, the question became who gets hired and how. Ask: what separates a service from mere employment, and what did Cornwallis 86-93 NOT introduce? 3.1 Issues in civil services, and what a "service" means The seven design questions for any civil service, as his board lists them: (1) nomination or examination? (2) if exam, by a specialised body like the UPSC or not? (3) syllabus: Indian or Western? (4) exam location: London, or India and London? (5) age limit: low or high? (6) organisation of the services (today IAS, IPS, IFS, IRS and more): one common exam or a separate exam for each service? (7) training: on the job or in a training institute? Read the rest of the chapter as the EIC's answers to these seven, in order. In any organisation officials may be simply employed, or organised into a service. A service means a pre-defined career path, fixed rules for pay, promotion and removal, and a clear structure of seniority and accountability: the difference between being an employee and being a member of a cadre. The history of the EIC's civil services is a move from a chaotic, patronage-based system to a structured, merit-based administrative cadre, with an extra tension: how many Indians would be allowed in? Teacher's board: "issues in CS" (in an oval) Without a service: "No career ladder" = "Total discretion," that is, total discretion in employment and in promotion. The boss alone decides who is hired and who is promoted. A service replaces discretion with rules. 3.2 Recruitment: from patronage to examination Initially EIC officials were recruited by nomination, not merit. Posts were either purchased or handed out through patronage. EIC Directors actively lobbied British Parliamentarians with offers of jobs for their sons. This bred corruption and incompetence. 3.3 Training Until 1800 Essentially on the job 1800-1806 Fort William College, Calcutta, set up by Wellesley 98-05 for training in Indian laws, customs and languages 1806-1858 Haileybury College, London (East India College) 1858 onwards British universities 3.4 Cornwallis 86-93: founder of civil services Cornwallis 86-93 brought the first proper structure to the civil services. He organised ("ORGanised") EIC employees into two tiers: Today's parallel Like today's Group A Like today's Group B Who Senior officers who signed a formal legal contract, a "covenant," with the EIC's Court of Directors in London before sailing to India Junior officers hired locally in India by the GG or provincial governors Pay and path High defined pay, clear career path Lower pay, less formal Access Under Cornwallis 86-93 reserved strictly for Europeans The space where Indians were allowed to serve: at first very low-level clerical roles, then Deputy Collectors and Deputy Magistrates by the 1830s-40s as the empire grew and needed cheaper local administrators "Organised employees into...": this is what the word "service" means (Section 3.1): from a pool of employees to ranked cadres. Beside the CCS access cell: Europeans-only = "Authoritarian" (the same Cornwallis 86-93 who removed Indians from all senior judicial posts). Beside the UCS: "Indians + British": the UCS was not Indians-only; it held both, which is why it is the space where Indians could enter. DID Two tiers CCS plus UCS: the first proper structure DID Strict seniority for promotions London bosses could no longer push underqualified relatives over experienced officers (the slide calls it "Merit @ Promotions") DID Massively higher salaries To reduce the incentive to be corrupt DID Curbed private trade by EIC officials (see the Dastak and private trade story in [[10 Chapter 10]]) DID Separation of Powers DC stripped of judicial powers in 1793 DID NOT Merit-based selection for entry Entry stayed patronage-based: nomination by the EIC's Court of Directors in London, right until the Charter Act 1853 This is why he is called the founder of civil services in India: he converted a corrupt, patronage-ridden set of employees into a structured, professionalised service. Prelims 2010 trap (handout, Section 3.4). "Who among the following GGs created the Covenanted Civil Service, which later became the Indian Civil Service?" Correct: (c) Cornwallis 86-93. (a) Hastings 73-85 is wrong: first GG of Bengal under the Regulating Act 1773, introduced a judicial plan but not the CCS structure. (b) Wellesley 98-05 is wrong: set up Fort William College 1800 for CCS training but did not create the service structure. (d) Bentinck 28-35 is wrong: opened the UCS to Indians under the Charter Act 1833 and encouraged some senior Indian recruitment, but did not create the CCS. Also: the CCS was later renamed ICS in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94, per the Aitchison Commission 1887, NOT by the Indian Councils Act 1892. 3.5 Charter Act 1833 and Bentinck 28-35 The Charter Act of 1833 opened the Uncovenanted Civil Services to Indians, primarily to reduce administration cost by using cheaper Indian labour in junior roles. Bentinck 28-35 went slightly further and encouraged recruitment of Indians to some senior positions. 3.6 Charter Act 1853: the exam opened to Indians The Charter Act of 1853 was a landmark: it mandated a Civil Service Examination for the CS and Indians were eligible to appear. 1854: a Select Committee of Parliament under Macaulay recommended replacing patronage-based recruitment with exam-based recruitment for a permanent civil service. This led to the Civil Services Commission (1854) in London, which held its first examination in 1855. Eligibility on paper did not mean access in practice: Age limit The maximum age ranged from 18 to 23, kept deliberately low. 1859: the Crown cut the maximum entry age to 23. Then 22 in 1860, 21 in 1866, and 19 in 1876 (implemented 1878 so as not to hit aspirants already preparing) Syllabus Dominated by English Literature, designed to produce what Macaulay called "Brown Sahibs": Indians educated in English culture and values, culturally loyal to Britain Venue Held only in London For an Indian candidate Cost of travel to England; inferior preparation compared with British candidates; a syllabus that rewarded English cultural knowledge over Indian First Indians through 1864: Satyendranath Tagore (brother of Rabindranath Tagore) was the first Indian to clear the CCS exam. 1867: four more Indians cleared it Why low age, English Literature and a London exam? "To prevent entry of Indians into CS." The age ladder itself he marks "not imp" (do not memorise every step). "Literature = source of values": English Literature on the syllabus carried English values, which is how the Brown Sahib is made. And the last row's point in his words: the exam tested "culture's knowledge," and western education in Britain was better than in India, so a Briton had the advantage. 3.7 The fight for Indianisation (1860 onwards) From 1860 the western-educated Indian middle class (WEMC), the very product of British educational policy, began demanding Indianisation of the civil services. Two core demands: Simultaneous examination in India (not just London). A higher maximum age limit. The British response was hostile. Post-1857 British administrators were insecure about Indian assertion and determined to keep Indians out of senior positions. WEMC = Western Educated Middle Class [1835+]. The date is the western education of 1835 (see the "Western Edu 1835" note on slide 27): the class that demands entry is the one the British made. And on the same row, beside the British response, "1st exam in India = 1922" (the answer to demand 1, which came only with the GOI Act 1919; see Section 3.9). 3.7.1 The Statutory Civil Services Act (Lytton 76-80) Parliament had given directions for Indianisation in 1870. Instead of holding the exam in India or raising the age limit, Lytton 76-80 (Viceroy 1876-1880) brought lateral entry via nomination through the Statutory Civil Services Act. Under it loyal elite Indians could be nominated to posts previously reserved for CCS officers, but only carefully vetted, politically loyal individuals were selected. The statutory authority over the rules, regulations, syllabus and age limits for the civil service was vested in the Secretary of State for India after the GOI Act 1858. (The handout adds a note: books put responsibility on Lytton 76-80 for reducing the age limit and credit Ripon 80-84 for increasing it, because the SoSforIndia was greatly influenced by the GG's input, but that is not the legal truth.) He links the 1870 directions to the 1858 Proclamation and the Charter 1833 (the "star" note on the slide), and labels the Statutory Civil Services Act "[unimportant ACT]." Underlined: lateral entry, Statutory CS, only loyalists. Learn it in one line: nomination of loyal elite Indians, instead of an exam in India. Handout versus slide on the Statutory Civil Services Act. The handout writes "Statutory Civil Services Act 1878 (under Lytton 76-80)" and says the Statutory Civil Services were "created 1878" (Section 3.7.2). The slide title and body write "Statutory CS 1879," with "rules framed in 1879 under GOI Act 1870." Reading them together: the Act is 1878 in the handout; the rules were framed in 1879 on the slide. The teacher calls it an "unimportant act," so memorise only Lytton 76-80, lateral entry, loyalists. Slide 40 strikes out "ICS" and writes "CCS" in the SoSforIndia row, while the handout says authority over the "Indian Civil Service." The slide's correction is the logical one (the service in 1858 was still the CCS; it became ICS only in 1892, Section 3.7.2). Handout only (no class notes): Lecture 20 stops at slide 40, so everything from here to the end of the chapter comes from the handout alone 3.7.2 Aitchison Commission (1887) Dufferin 84-88 appointed it in 1886; the report came in 1887. It recommended dropping the terms "Covenanted" and "Uncovenanted" and dividing the services into three tiers: Imperial Civil Service (ICS), Provincial Civil Service (PCS) and Subordinate Civil Service. Implementation came in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 (NOT a provision of the Indian Councils Act 1892, a classic exam trap; see Chapter 28: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (Lord Cross Act), Section 9). CCS became ICS, UCS became PCS, and the Statutory Civil Services (created 1878) were abolished (partly through moderate nationalist pressure). The Provincial Civil Services were recruited through exams and selection held in India, to ensure greater Indian participation in administration. 3.8 Islington Commission (1912) Context in the national movement: Swadeshi Movement (1905-11), Delhi Conspiracy Case (1912), Ghadar Movement (1913-15), Home Rule Leagues (1916-18) and British wartime claims of fighting for democracy in WW I (1914-19). The Commission was set up in 1912 but published its report only in 1917. It recommended 25% Indians in senior positions, via exam and via promotion from the PCS. It rejected the nationalist demand for simultaneous examination in India, arguing that educational standards in India were not uniform enough. (The handout's reading of the real reason, unstated: the British feared an exam in India would produce more Indian candidates than they were comfortable with.) 3.9 Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms / GOI Act 1919 Context: Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919). The GOI Act 1919 mandated: Simultaneous examination in India (first held in 1922). A Public Service Commission for India (established in 1926). A gradual increase to 33% Indians in senior positions. The ICS was also restructured. Since the Act divided subjects between the Centre and the Provinces (Dyarchy), the ICS was split into All India Services (AIS) and Central Civil Services. (The AIS and Central Services structure of today is essentially this 1919 structure, continued and modified by the Constitution.) 3.10 Lee Commission / Royal Commission on Superior Civil Services (1923) Context: Khilafat Movement (1920-24) and Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22). It had equal numbers of British and Indian members. Its report (1924) recommended: 20% of senior positions Filled by promotion from the PCS 40% Indians via exam 40% Europeans via exam 50:50 ratio Between Indians and Europeans within 15 years via exam Public Service Commission As originally mandated by the GOI Act 1919, should be established Structure AIS (ICS, IPS, Indian Forest Service and so on), Central Services (Foreign Affairs, Customs, Railways and so on) and Provincial Services (Health, Education and so on) 3.11 GOI Act 1935 Context: Hindustan Republican Army (1924), CPI (1925), HSRA (1928), Anti-Simon agitations (1928), Lahore Conspiracy Case (1928), Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34), Chittagong Armoury Raid (1930-33), the martyrdom of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and Chandrashekhar Azad (1931). The Act made the federal distribution of subjects between Centre and Provinces a formal constitutional structure. It mandated a Federal Public Service Commission (set up in 1937, replacing the 1926 PSC, the direct predecessor of today's UPSC) and Provincial Public Service Commissions for each Province or group of Provinces. By 1947 more than 50% of civil service positions had been Indianised. On 26 January 1950 the Federal PSC became the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) under Article 378 of the Constitution. (Article 378 is a transition provision: it ensures membership of the British-era UPSC and State PSCs continued seamlessly. Articles 315 and 316 govern the UPSC and State PSCs. Article 312 governs All India Services.) The civil services: from patronage to the UPSC Early EIC: nomination, purchase and patronage; Directors lobby Parliamentarians for sons' jobs 1793 (Cornwallis 86-93): CCS plus UCS, higher pay, private trade curbed, seniority for promotion; entry still by nomination Training: on the job until 1800; Fort William College 1800-06; Haileybury 1806-58; universities from 1858 1833: UCS opened to Indians (cheaper junior labour); Bentinck 28-35 encourages some senior posts 1853-55: exam mandated, London-only; first exam 1855; Satyendranath Tagore 1864; four more 1867 1860 onwards: Indians demand a simultaneous exam and a higher age; British hostile; Lytton 76-80 offers lateral entry (Statutory CS 1878-79) 1887-92: Aitchison; ICS, PCS, Subordinate by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94 1912-17: Islington: 25% Indians, no simultaneous exam 1919-26: GOI Act 1919: exam in India 1922, PSC 1926, 33% 1923-24: Lee: 20-40-40, 50:50 in 15 years 1935-50: Federal PSC 1937; over 50% Indianised by 1947; UPSC under Article 378 on 26 January 1950

Because the third pillar was the most sensitive, the Mughal chain was kept for the longest time. Ask: why did the Daroga system fail, and why was Napier's Sindh model chosen? Handout only (no class notes). Lecture 20 has no slides on the police, so there is no teacher ink in Sections 4 and 5. The teacher's title-slide verdict (few and rare Prelims questions) still applies. 4.1 The inherited system (pre-1781) The EIC treated law and order as extremely sensitive, so the Mughal system of policing was left untouched for the longest time. Under it in Bengal: Overall head Naib Nazim (Deputy Subadar) Rural districts (Sarkars) Faujdars (Sarkar here means a sub-divisional unit, not government; the meaning differs by region) Towns and urban areas Kotwals Villages Zamindars held police duties and paid Village Watchmen from their own resources 4.2 Warren Hastings 73-85's reforms of 1781 The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 had led to a sharp increase in crime. Hastings 73-85 replaced Faujdars with English Magistrates (DC/DM) in rural districts. Zamindars kept their police duties under the DM's supervision. The problem: very few DMs, and poor supervision of zamindars, who continued to oppress the masses freely. 4.3 The Daroga system of Cornwallis 86-93 (1793) Ended the police powers of zamindars: under PS1793 zamindars were to be agrarian capitalists, not local police authorities. Divided each district into thanas of 30 square miles each. Each thana was under a new officer, the Daroga (Indian), appointed and supervised by the DM. The English District Magistrate (DM) was made the absolute, supreme head of law and order within his district. Rather than an intermediary like an English Naib Nazim or an Inspector General, Cornwallis 86-93 centralised ultimate oversight of criminal and police administration in the GG and his Council. Chain of command: Darogas, then DM, then the central government. 4.3.1 DC and DM: two roles, usually one person In most of British India (and in India today) the District Collector and District Magistrate are the same person holding two roles. Cornwallis 86-93 separated the judicial function from this officer (the DC/DM lost the power to be a judge), but the revenue and law-and-order functions stayed combined: DC (revenue) Collects land revenue, manages government land, maintains land records, collects various taxes The Mughal Diwani / Amalguzar function DM (law and order) Heads the district's criminal administration; coordinates with the SP to keep peace, prevent riots and issue executive orders such as Section 144 of the CrPC The Mughal Nizamat / Faujdari function 4.3.2 Result: the Daroga-Zamindar nexus A Daroga-Zamindar nexus quickly developed: zamindars bribed Darogas and kept private armed men (lathiyals). The nexus became the primary instrument of oppression of the rural poor in the early 1800s. The British blamed "Indian corruption" rather than the structural weaknesses of the system. 1799: Wellesley 98-05 restored police powers to zamindars, in effect admitting the Daroga system had not worked. 1802: the Daroga system was extended to Madras but was later abolished there too because of its failures. The resulting atrocities of revenue officials were exposed by the Madras Torture Commission report of 1855, which led to corrective measures. 4.4 The Police Act 1861 The Daroga system had failed. The British looked for a proven alternative and found it in the Irish Constabulary model: a centralised, hierarchical, quasi-military police force, effective in Ireland since 1787, designed as much for suppressing political agitation as for preventing ordinary crime. (The British were not primarily building a crime-prevention force; they were building a political control mechanism.) 4.4.1 Province-by-province road-test (pre-1861) Sindh 1843 (annexed) Charles Napier, the military general who conquered Sindh, set up the Sindh Police on the Irish Constabulary model immediately after conquest Punjab 1849 Post-annexation Bombay 1853  Madras 1859  The 1st Police Commission (1860) was set up by Canning 56-62 under M.H. Court. It simply formalised what had already proved effective on the ground and borrowed heavily from the Sindh model when drafting the 1861 Police Act. A common UPSC trap: Charles Napier did NOT head the 1860 commission (many guidebooks wrongly say he did). Napier gave the blueprint (Sindh); M.H. Court's commission drew the national map using it. 4.4.2 The Police Act 1861 The Police Act, 1861 was passed in March 1861 by the GG's Council (as last restructured by the Charter Act 1853). (The Indian Councils Act 1861 came in August 1861 and created the Imperial Legislative Council (ILC); do not mix them.) It created the provincial police structure across all provinces: each Province to have its own police organisation, with a clear hierarchy: Inspector General (IG) The provincial police The Governor / Lieutenant Governor (LG) Superintendent of Police (SP) The district police The DC / DM Sub-Inspector (SI) The thana The SP (not to the DC as earlier) Operational accountability ran upward through the police chain: SI, SP, IG. Political accountability ran to civilian authority: SP to DC/DM, IG to LG / Governor. This was only the organisational chart. In 1861 the British simply posted military officers or nominated European men into the senior posts: no formal cadre, no competitive exam, no unified service, just employees of provincial governments. The posts existed; the service did not yet. From 1857 onwards a "Police Raj" was created: Indians were excluded from all senior positions, and the emphasis was on effective policing, intelligence collection and political surveillance. 4.4.3 Formalisation into a structured cadre 1893 First open competitive exam for senior police posts, held in London; top candidates became probationary Assistant Superintendents of Police under the Secretary of State for India 1902-03 Curzon 99-05 set up the 2nd Police Commission under Sir Andrew Fraser; report 1903. It organised superior police officers into one unified all-India cadre, the Imperial Police (IP) (informally the Indian Police); scheme implemented from about 1905 (Fraser's package) Provincial Police Service (PPS) created, with a new rank Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) that accommodated Indians at officer level, always junior to the British IP. CID set up in every province, plus a central intelligence bureau, the Department of Criminal Intelligence (1903), forerunner of today's IB. But the IP itself stayed closed to Indians: Fraser did NOT recommend appointing Indians to it 1920 Direct entry into the IP officially opened to Indians (simultaneous exams in England and India from 1921), largely a result of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (GOI Act 1919) By 1931 Only 20% of SPs were Indians From 1939 More Indians posted as SP because British candidates were unavailable (recruited for World War II, 1939-45) 1948 The IP was administratively replaced by the Indian Police Service (IPS) by a Home Ministry resolution; statutory backing came from the All India Services Act, 1951 1861 built the structure, 1902-03 built the service, 1948-51 built the IPS. (Today's IPS is an All India Service under Article 312, with State police under State governments, directly inheriting the 1861 framework.)

items.t: 5 · The three-pillar administrative legacy (handout only, no class notes)
items.x: Because each pillar moved only when pushed, the handout ends with one pattern. Ask: which two triggers drove reform, and what three legacies were left? The EIC's administrative evolution across judiciary, civil services and police shows a consistent pattern: structural improvement followed political convenience, not principle. Each major reform was triggered by a crisis (the Great Bengal Famine 1770, the 1857 revolt) or was a concession wrested by the Indian National Movement after sustained pressure. The British never voluntarily Indianised their administration beyond what was economically necessary (to reduce costs) or politically unavoidable (to manage nationalist pressure). They left behind, however inadvertently, a set of institutions that independent India would inherit, adapt and build upon: codified law, an organised civil service, a hierarchical police. Judiciary Diwani Adalats (civil; Pandits and Maulvis) plus Nizamat Adalats (criminal; Kazis, Muftis, Faujdars) Hastings 73-85's 1772 plan; 1774 Supreme Court at Calcutta; Cornwallis 86-93 Code 1793 with Anglo-Muhammadan law Charter Act 1833 (Macaulay, Law Commission 1834) leading to CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861; High Courts Act 1861 (High Courts at Madras, Bombay, Calcutta 1862) GOI Act 1935: Federal Court (1937), then Supreme Court of India 1950; CPC, IPC and CrPC replaced in 2024 by BNS, BNSS and BS Civil services Mansabdari nobility under Mughal patronage Cornwallis 86-93 (1793): founder of CCS plus UCS; salaries raised; seniority for promotion Charter 1853: exam mandated, Indians eligible (London only); ICS renamed by executive order 1892 (Lansdowne 88-94, per Aitchison 1887, NOT by ICA 1892) Lee Commission 1923 leading to PSC 1926; GOI 1935 Federal PSC (1937) then UPSC 1950 (Article 378); AIS under Article 312 Police Naib Nazim to Faujdars (rural) and Kotwals (towns), plus Zamindars (villages) Hastings 73-85's 1781 reforms; Cornwallis 86-93's Daroga System 1793 (failed through the Daroga-Zamindar nexus) Irish Constabulary road-test (Sindh 1843 Napier, Punjab 1849, Bombay 1853, Madras 1859); 1st Police Commission 1860 (M.H. Court) leading to the Police Act 1861 (March 1861) 2nd Police Commission 1902-03 (Fraser) leading to the Imperial Police (IP) cadre; 1948 Home Ministry resolution leading to the IPS; AIS Act 1951 plus Article 312 The handout's scrambled table. In the PDF this summary table is broken (words split across cells; the last cell of the judiciary row is cut). A trading company must run a state. Administration is the machinery by which a State carries out its policies, laws and schemes on the ground. When the EIC turned from a trading company into a Company State (1765-1858; the Charter Act 1833 ended its commercial function) it had to decide how much Indian machinery to keep and how much to replace. Three pillars carry the story: judiciary, civil services and police. The teacher calls the whole chapter the history of Public Administration in British India. The Mughal ladders of Bengal. Before 1772 Bengal had two separate hierarchies. In civil matters (Diwani) courts ran up to the Sadar Diwani Adalat, with Pandits and Maulvis judging personal law and the Zamindar's Kachari handling land revenue disputes. In criminal matters (Nizamat) Islamic law applied to everyone: the Kazi judged, the Mufti interpreted and the Faujdar, like today's SP, caught the accused and carried out the sentence. One man, two hats. After the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 the EIC held the Diwani and the Nawab kept the Nizamat: a Dual Government. Guided by Orientalism, the EIC let Muhammad Reza Khan head both and cared mainly about revenue. Revenue fell, law and order broke down, and the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 killed about one-third of Bengal. Hastings 73-85 steps in. In 1772 Hastings 73-85 ended the Dual Government. The British DC sat as judge in the civil courts, while in criminal courts the Kazi and Mufti stayed as judges under the DC's watch, because law and order was too sensitive to replace. The Regulating Act 1773 led to the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774 for British subjects under British law, with Madras (1800) and Bombay (1823) to follow. Laws were written down too: the Gentoo Code (1776), the Hedaya (1791) and the Code of 1781. Cornwallis 86-93's Code of 1793. With the Permanent Settlement of 1793, zamindars became property owners and needed courts they could trust: if the DC auctioned an estate and then judged the owner's appeal, there was a conflict of interest. Cornwallis 86-93 stripped the DC of all judicial power (the Prelims 2010 answer), divided Bengal into four divisions with Provincial Courts of Appeal and Courts of Circuit, created Anglo-Muhammadan law, removed Indians from all senior posts and permitted lawyers. Ryotwari, Bentinck 28-35 and the codes. Courts clogged after 1793: the DC could no longer settle disputes on the spot, court fees were abolished (back in 1795), and lawyers prolonged cases. In Ryotwari areas, with many small landowners, Madras (1814, on Munro's advice) and Bombay (1819, Elphinstone) merged the DC's roles again. Bentinck 28-35 abolished the divisional courts, replaced Persian in 1835, and the Charter Act 1833's Law Commission under Macaulay led to the CPC 1859, IPC 1860 and CrPC 1861. High Courts came in 1862 and the Federal Court in 1937. From patronage to a service. A service means a career ladder with rules, not total discretion. Early EIC officials came by nomination and patronage, and Directors lobbied Parliamentarians with jobs for their sons. Cornwallis 86-93 organised them into the Covenanted Civil Service (senior, signed a covenant in London, Europeans only, like Group A) and the Uncovenanted (junior, hired locally, where Indians served, like Group B), with higher pay, curbed private trade and strict seniority; but entry stayed by nomination until the Charter Act 1853. The exam and its three locks. The Charter Act 1853 mandated an exam for the CCS and the first exam was held in London in 1855. Indians were eligible on paper, but the age limit was kept low, the syllabus was dominated by English Literature (to produce Macaulay's Brown Sahibs) and the venue was London. Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to clear it in 1864 and four more followed in 1867. The long fight for Indianisation. From 1860 the WEMC demanded a simultaneous exam in India and a higher age limit. The British answered with Lytton 76-80's lateral entry for loyal elite Indians (a Statutory Civil Services Act the teacher calls unimportant). Aitchison 1887 led to the ICS, PCS and Subordinate services in 1892 by executive order under Lansdowne 88-94; Islington (1912, report 1917) offered 25% and refused a simultaneous exam; the GOI Act 1919 brought the exam to India in 1922, the PSC in 1926 and a 33% target; Lee (1923-24) set 20-40-40; the GOI Act 1935 gave the Federal PSC (1937), over 50% were Indianised by 1947, and Article 378 made it the UPSC in 1950. From Faujdar to Daroga. Under the Mughals the chain ran Naib Nazim, Faujdar, Kotwal, Zamindar. After the 1770 famine raised crime, Hastings 73-85 put English Magistrates in place of the Faujdars in 1781. Cornwallis 86-93 ended the zamindars' police powers in 1793: thanas of 30 square miles under an Indian Daroga, the DM supreme in his district. But a Daroga-Zamindar nexus of bribes and lathiyals oppressed the rural poor; Wellesley 98-05 restored the zamindars' powers in 1799, and the Madras trial of 1802 ended in the Torture Commission report of 1855. The Police Act 1861. The British turned to the Irish Constabulary model, a centralised, quasi-military force built as much for political control as for crime. It was road-tested in Sindh (1843, Charles Napier), Punjab (1849), Bombay (1853) and Madras (1859); M.H. Court's 1st Police Commission (1860), set up by Canning 56-62, borrowed from Sindh, and Napier did not head it. The Police Act (March 1861) set up the IG, SP and SI hierarchy; Fraser's commission (1902-03) created the Imperial Police cadre; the IPS came in 1948 and the AIS Act in 1951. Crisis or pressure. Each major reform followed a crisis (the 1770 famine, the 1857 revolt) or a concession won by the Indian National Movement. The British Indianised only as far as cost or politics demanded. What they left behind, however inadvertently, was codified law, an organised civil service and a hierarchical police, which independent India inherited and adapted.
